chunks.title: Bereavement
chunks.text: You may be able to get help to pay for funeral expenses or travel to a funeral or tangi. When a client dies, we need to know. Please call us to let us know. Phone us If they were getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension you can tell us by filling out our online form. Online formexternal

chunks.title: Funeral expenses
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for some funeral expenses if the person who had died has little or no money to pay for this. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for a Funeral Grant and you don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We may be able to pay a Funeral Grant of up to $2,697.43 if the estate of the person who has died can't pay. This money can be used for costs such as: - professional services for preparing the body for cremation or burial (e.g. embalming) - the cost of a casket - newspaper death notice costs - hearse fees - compulsory fees for buying a burial plot - cremation fees. Funeral Grant

chunks.title: If the person died from an injury or accident
chunks.text: If someone close to you has died from an injury or accident, ACC may be able to give you financial support. They can help with funeral or memorial costs, one-off payments and loss of income. Financial support if someone has died from an injury (ACC)external

chunks.title: Travel to a funeral or tangi
chunks.text: We may be able to help you if you can't afford to travel to a funeral or tangi. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for help and you may have to pay the money back depending on your situation. How much you get depends on your situation. You may be able to get help with your travel costs if someone has died and you are either their: - Partner (if you were living together at the time of their death) - child (including step-children, foster children and whāngai) - grandchild or mokopuna - sibling (including half-siblings and step-siblings) - parent (including step-parents and foster parents) - grandparent.

chunks.title: If you're on a benefit
chunks.text: Advance Payment of Benefit You may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit to help with your travel costs.

chunks.title: If you're not on a benefit
chunks.text: Recoverable Assistance Payment You may be able to get a Recoverable Assistance Payment to help with your travel costs.

chunks.title: Bond Grant
chunks.text: If you don't have enough money to pay bond to your landlord, you may be able to get a Bond Grant. - You don't need to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll need to pay the money back. We'll put a repayment plan in place to suit your financial circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Bond Grant if you need to pay bond because you're entering a tenancy that the Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) applies to, for example a tenancy agreement. You can also apply if your existing bond is being increased because of a rent increase. You can apply for a bond grant for a General Bond or a Pet Bond. We'll also take into account other factors, such as: - your situation - if you can afford to stay in the accommodation long-term. - how long you’ll be living in your accommodation (generally this needs to be at least 28 days) - if this is the best payment for you - what other help is available to you. There are also residency and income criteria you need to meet. If you're not entering a tenancy under the RTA, we may still be able to help. You may be able to get an Accommodation Security Cover Grant to help with outstanding costs when you leave your accommodation.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: Accommodation Security Cover Grant

chunks.title: Residency criteria
chunks.text: You must be either: - getting a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, or - ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: a New Zealand citizen have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. - a New Zealand citizen - have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or - getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.

chunks.title: Residency criteria
chunks.text: Main benefit Ordinarily resident

chunks.title: Income criteria
chunks.text: Getting a Bond Grant also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: Weekly income (before tax) is less than:
chunks.text: Single, 16+ years $1,353 Couple without children $2,006 Couple with children $2,337 Sole parent, 1 child $1,846 Sole parent, 2+ children $2,126

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: Assets include money in the bank, or things like a caravan or second property. Assets don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, like the home where you live or your car.

chunks.title: Your assets are worth less than:
chunks.text: Single $8,100 Married, civil union or de facto couple (with or without children) or sole parent $16,200

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: The Bond Grant is to help pay the cost of your bond, including an increase to an existing bond due to a rent increase, even if you have more than one bond. For example you may have to pay for a General Bond and a Pet Bond. We pay for whichever is the lowest of: - 4 weeks rent, or - the amount your landlord asks for, or - your share of the bond. The most you can get is 4 weeks rent. If your bond is being increased, the grant can cover the increase up to these same limits. You need to pay the Bond Grant back. The Bond Grant and Accommodation Security Cover Grant are paid for similar reasons. This means you can only get these payments a total of twice in 52 weeks (i.e. 1 year). So within 52 weeks, you could get either:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: - 2 Bond Grants - 2 Accommodation Security Cover Grants, or - 1 Bond Grant and 1 Accommodation Security Cover Grant. You may be able to get another grant if there's an exceptional situation outside your control, for example: - you need to move unexpectedly through no fault of your own, or - you're in a family violence situation.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 We may need to book you an appointment either to come in and see us, or a phone appointment. We'll let you know if this is the case. You'll need to provide proof of the amount of bond, for example a: - tenancy agreement, or - bond form which is signed by the landlord, or - written notice from your landlord showing the bond increase due to a rent increase.

chunks.title: If you have a shared tenancy
chunks.text: If you share your tenancy with: - your partner, you can apply for your portion and your partner's portion of the bond. Or your partner can apply separately for their portion. - someone else, you can only apply for your portion of the bond. The other person will need to apply separately for their portion of the bond. If your bond is being increased due to a rent increase, you can only apply for your portion of the increase. Anyone else who needs to pay (e.g. your partner or flatmates) must apply separately for their own portions.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll pay the bond directly to the landlord. We'll check if your landlord's already a supplier with us. If they're not, we'll ask them to register as a supplier by completing a 'Supplier Registration Form'. This is so we can make the payment to them. Register as a supplier

chunks.title: Budgeting
chunks.text: We can provide support and practical information to help you budget. Budgeting gives you control of your money – and your life. It helps you to - see how much money you have - look at what you spend your money on, and - think about ways to make your money go further. Thinking carefully about where your money goes also gives you opportunities to explore ways to improve your situation. By budgeting, you can: - pay off your debts faster - keep up with your bills - save for the things you want - be more prepared for unplanned expenses.

chunks.title: Work out if you need a budget
chunks.text: To work out if you need to budget, ask yourself: - do I worry about money? - do I often have no money to pay my bills? - does talking about money with my family cause arguments? - am I unable to afford the things I want? - am I always in debt? - have my costs increased for some reason? - have I given up hope of having money for holidays or retirement? If your answer is YES to any of these, it may be a good idea to start budgeting.

chunks.title: Ideas to pay off debt or save
chunks.text: Here are some ideas on how you could help to pay off your debt, or save some money.

chunks.title: Open a separate bank account for savings
chunks.text: Open a separate bank account and make an automatic payment into it every time you get paid. This can be your savings account and you can see it build up over time. You can ask your bank about setting up an automatic payment.

chunks.title: Put some money towards your debt every time you get paid
chunks.text: Pay off your debts as soon as you can. The longer you have a debt, the more interest you're charged and the more money you owe. An easy way to pay off a debt is to put a bit towards it every time you get paid (but only after you've paid your bills). You can organise to pay it straight from your bank account so you don't have to think about it. Then you're not tempted to use the money for other things. Ask your bank about setting up an automatic payment. Only buy the things you need if you really want to pay off your debts and get closer to reaching your goals.

chunks.title: Plan a budget
chunks.text: Putting together and planning a budget helps you understand more about how to manage your money. Everyone can benefit from managing their money better and it's a good idea to do a budget plan, or redo the one you have, to make sure it's still helping you. There are 3 steps listed below to help you make your plan, with a separate worksheet for each step. You can print these off and use them to make your plan. You should do them one-by-one to build your plan over time.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Your money
chunks.text: Budgeting is not just about how much money you spend, it's also about where you spend your money. You can use this to write down the money you get. This can help you to set goals to see if there are any ways to reduce your costs and money you owe. It also helps you think of ways to start saving.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Your goals
chunks.text: Setting goals is a good way to start helping you decide how you spend your money in the future. It is about changing the way you manage your money to see if there are any ways to spend less and increase the money you get.

chunks.title: Step 3 - Managing your money
chunks.text: A budget plan needs to change when something different happens in your life. You might move house and have to pay more or less than you were paying before. Or you might get part-time work which means you have more money now. Your budget plan should show any new income or costs for you and your family/whānau. You might need to set some new goals so you keep planning ahead for you and your family/whānau.

chunks.text: Enter your income and expenses into this budget worksheet to get you started. Budget worksheet

chunks.title: Calculating your rent payments
chunks.text: When you live in public (social) housing, the amount of rent you pay is based on your income, and the income of people you live with. This is called Income Related Rent. Income Related Rent means: - you pay some of the rent - the government pays some of the rent. We'll generally pay your rent directly to your landlord if you get either: - a main benefit, for example Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support - NZ Super, or - Veteran's Pension. Otherwise you'll need to arrange to pay it to your landlord.

chunks.title: Step 1 - Work out your weekly household income
chunks.text: We work out what your total weekly household income is after tax. This includes any income that you, your partner, anyone else on the tenancy agreement and their partners, get. Income can include: - a benefit from Work and Income - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension - Student Allowance - wages - salary - commission - parental leave payments - most child support payments - income from assets (e.g. income from a rental property you own, or interest on savings) - minimum family tax credits. If your income changes often, we may work out your weekly income in a different way.

chunks.title: Your income changes often
chunks.text: If your income changes often (e.g. you work casual hours, or are self-employed), we look at your total income over a longer period of time (at least 4 weeks). We then work out your average weekly income based on this. For example, you earn the following amounts (after tax) over 4 weeks: - Week 1: $400 - Week 2: $300 - Week 3: $700 - Week 4: $420 Altogether this comes to $1,820 after tax. We divide this by the number of weeks it covers (4). This would make your average weekly income $455 after tax.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Check your income threshold
chunks.text: We find out what your living situation is. Then, using the table below, we check what your income threshold is. For example, if you're single and living by yourself, your weekly income threshold (after tax) is $555.15.

chunks.title: Weekly income threshold (after tax)
chunks.text: Have a partner (with or without children) $854.08

chunks.title: Step 3 - Calculate your rent payment
chunks.text: We check if your total weekly household income (after tax) is higher or lower than your income threshold.

chunks.title: Income is higher than your income threshold
chunks.text: If your total weekly household income (after tax) is higher than your income threshold, first we: - take your income threshold, and - calculate 25% of it. Then we: - take your total weekly household income (after tax) - work out how much is over the income threshold - calculate 50% of this amount. Then we add these two amounts together to work out your rent payment.

chunks.title: For example:
chunks.text: - Your income threshold is $854.08. - 25% of that threshold is $213.52. Then: - Your income is $890 (after tax) a week. - This is $35.92 over the income threshold. - 50% of $35.92 is $17.96. We add $213.52 and $17.96 together, which makes your rent $231.48 per week.

chunks.title: Income is lower than your income threshold
chunks.text: If your total weekly household income (after tax) is lower than your income threshold, we: - take your total weekly household income (after tax) - calculate 25% of it.

chunks.title: For example:
chunks.text: - Your total household income is $650 (after tax) a week (your income threshold is $854.08). - 25% of your income is $162.50. This makes your rent $162.50 per week.

chunks.title: Step 4 - Family tax credits
chunks.text: If you get family tax credits (not including Best Start, In-Work and Minimum family tax credits), we work out the lowest amount of either: - 25% of your weekly family tax credit payment, or - $36.07 (25% of the first or only child weekly family tax credit payment). We then add the lower amount to your rent payment.

chunks.title: Step 5 - Income from boarders
chunks.text: A boarder is any person, who is not a tenant, who pays you to live in that home – regardless of whether the payment includes other costs like food. If you get payments for board, 62% of the board payment will be added to your rent payment.

chunks.title: Step 6 - Finalise your rent payment
chunks.text: Once we've worked out your rent payment, we round it down to the nearest dollar.

chunks.title: Step 7 - Check against market rent or minimum rent required
chunks.text: If you're not sure what the market rent price is for your property, you can find this out from your property provider or landlord.

chunks.title: Rent calculation is more than market rent
chunks.text: If the rent payment we've worked out for you is more than the actual market rent price for the property, you'll only pay the market rent amount.

chunks.title: Rent payment is lower than the minimum amount required
chunks.text: There is a minimum amount of rent you have to pay, depending on your circumstances. This amount is the lowest rent that a public housing provider can charge. If the rent amount we've calculated for you is lower than the minimum amount, you'll need to pay the minimum amount instead. The table below shows the minimum rent payment for each circumstance.

chunks.title: Sole parent
chunks.text: Julie is a sole parent with an 8 year old son. She gets a Sole Parent Support payment of $521.52 a week. Her living situation is single with children. - Her total household income is $521.52 a week (after tax). - Her income threshold is $854.08. Because Julie’s total household income ($521.52) is lower than her income threshold ($854.08), we calculate 25% of her household income. - 25% of $521.52 is $130.38. - Julie also gets family tax credits of $151.91 per week. We work out 25% of $151.91, which comes to $37.97. We then add $130.38 and $37.97 together (and round it down to the nearest dollar). This makes Julie’s rent $168 a week.

chunks.title: Couple with children
chunks.text: Sam and Jo live with their 2 year old daughter and 6 year old son. They both work part-time, and are paid $450 (after tax) each. - Their total household income is $900 (after tax) a week. - Their income threshold is $854.08. Because Sam and Jo’s income is higher than their income threshold, we: - take their income threshold ($854.08) - calculate 25% of it, which is $213.52. Then we: - take their total household income ($900) - work out how much is over the income threshold, which is $45.92 - calculate 50% of this amount, which is $22.96. We then add $213.52 and $22.96 together, which is $236.48. They also get a family tax credit payment of $275.69 per week. This means we work out the lowest amount of either:

chunks.title: Couple with children
chunks.text: - 25% of $275.69 which is $68.92, or - $37.97 of their weekly family tax credit payment. We then add $236.48 and $37.97 together (and round down to the nearest dollar). This makes Sam and Jo’s rent $274 per week.

chunks.title: Single, living on your own
chunks.text: Barry is single and living on his own. He does casual work, and his hours change from week to week. For the past 4 weeks, Barry has earned the following amounts: - Week 1: $600 (after tax) - Week 2: $500 (after tax) - Week 3: $700 (after tax) - Week 4: $450 (after tax) Altogether this comes to $2,250 (after tax). We divide this by the number of weeks this covers (4), which makes Barry’s average weekly income $562.50. - His total household income is $562.50 (after tax) a week. - His income threshold is $555.15. Because Barry's income is higher than his income threshold, we: - take his income threshold ($555.15). - calculate 25% of it, which is $138.78. Then we: - take his total household income ($562.50)

chunks.title: Single, living on your own
chunks.text: - work out how much is over the income threshold, which is $7.35 - calculate 50% of this amount, which is $3.67. We then add $138.78 and $3.67 together (and round it down to the nearest dollar). This makes Barry’s rent $142 per week.

chunks.title: Disagree with rent amount
chunks.text: If you disagree with a decision about your rent, talk to us. We may be able to solve the problem or explain the decision. If you still disagree, you can apply for a review of decision. Making a complaint

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Canada
chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Canada to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Canadian payments (paid by Service Canada). NZ payments covered by this agreement are: - New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) - Veteran's Pension - Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability - Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers. Canadian payments covered by this agreement are: - Old Age Security Pension - Canada Pension Plan (if you get the Quebec Pension Plan, this is not covered by the agreement). It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Living in Canada
chunks.text: If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in Canada, you may be able to get some payments. Social Security Agreement with Canada - living in Canada

chunks.title: Living in New Zealand
chunks.text: If you've lived in Canada and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments. Social Security Agreement with Canada - living in New Zealand

chunks.title: Vehicle Modification Funding
chunks.text: If you have a serious disability and need help to buy or modify a car or other vehicle, you may be able to get Vehicle Modification Funding.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: For information about who can get this payment, go to the Disability Support Services website. Vehicle modifications - Disability Support Servicesexternal

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on: - the cost of the vehicle or modifications - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. View the maximum payments - Manual and Procedures websiteexternal

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to talk to an occupational therapist who will do an assessment of your needs. They will submit an application to one of the service providers, Accessable or Enable New Zealand. For information about how to apply, go to the Disability Support Services website. Vehicle modifications - Disability Support Servicesexternal

chunks.title: Car repairs
chunks.text: If your car needs to be fixed, we may be able to help. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get help if: - you're 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - you're a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - you normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - you have an immediate or essential need - you need the car for you, your partner or children - you need the car because of either: a health condition disability employment lack of access to public transport - a health condition - disability - employment - lack of access to public transport - you or your partner own the car, i.e., you bought the car or were gifted it. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Youth Servicesexternal

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Generally we can pay up to $400 to help with some car repairs. We don't usually pay for standard car costs, e.g.: - fuel - warrant of fitness - car insurance - car registration - regular servicing costs.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Caring for a child with a health condition or disability
chunks.text: If you're caring for a child with a health condition or disability, we may be able to help.

chunks.title: Child has a serious disability or health condition
chunks.text: Your dependent child needs constant care and attention, over and above what a child or young person of the same age would need, because of a serious disability or health condition. Child Disability Allowance If you get the Child Disability Allowance, we may be able to help with extra childcare assistance. Childcare A Community Services Card can help with the costs of healthcare. You'll pay less for some health services simply by showing your card. Most people who are on a benefit automatically get one of these cards. If you're on a low income you can also apply for one. Community Services Card

chunks.title: Help with disability costs
chunks.text: You need help to cover the ongoing costs of your child's disability. Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Caring for someone else's child
chunks.text: If you're caring for someone else's child there are also other kinds of help you may be able to get. Caring for someone else's child

chunks.title: Unsure of what you'll be able to get
chunks.text: You may also be able to get a benefit or help with other expenses, eg living expenses. Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.

chunks.title: Caring for someone with a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text: If the person you're caring for would need hospital, rest home or residential care without you, we may be able to help.

chunks.title: Caring for someone ill or disabled
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Supported Living Payment if you're caring for a person at home who would otherwise need hospital-level, rest home or residential care (or the equivalent). This includes caring for your own child but not your partner. The person you're caring for can also apply for a Supported Living Payment. We'll need to see a medical certificate for the person you're caring for. It needs to be completed by their health practitioner. Supported Living Payment

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: If you're caring for your partner at home and they would otherwise need hospital-level care or residential care (or the equivalent), they may be able to get a Supported Living Payment. They will need to apply for this benefit and you can be included in it. We'll need to see a medical certificate from their health practitioner. Supported Living Payment

chunks.title: Special Disability Allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit and your partner is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks, you may be able to get a Special Disability Allowance. Special Disability Allowance

chunks.title: Guide for carers
chunks.text: There is help available from other government agencies and organisations. A guide to services and support available for carers (Ministry of Social Development)external

chunks.title: Applying on someone else's behalf
chunks.text: You can apply for help from us on someone else's behalf, but only if they've filled out a form to appoint you as their agent. Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: Caring for someone else's child
chunks.text: If you're caring for someone else's child, we may be able to help. What you get will depend on both your and the child's circumstances.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Unsupported Child’s Benefit A weekly payment that helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents can't care for them because of a family breakdown. Orphan’s Benefit A weekly payment that helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents have died or can't be found, or can't look after them because they have a serious long-term health condition or incapacity. Sole Parent Support A benefit that helps single parents and caregivers of dependent children under 14 get ready for future work, supports them to find part or full-time work and provides financial help through a weekly payment. Away from Home Allowance A weekly payment which helps carers with the living costs for 16 or 17 year olds who are living away from home while on a tertiary or training course. We pay the allowance to the carer of the young person.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: There are other types of help you may be able to get, it depends on your situation. Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.

chunks.title: Getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit
chunks.text: Clothing Allowance If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you'll also automatically get a Clothing Allowance for children in your care, to help you pay for their clothing. Establishment grant Establishment grant is paid automatically when you first get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. This is a once only payment of $350 for each child you're caring for. This money helps you buy things like a bed, bedding and clothing. You won't be taxed on this money, and you won't have to pay it back. Holiday and Birthday Allowance You automatically get the Holiday and Birthday Allowance if you already get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas.

chunks.title: Getting Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit
chunks.text: School and Year Start-up Payments Help with the costs that mostly happen at the beginning of the year, in particular pre-school and school-related costs, eg clothing, school fees and stationery. Extraordinary Care Fund This fund helps support children to develop their skills and talents. It can also help children who are experiencing difficulties that are significantly impacting on their development.

chunks.title: On a benefit
chunks.text: If a child comes into your care while you're on a benefit, you may have a change in obligations or your benefit could be affected.

chunks.title: Getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: It's different for people getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension - your payments stay the same whether or not you include the child in your payments. You may qualify for Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue, depending on your income. You'll need to apply by calling 0800 227 773 or visiting www.ird.govt.nzexternal Remember, any extra income you get can affect your other payments. It's probably better for you to get the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit if you qualify. Contact Work and Income to find out which is the best option for you.

chunks.title: Wages from casual work
chunks.text: If you do a one-off job and get paid, you need to let us know. The amount you earn may affect your benefit and any other payments you get from us. If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back. Do you need to declare income?

chunks.title: Tell us before you get paid
chunks.text: You need let us know the week you earn the money, not when you've been paid. We need to know by Friday 6pm. If you're working the weekend, include this time too. The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed.

chunks.title: Make an estimate
chunks.text: If you don't know what you'll earn tell us what you think it will probably be.

chunks.title: What we need to know:
chunks.text: - the amount before tax (gross) or estimate for the work, or the hourly rate - the number of hours you worked.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us about your earnings is to use MyMSD. You'll need your client number to register then follow a few simple steps. About MyMSD

chunks.title: If you can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: Call us or come into one of our service centres. If you're declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed. Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: How your main benefit will be affected
chunks.text: Other payments from us such as Accommodation Supplement, may also be affected. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Made a mistake or need to change your estimate?
chunks.text: If you think the amount you entered in our online services isn't right, correct this as soon as you can by logging back in. If you need to change your estimate after 6pm on Friday, call us before midday on the following Monday.

chunks.title: Change in your circumstances
chunks.text: If you get a Childcare Subsidy or before, after-school or holiday care for your child, you need to tell us straight away if something changes in your life as it can affect how much childcare we pay.

chunks.title: What you need to tell us about
chunks.text: We need to know if: - your income or your partner's income changes - the number of hours you or your partner work, train or study each week changes - your child stops attending childcare - your child moves to another childcare provider - there's a change to the number of hours your child attends childcare - your relationship status changes, eg you become single or are now in a relationship - you have another child - a child is no longer in your care - the reason why your payments change, eg your health improves or you stop working or studying - your child now needs before, after-school or holiday care - your child is going to a cohort entry school - your child starts or stops receiving 20 Hours ECE - you want to have another child in childcare.

chunks.title: Change in hours
chunks.text: If the number of hours your child attends childcare changes, you must tell us straight away as it could affect how much we pay for childcare.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to complete a change in circumstances form for each child. You can complete the form online and print it. - View or download Childcare Assistance change of circumstances form. Childcare Assistance change of circumstances form (PDF 825 KB) - Get your childcare provider to sign the form. - If you or your partner are studying, your education provider will also need to sign it. - Post the signed form with supporting documents (the Change of Circumstances form will tell you what you'll need to provide) to your local service centre, or drop off at one of our service centres. If you can't print the form, contact us on 0800 559 009 and we’ll send one to you. Find your nearest service centre

chunks.title: Change to the reason you get a childcare payment
chunks.text: If the reason you get a childcare payment changes, eg your health improves, your child leaves hospital or you're no longer working or training, you must tell us straight away as it can affect how much childcare we pay.

chunks.title: What you need to tell us about
chunks.text: You need to tell us if: - you're no longer studying or working - your health improves - your child leaves hospital.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: - Complete the Childcare Assistance - Change of circumstances form (you'll need to complete a form for each child) - Get your childcare provider to sign the form. - If you or your partner are studying, your education provider will also need to sign it. Childcare Assistance change of circumstances form (PDF 825 KB) You can get your application form and proof of costs to us by either: - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first) Phone us - dropping them in to your nearest service centre, or - posting them to your nearest service centre. chunks.title: Change of costs for Disability Allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a Disability Allowance and you have a new cost that you need help with, or a cost has changed, you need to let us know straight away. If you're not sure what costs are included in your Disability Allowance, you can check in MyMSD. Find out about MyMSD

chunks.title: A new cost
chunks.text: If you have another cost that you want the Disability Allowance to help with and you're getting less than the maximum amount of $82.85 a week, we may be able to help. - Your health practitioner needs to complete a Disability Certificate form - You need to get proof of the new cost. Call us to talk about how to get these to us. Contact us If the cost is approved, we'll include it in your Disability Allowance from the date the cost started. Disability Allowance - Types of costs (Maps and Procedures)external If you're already getting the maximum amount of Disability Allowance, we may still be able to help. Call us to talk about this. Contact us

chunks.title: Cost has increased
chunks.text: If a cost you're getting Disability Allowance for has increased, you need to let us know. You need to get proof of the change of cost. Call us to talk about how to get this to us. Contact us If the cost is approved, we'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date the cost increased.

chunks.title: Cost has stopped or decreased
chunks.text: If a cost you're getting Disability Allowance for has stopped or decreased, you need to let us know straight away. Call us and tell us: - the date the cost stopped or decreased - how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased). We'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date you call us. Contact us If you don't tell us straight away, we'll reassess your Disability Allowance from the date the cost stopped or decreased. This means you may get a debt.

chunks.title: Change of costs for Temporary Additional Support
chunks.text: If you're getting Temporary Additional Support and you want to include a new essential cost, or one of your costs has changed, you need to let us know straight away. Allowable costs (Manuals and Procedures)external If you're not sure what costs are included in your Temporary Additional Support, you can check in MyMSD. Find out about MyMSD

chunks.title: Add a new cost or cost has increased
chunks.text: If you have another essential cost, or one of your costs has increased, you need to let us know straight away. You can tell us about this in MyMSD, or you can call us. Phone us Find out about MyMSD

chunks.title: You need to provide proof
chunks.text: You'll need to provide proof of: - the amount of the new cost or change in cost, and - the date the cost started or changed. You'll be able to upload this proof in MyMSD as you go. If you call us, we'll let you know how you can get it to us. If your cost is formula assessed child support through Inland Revenue, you can give consent in MyMSD for IR to share this information with us.

chunks.title: If your application is approved
chunks.text: If it's approved, we'll reassess your Temporary Additional Support from either: - the date you tell us about the new cost, or - the date an existing cost changed.

chunks.title: Cost has stopped or decreased
chunks.text: If a cost you're getting Temporary Additional Support for has stopped or decreased, you need to let us know straight away. You can tell us about this in MyMSD, or you can call us. Phone us Find out about MyMSD We'll need to know: - the date the cost stopped or decreased, and how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased). - the date the cost stopped or decreased, and - how much the cost has decreased to (if the cost decreased). We'll reassess your Temporary Additional Support from the date you tell us. If you don't tell us straight away, you may get a debt.

chunks.title: Changing your tax code for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Tell us straight away if you need to change your tax code, eg, if you stop working, so we can pay you the right amount of NZ Super or Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Find out your tax code
chunks.text: If you don't know what tax code you should be on, go to Inland Revenue's website. Tax codes and tax rates for individuals (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: How to change your tax code
chunks.text: Select the 'Change tax code' button above to complete the 'Change tax code' form.

chunks.title: What you'll need
chunks.text: You'll need the following information to complete the form: - client number - name - IRD number - current tax code - new tax code.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll change your tax code and send you a letter to let you know how it affects your payments.

chunks.title: Tailored tax code
chunks.text: If you have a tailored tax code, you need to renew it with Inland Revenue at the end of each financial year. If you don't renew your tailored tax code, you need to change it to a standard tax code and let us know. If you don't renew or change your tailored tax code before the end of the financial year, your tax rate will default to 45% on 1 April. What is a tailored tax code? (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: If you use myIR
chunks.text: When it's time to renew your tailored tax code, Inland Revenue will send you a letter through myIR, and you'll be able to complete the form online. Inland Revenue will let us know what your tax code is. Apply for a tailored tax code (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: If you don't use myIR
chunks.text: When it's time to renew your tailored tax code, Inland Revenue will send you a renewal form. You need to fill it out and send it back to them. Inland Revenue will let us know what your tax code is.

chunks.title: How to change to a standard tax code
chunks.text: To change your tailored tax code to a standard tax code, you need to complete the 'Change tax code' form.

chunks.title: What you'll need
chunks.text: You'll need the following information to complete the form: - client number - name - IRD number - current tax code - new tax code.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll change your tax code and send you a letter to let you know how it affects your payments.

chunks.title: Check your payments
chunks.text: How to check your payments and information about payment issues.

chunks.title: Do it online
chunks.text: You can check your payments online in MyMSD. My MSD If you have no upcoming payments or if your payment has been suspended, MyMSD will tell you. If you think this isn't right, call us. If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, you also need to contact your Youth Service provider directly to discuss your payments. Phone us Find your nearest provider (Youth Service)external

chunks.title: Don't have MyMSD
chunks.text: It's easy to set up MyMSD - all you need to get started is your client number. How to register for MyMSD

chunks.title: Payments don't match
chunks.text: If your payment doesn't match what's in MyMSD there could be a number of reasons for this. If you and your partner both get extra help payments (eg, Accommodation Supplement), we split the total amount evenly between you. If the split is uneven by a number of cents, one of you will get 1 cent more in your account. For example, if your total payment is $100.03, it splits into $50.015 each. So one of you will get $50.01 and the other person will get $50.02. If you get another extra help payment as well (eg, Disability Allowance) and the split is uneven again, the payment breakdown in MyMSD may show you getting a few cents more or less than what you get in your account.

chunks.title: Extra payment not showing in MyMSD
chunks.text: When you have a change in your circumstances, you need to tell us right away as it could affect your payment. If you don't tell us before your regular payment is finalised, you might be paid the wrong amount, (either too much or not enough). If we don't pay you enough, we'll pay you the extra amount in a one off payment. This will be paid to you before your regular payment and won't show in MyMSD.

chunks.title: Payments around public holidays
chunks.text: Sometimes your regular pay day will fall on a public holiday. When this happens, we'll always make sure you get your payments either the day before or on your regular pay day. For example, if you're usually paid on Wednesdays, and Wednesday is a public holiday, your payment will be available from Tuesday.

chunks.title: Regional anniversary holidays
chunks.text: If your regular pay day falls on a regional anniversary (eg. Wellington or Auckland anniversary), you will still be paid on your usual pay day. This is because pay dates only change when there is a national holiday for the whole country.

chunks.title: If you have any questions about your payment information
chunks.text: Call us and say "payments". This will direct you to our Self Services where you'll be given details of your next payment. If this is still not what you were expecting or you have any questions, you can choose to talk to us. Phone us

chunks.title: Money management for youth clients
chunks.text: When you are working with a Youth Service provider, your payments may be subject to money management. Money management means your provider will help you manage your payments so that all your important costs are paid. This means: - your rent or board and things like your power bill and any debts will be paid straight from your payment. You won't get this money yourself. - you will get paid a weekly allowance of up to $50 into your personal bank account. - any money left over will be put onto your personal payment card. This is like a debit card that you can use to buy your food and groceries at approved stores. Payment cards

chunks.title: Money management and extra help
chunks.text: The following will be paid directly to your bank account: - Disability Allowance - Child Disability Allowance - Unsupported Child's Benefit - Orphan's Benefit - Training Incentive Allowance - weekly ongoing costs. The following will be subject to money management: - Temporary Additional Support - Family Tax Credit - Accommodation Supplement For example, an 18 year old sole parent with a one year old disabled child, renting in Kaitaia, would have their money managed as follows: For more detail see our: Manuals and procedures (MAP) - Young Parent Paymentexternal Manuals and procedures (MAP) - Youth Paymentexternal If you are new to Youth Service, your provider will set this up for you when you meet with them. They will set up the payment of your rent and bills with you and give you a payment card.

chunks.title: Money management and extra help
chunks.text: You can manage your whole payment yourself if you show your Youth Service provider that you can do this responsibly. You should talk to them about how you can prove this. Once you have proven you are capable of managing your money yourself, your payment will go straight into your bank account and you will be responsible for paying all of your own costs.

chunks.title: Incentives and money management
chunks.text: If you are doing all the things you need to with your education, training or work-based learning, budgeting and parenting you can get extra incentive payments. If you are subject to money management, extra incentive payments will be added to the total amount that goes through money management. If you are not subject to money management and you earn an incentive payment, this will be paid straight to your bank account. When you have been successfully in education, training or work-based learning for 6 months you can get an extra $10 a week. If you finish a budgeting programme and have regular budget talks with your Youth Service provider for 3 months, you can get an extra $10 a week. If you are receiving Young Parent Payment, you can get a further $10 a week if you have met all your parenting requirements and had regular talks with your Youth Service provider for three months.

chunks.title: Incentives and money management
chunks.text: This includes: - completing an approved parenting programme - enrolling your child with a health practitioner and keeping up to date with WellChild checks - registering your child in an approved early childhood education programme or other suitable childcare while you are in education, training or work-based learning or part-time work. Incentive payments are earned by each person separately. For example, if only one parent attends a parenting programme only they can get the extra payment. If both parents go, both can get the payment.

chunks.title: Once you are getting the extra payment you need to keep up the good work
chunks.text: If you are away from education, training or work-based learning without a good reason, or don't complete the required course work, or you get suspended, you will lose the education incentive payment. If you get into trouble with your money and are not managing it properly you will lose the budgeting incentive payment. If your child is not being well looked after, you will lose the parenting incentive payment. Your provider must tell Work and Income if you have stopped doing what you need to do to get your incentive payments.

chunks.title: Sanctions and money management
chunks.text: If you are on Youth Payment, a first or second failure to meet your obligations results in the in-hand allowance and any incentive payments being suspended. If you don't recomply within 4 weeks your payment will be automatically cancelled and you will have to reapply. A third failure will result in Youth Payment, Temporary Additional Support, Accommodation Supplement and any incentive payments being cancelled immediately. Disability Allowance can continue to be paid if you still meet the eligibility criteria for it. If you receive Young Parent Payment (YPP) a first or second sanction means your in hand allowance and any incentive payments are suspended until you recomply. For a third failure, 50% of your YPP is cancelled, but you can continue to receive the full rate of Accommodation Supplement and Temporary Additional Support. For couples, these payments are reduced by half and paid to the non-sanctioned partner. Disability Allowance, Child Disability Allowance, Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment & Childcare Assistance can continue to be paid if you continue to meet the eligibility criteria for these forms of assistance.

chunks.text: For more detail see: Young Parent Payments (MAP)external Youth Payments (MAP)external Young Parent Payment Obligations (MAP)external Youth Payment Obligations (MAP)external Young Parent Sanctions (MAP)external Youth Payment Sanctions (MAP)external

chunks.title: Income rules for Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: You only have to tell us about any income if you get another benefit as well as Child Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Do you get any other benefits
chunks.text: If you only get Child Disability Allowance you don't have to tell us about any regular income, one-off payments or any assets you have. If you get any other benefits or allowances, check the income rules for them to find out if you need to tell us about your income and one-off payments. Do you need to declare income?

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Child Disability Allowance is a fortnightly payment made to the main carer of a child or young person with a serious disability. It is paid in recognition of the extra care and attention needed for that child.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get a Child Disability Allowance if: - you are the main carer of the child (or if there is no main carer, you have care of the child for the time being) - you are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - the child has been assessed as needing constant care and attention for 12 months or more because of a serious disability, and - the child or young person is under 18. Both you and the child should also normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. You may be able to get both the Child Disability Allowance and the Disability Allowance for the same child. Disability Allowance

chunks.title: When you can't get this payment
chunks.text: You can't get a Child Disability Allowance if: - the child you're looking after is in the care of Oranga Tamariki, or - the child already gets a benefit (unless they get the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit). If the child is 16 or over, they may be able to get Supported Living Payment instead.

chunks.title: Check if you can get Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Child Disability Allowance and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: The Child Disability Allowance is $62.43 a week for each child who qualifies. This is a set amount and doesn't depend on your income, assets or costs. This allowance is paid into your bank account every 2 weeks and is paid separately from any other assistance you may get. In most cases, it won't affect any other assistance you may get from us.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You may be granted financial assistance from the date you request it. Contact us now if you haven't already done so. Phone us You have 20 working days from the date you first contact us to complete the application process. You need to complete the Child Disability Allowance application form. Your child's health practitioner (e.g. doctor) also needs to complete the medical certificate inside this form. The form tells you what documents you need to provide. If you can't print the form out, you can call us to get one sent to you. Phone us You can bring the completed form into a service centre. Find a service centre If you can’t bring the form into a service centre, call us to find out how to get it to us.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Phone us If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you need to bring your original government-issued ID into a service centre so we can check it. Checking ID in person helps us make sure we give support to the right person and protect your identity. Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance obligations
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting a Child Disability Allowance. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell us immediately if either you or the child or young person: - intends to travel overseas - have changes to your living situation, eg the child or young person leaves your care or enters residential care - are imprisoned / held in custody or remand - have any other change that may affect your entitlement.

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. Contact us If you don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your payment entitlement, or rate, then: - your payment may be reviewed and cancelled - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you've received - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined and/or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text: If you intend to travel overseas and don't let us know before you leave New Zealand, your payment will be stopped the day after you leave New Zealand.

chunks.title: A child enters or leaves your care
chunks.text: If a child enters or leaves your care you must tell us as soon as possible as it could affect your payments and whether you need to look for work.

chunks.title: Child enters your care
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 and tell us: - the date the child entered your care - the child's relationship to you - the circumstances - this can affect what payments you'll get from us. We'll work out if the change affects the benefits you're getting from us. We may book you an appointment to come in and see us. If we book you an appointment, we'll let you know what you need to bring. You may also need to apply for child support.

chunks.title: Child leaves your care
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 and tell us: - the date the child left your care - the circumstances - this can affect when payment may reduce or stop. We may book you an appointment to come in and see us. If we book you an appointment, we'll let you know what you need to bring.

chunks.title: Child under 1
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit that requires you to look or prepare for work and you have a child come into your care, you will be expected to prepare for work until the child turns 1 year old. When the child turns 1 you may have a change in your obligations, depending on the age of your next youngest child. If your next youngest child is: - under 3 years old, you'll need to continue to take practical steps to prepare for work - between 3 and 13, you'll be expected to actively seek part-time work of at least 20 hours a week and accept any suitable job - 14 or older, you'll be expected to actively seek full-time work of at least 30 hours a week and accept any suitable job.

chunks.title: Child over 1
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit that requires you to look or prepare for work and you have a child come into your care who's over 1 year old, your obligations won't change.

chunks.title: Helping you get back into work
chunks.text: We can help you access training and a range of other support to help you get ready to move into work. You may be able to get assistance with the cost of childcare while you're working, attending training or doing some other activity that will help you move into work. The Childcare Subsidy is for preschool children and the Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy is for before and after school care and holiday programmes for children aged five - 13 years. For more information, read: Help with childcare costsLooking for a job

chunks.title: Having a baby
chunks.text: If you're having a baby, you need to let us know as it could affect your payments and whether you need to look for work. Having a baby while on a benefit

chunks.title: What happens if you don't tell us
chunks.text: If you don't tell us about children coming into or leaving your care, we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.

chunks.title: Child moves childcare providers
chunks.text: If your child moves to another childcare provider or programme you must tell us as soon as possible.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to complete a change in circumstances form for each child. You can complete the form online and print it. - View or download Childcare Assistance - Change of circumstances form. - Get your childcare provider to sign the form. - If you or your partner are studying, your education provider will also need to sign it. - Post the signed form to us with supporting documents (the Change of Circumstances form will tell you what you'll need to provide) to your local service centre, or drop off at one of our service centres. If you can't print the form, contact us on 0800 559 009 and we'll send one to you. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Your child starts or stops getting 20 Hours ECE
chunks.text: If your child starts or stops getting 20 Hours ECE, you need to tell us as soon as possible as it can affect how much childcare we pay. You can only get Childcare Subsidy for the same hours you're getting 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) if: - your child is at a home-based educator, and - the home-based educator is charging a top up payment for the same hours as 20 Hours ECE. Home-based educators may charge you a top up payment to cover the difference between their normal hourly rate and the 20 Hours ECE. 20 Hours ECE - Ministry of Educationexternal

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: - Complete the Childcare Assistance - Change of circumstances form (you'll need to complete a form for each child) - Get your childcare provider to sign the form. - If you or your partner are studying, your education provider will also need to sign it. Childcare Assistance - Change of circumstances form (PDF 825 KB) You can get your application form and proof of costs to us by either: - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first) - dropping them in to your nearest service centre, or - posting them to your nearest service centre. chunks.title: Child support
chunks.text: All child support payments from a private arrangement and Inland Revenue are counted as income. If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit, there are different rules for how we treat child support as income.

chunks.title: Child support through a private arrangement
chunks.text: You need to tell us about any child support payments you get through a private arrangement. This includes any child support you get from an overseas agency. The easiest way to do this is online, using MyMSD. See instructions on this page under 'How to tell us about child support using MyMSD'. How to tell us about child support using MyMSD

chunks.title: Child support through Inland Revenue
chunks.text: If you get child support through Inland Revenue (IR), they share your child support payment information with us. They do this under our Approved Information Sharing Agreement. This means you don't need to tell us about most types of IR child support payments. Information sharing with MSD - IR websiteexternal

chunks.title: IR child support you still need to tell us about
chunks.text: There are some types of IR child support payments you still need to tell us about. This includes child support you get: - through IR that relates to a period before 1 July 2023 - for a child you get an Unsupported Child's Benefit for - if you get Residential Care Subsidy or Residential Support Subsidy - if you're a student and get a Student Allowance from StudyLink - if you're living overseas and get a benefit under a reciprocal agreement, and - if they're Court Ordered lump sum payments. The easiest way to tell us about these payments is online, using MyMSD. See instructions on this page under 'How to tell us about child support using MyMSD'. How to tell us about child support using MyMSD

chunks.title: How to tell us about child support using MyMSD
chunks.text: Once you've logged in to MyMSD, select 'Declare wages' and then 'Change other income'. If there's already a child support payment recorded in MyMSD, they'll show on the home screen. You can change them from there. The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed. If your payment amount changes and you don't tell us, you could get into debt.

chunks.title: Information you need to tell us
chunks.text: You need to tell us: - how much the payment is - when you're paid - how often you get this payment.

chunks.title: Log in to MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD, you can call us. Phone us

chunks.title: When IR shares your child support information
chunks.text: Inland Revenue (IR) shares your child support payment information with us under our Approved Information Sharing Agreement. This means you don't need to tell us about most types of child support payments.

chunks.title: How we treat your child support as income
chunks.text: When we get your child support payment information from IR, our system will automatically treat this as income for the next month. This means the next 4 or 5 weeks from the date you receive the child support payment. It could be 4 weeks, or 5 weeks, it depends on the number of weeks until you get your next child support payment from IR (as long as the paying parent has paid on time). Our system will: - take the total amount of child support that IR has told us about - average it out over these 4 or 5 weeks so it's a weekly amount, and - update your benefit and other payments you get from us, based on this weekly income amount. Examples of how we treat your child support as income

chunks.title: When we'll send you a letter
chunks.text: We'll send you a letter if IR shares your child support information with us and your payments from us change. The letter will tell you: - the amount of child support IR shared with us - what your average weekly amount of income is, and - how much your benefit or payment from us will be. If you think there's an error with the child support information we've used, you can talk to us. We may need to contact IR to confirm your information.

chunks.title: You get Unsupported Child's Benefit
chunks.text: If you get child support from Inland Revenue and Unsupported Child's Benefit (UCB) for the same child, there are different rules for what's counted as income.

chunks.title: Most people must apply for child support through IR
chunks.text: Most people who get UCB must apply for IR to assess and administer their child support payments. IR does this using a formula assessment. The Government keeps the amount of child support that's equal to your benefit payment, and IR passes on any excess amount to you. For example, your benefit payment is $300. Your child support payment is $350. The Government keeps $300 and IR passes on $50 to you.

chunks.title: How we treat your child support as income
chunks.text: The excess amount you get from your formula assessment is only counted as income for these payments: - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR Subsidy. The excess amount is not counted as income for your Unsupported Child's Benefit. This means you only need to tell us about your child support payments if: - you get an excess amount from IR, and - you get one of the payments listed in the bullets above.

chunks.title: How your benefit will be affected
chunks.text: You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Automated decision-making
chunks.text: We use automated decision-making to help process child support payments. Automated decision-making for child support paymentsexternal

chunks.title: Examples of how we treat your child support as income
chunks.text: Inland Revenue shares most types of child support payment information with us. Our systems automatically treat these payments as income when working out your benefit and most other payments you get from us. This page has examples of how this will work.

chunks.title: How we treat your child support as income
chunks.text: IR shares monthly child support information with us around the 21st of every month, if the paying parent pays on time. If the paying parent pays late, IR shares it with us on the day they pay it. When we get your child support payment information from IR, we treat this as your income for the next month. This means the next 4 or 5 weeks from the date you receive the child support payment. It could be 4 weeks, or 5 weeks, it depends on the number of weeks until you get your next child support payment from IR (as long as the paying parent has paid on time). We take the total amount of child support that IR has told us about and average it out over these 4 or 5 weeks so it’s a weekly amount.

chunks.title: How much child support we treat as income
chunks.text: You're entitled to a certain amount of child support each month. IR call this your 'child support entitlement' and it's the amount the paying parent should be paying to IR. If the paying parent pays less than the full amount for the month, IR will give you whatever amount they have paid. This is the amount they share this with us and we treat as income. When the paying parent pays the rest of what's owed, IR will pay it to you straight away and then share it with us. This is treated as income once IR have paid it to you.

chunks.title: If you get paid weekly
chunks.text: Weekly pay cycles are from Monday to Sunday. If you get paid weekly, the next month is the next 4 weeks, or 5 weeks, from the Monday of the week you receive the child support payment. We'll take it that you have received the child support payment the day after IR pay you. This is to allow for banking time.

chunks.title: Example for the month of August (4 weeks)
chunks.text: - Paying parent must pay $800 child support to IR on Monday 21 August (for period 1 July to 31 July). - Paying parent only pays $600 child support to IR on Monday 21 August (for period 1 July to 31 July). - IR pays you (the receiving parent) $600 on Tuesday 22 August. - IR shares this info with us ($600) on Tuesday 22 August. - We’ll take it that you have received the payment on Wednesday 23 August, to allow for banking time. We’ll then average out this $600 of child support as weekly income of $150 a week from Monday 21 August to Sunday 17 September. Your first payment from us with this child support counted as income will be in the week of Monday 28 August (as we pay for the week that’s just been).

chunks.title: When paying parent pays remaining $200
chunks.text: Once the paying parent pays the remaining $200, IR will pay this to you straight away. They will then share this information with us. We'll then average out this $200 child support as weekly income over the next 4 or 5 weeks.

chunks.title: Example for the month of September (5 weeks)
chunks.text: - Paying parent must pay $800 child support to IR on Wednesday 20 September (for period 1 August to 31 August). - Paying parent pays $800 child support to IR on Wednesday 20 September (for period 1 August to 31 August). - IR pays you (the receiving parent) $800 on Thursday 21 September. - IR shares this info with us ($800) on Thursday 21 September. - We’ll take it that you have received the payment on Friday 22 September, to allow for banking time. We’ll then average out this $800 of child support as weekly income of $160 a week from Monday 18 September to Sunday 22 October. Your next payment from us with this child support counted as income will be in the week of Monday 25 September (as we pay for the week that’s just been).

chunks.title: If you get paid fortnightly
chunks.text: Fortnightly pay cycles are from Wednesday to Tuesday across 2 weeks. If you get paid fortnightly, the next month is the next 4 weeks from either: - the Wednesday of the week you receive the child support payment, if you get the child support in the first week of your pay cycle, or - the Wednesday of the week after you receive the child support payment, if you get the child support in the second week of your pay cycle. We'll take it that you have received the child support payment the day after IR pay you. This is to allow for banking time.

chunks.title: Example for the month of August
chunks.text: - Paying parent must pay $750 child support to IR on Monday 21 August (for period 1 July to 31 July). - Paying parent pays $750 child support to IR on Monday 21 August (for period 1 July to 31 July). - IR pays you (the receiving parent) $750 on Tuesday 22 August. - IR shares this info with us ($750) on Tuesday 22 August. - We'll take it that you have received the payment on Wednesday 23 August, to allow for banking time. Your pay cycle is from Wednesday 16 August to Tuesday 29 August. You've received the child support payment in the second week of your pay cycle. So we’ll average out this $750 child support as weekly income from Wednesday 30 August to Tuesday 26 September. Your first payment from us with this child support counted as income will be from Wednesday 13 September (as we pay for the fortnight that’s just been).

chunks.title: Childcare
chunks.text: If you have children who need looking after, we may be able to help pay for childcare. We can pay for up to 50 hours a week depending on your circumstances. We pay childcare for public holidays like Waitangi Day and anniversary days. However, most programmes close between Christmas and New Year, so payments won’t be made during this time.

chunks.title: Pre-school childcare
chunks.text: Childcare Subsidy is a payment that helps families with the cost of pre-school childcare. Childcare Subsidy

chunks.title: Teen parent
chunks.text: You may be able to get the Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment (GCAP) to help with the cost of childcare if: - you're under 20 - you're in full-time education, training or work-based learning, and - your child is aged either: under 5, or over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. - under 5, or - over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. There are also other criteria you need to meet. Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment

chunks.title: Child is in a Family Start or Early Start Programme

chunks.title: Childcare absences
chunks.text: When your child is away from the childcare centre (eg, they're sick), we may be able to keep paying the childcare provider.

chunks.title: Absence due to COVID-19
chunks.text: If your child is absent due to COVID-19, we may be able to continue to pay childcare assistance. For example, they could be: - sick with COVID-19 and cannot attend childcare - at high risk of severe illness if they get COVID-19, based on Ministry of Health guidelines - in self-isolation or quarantine due to COVID-19 public health requirements - connected to a confirmed or probable case of COVID-19. Your provider will let us know if your child is absent due to COVID-19.

chunks.title: Absence not due to COVID-19
chunks.text: If your child is absent for a non-COVID-19 related reason, we may be able to continue to pay childcare assistance. It depends how long they’re absent for.

chunks.title: Absences of fewer than 3 weeks
chunks.text: If your child is going to be away for a short time, you don't need to do anything. We'll pay the childcare provider while your child is absent.

chunks.title: Absences of more than 3 weeks
chunks.text: If your child is going to be away for longer than 3 weeks, they must have a medical reason. You'll need to: - let your childcare provider know - get a medical certificate (unless you get Child Disability Allowance or Group Special Education Funding). We can keep paying for your child's place at the programme for up to 6 weeks when a medical certificate is provided. You can email the medical certificate to us at Centralised_Childcare_Reviews@msd.govt.nz.

chunks.title: Absence from New Zealand
chunks.text: We may be able to continue to pay for childcare for up to 28 days if you're going overseas. But this is only possible if you let us know before you go. We'll assess it on a case by case basis. Call us before you leave NZ on 0800 559 009 and tell us: - the date you're leaving - when you're returning - reason for travel - whether your child is travelling with you or staying in New Zealand. If you don't tell us you're going overseas, your childcare payments may stop and you might have to pay back some of your childcare payments for the time you were overseas. This applies whether you're on a benefit or not.

chunks.title: Getting Early Learning Payment or Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment
chunks.text: If your childcare provider does not charge an absence fee, you need to let us know what dates your child is absent. You can do this by calling us on 0800 559 009. This is so we can adjust the payments to your provider.
