chunks.title: Dental treatment
chunks.text: If you're on a low income or benefit, we may be able to help you pay for immediate and essential dental treatment. Immediate and essential dental treatment includes treatment such as fillings and extractions, but not periodic cleaning or check-ups. See more examples in the 'What you can get' section. You can apply for up to $1,000 a year (any 52-week period), to help with immediate and essential dental treatment. You don't have to pay this back. We may still be able to help if the cost of your dental treatment is more than $1,000. You may need to pay some of this back, depending on your situation. Talk to us about how we can help. Phone us You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get help for dental treatment for yourself or a child, if immediate and essential work needs to be done. To apply, you need to: - be 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) Youth Servicesexternal - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. It also depends on: - how much you (and your partner) earn - any money or assets you (and your partner) have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of income or benefit you receive. The following income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We can help pay for immediate and essential treatment, which can include: - extractions - fillings for tooth restoration – not for cosmetic or for non-oral health issues - root canal treatment (except molars) - treatment of infection. It does not include: - regular dental check-ups - cosmetic treatment - scale and polish, and teeth cleaning (unless this treatment is required because of gum infection) - cast restorations - orthodontic treatment - molar root canal treatment - dentures. If you need help with dentures, there are other ways we can help, such as recoverable assistance or an advance payment of benefit. Talk to us about how we can help. Recoverable assistance Advance payment of benefit Phone us You can apply more than once a year (any 52-week period), up to a total of $1,000 for the period. You don't have to apply for all the assistance at once. You don't have to pay this money back.

chunks.title: Payments over $1,000
chunks.text: If you need help with immediate and essential dental treatment that's over $1,000, or that will bring your total payments within a 52-week period to over $1,000, we still may be able to help you meet this cost. You may need to pay some of this back. Talk to us about the options available to you. Phone us

chunks.title: Examples of how much we can pay
chunks.text: If you haven't had help from us for dental treatment in the last 52 weeks, we could pay up to $1,000 towards immediate and essential treatment. If you got $1,000 for dental treatment on 12 December 2024, you wouldn't have any dental treatment funds available until 12 December 2025. If you need more treatment talk to us, we may still be able to help you.

chunks.title: More than one payment in a year
chunks.text: If you got $300 for dental treatment on 1 July 2024, and you need more treatment 6 months later, you still have up to $700 available to you. From 1 July 2025, the $300 that was used on 1 July 2024, would again be available. If no other payments had been made in that period, then you would have a total of $1,000 available for immediate and essential dental treatment.

chunks.title: Step 1: Get a Dental Treatment information form
chunks.text: Your dentist or health agency needs to complete a Dental Treatment information form. They will already have this form and will fill it in when they examine you. The form will tell us: - what dental treatment you need - the cost of the treatment - who is providing the treatment, and - any other information that will help us assess your application. We can only make payments to dentists or health agencies who are registered suppliers with us. You can ask them if they are registered with us.

chunks.title: Step 2: Apply for dental treatment
chunks.text: How you apply depends on whether you're a client with us or not.

chunks.title: You're a client with us
chunks.text: The easiest way to apply is in MyMSD under 'One-off cost'. You can upload the Dental Treatment Information form during the application. Once you've completed the application, you'll need to check MyMSD again to see if it's been approved. This can take up to 1 working day. Otherwise you can either: - call us to apply over the phone. You'll need to upload the form through MyMSD (we can help you do this), or - drop or post the form to a service centre. Then call us so we can process this on the phone. Please allow enough time for us to get the form and add it to your file before calling. Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: You're not a client with us
chunks.text: You can either: - call us to apply over the phone. We'll set you up with a MyMSD login and help you upload the form through MyMSD, or - drop or post the form to a service centre. Then call us so we can process this on the phone. Please allow enough time for us to get the form and add it to your Phone us Find a service centre Phone us Find a service centre

chunks.title: Step 3: Get a payment card
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll load the money onto your Work and Income Payment Card. If you don't already have a Payment Card, you can pick one up from a service centre. You'll pay the dentist with your Payment Card (like an Eftpos card). In some cases, we may pay it directly to the dentist or health agency. You have 7 working days to pay your dentist or health agency before it expires. If you need more time, call us before the 7 day period has ended. You can also pay your dentist or health agency before you get the treatment, if you can't get an appointment within 7 days. You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when the payment expires.

chunks.title: Community Services Card
chunks.text: If you have a Community Services Card, you may be able to get dental treatment through your local hospital. Talk to a health practitioner, e.g. your doctor or dentist, about this. Community Services Card

chunks.title: ACC
chunks.text: ACC may be able to cover dental injuries caused by accidents, sports injuries, or as a result of medical or dental treatment. Injuries ACC covers (ACC)external

chunks.title: Health New Zealand
chunks.text: Health New Zealand has advice about emergency dental care, including how to find an after-hours dentist or how your local hospital can help. Dentists and emergency dental care (Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora)external You may be able to get publicly funded dental care if you're under 18 years of age, or have a Community Services Card, or have a disability or medical condition. Dentists (Health New Zealand - Te Whatu Ora)external

chunks.title: Information for dental providers
chunks.text: If you have a patient who needs help to pay for immediate and essential dental treatment, they may apply for financial support through Work and Income. You'll need to: - be registered as a supplier with Work and Income - complete a Work and Income Dental Treatment Information form. Register as a Work and Income supplier Dental treatment - information for dentists and health agencies

chunks.title: Alternate formats
chunks.text: The information on this page is available in alternate formats. Watch the New Zealand Sign Language video on YouTube: 0:01 Help with paying for immediate and essential dental treatment 0:06 Introduction: If you qualify, you can get help with up to one thousand dollars a year (any 52 week period) for immediate and essential dental treatment. You don’t have to pay this money back. The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) may be able to help. MSD includes Work and Income and StudyLink, who provide services for individuals and whānau (families) throughout New Zealand. 0:30 Do you qualify: To qualify, you need to 1. be 16 or over, 2. be a New Zealander (citizen or permanent resident), 3. live in New Zealand, 4. have an immediate and essential need for dental treatment. It also depends on 1. how much you and your partner earn, 2. any money or assets you and your partner have, and 3. and what type of dental treatment you need help with. Our website has more details about the criteria. Click on the link 'Dental Treatment - Work and Income' or at https://www.workandincome.govt.nz/dental-treatment

It does not include: 1. regular check-ups, 2. cosmetic treatments, 3. teeth cleaning – unless it’s for gum infections, 4. cast restorations, 5. orthodontic treatments, 6. molar root canal treatments, and 7. dentures. 2:07 Help with dentures: If you need help with dentures, there are other ways we can help, such as 1. recoverable assistance or 2. an advance payment of benefit, or 3. talk with us about how we can help.

chunks.title: Deported to New Zealand
chunks.text: If you've been sent back to New Zealand from another country, there's a range of support you may be able to get to help you get on your feet. It's important you contact us right away as there may be a stand-down period before you get the first payment of any benefit.

chunks.title: You've been in prison
chunks.text: You may be able to get help with initial set up costs if you've: - been in prison or remand for 31 days or more - been sent back to New Zealand straight after your release. It can help with things like: - housing - living expenses, eg power, a phone connection or food - other essential costs, eg bedding, clothing, appliances or toiletry items. Steps to Freedom grant

chunks.title: Haven't lived in New Zealand for 2 years
chunks.text: If you've got New Zealand residency or citizenship but haven't lived in New Zealand for 2 years, we may still be able to help, depending on your circumstances. Call us to discuss your situation. Phone us

chunks.text: You're looking for full-time work and need help to pay day-to-day living expenses until you find a job. Jobseeker Support When you apply for Jobseeker Support, there may be some things you need to do before you can get it. Online application process

chunks.title: Direct Career Service
chunks.text: Get free advice from qualified career practitioners. Whether you’re looking for work, thinking about a change or unsure where to start, a career practitioner can give you clear guidance and practical support.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can get one-on-one help to understand your skills and explore new career opportunities. This can include: - planning your next steps into work or training - understanding your skills and how you can use them in a new job - looking for a new direction or exploring training options and more. This service will not affect the support you get from us.

chunks.title: Who can use this
chunks.text: This service is available to all New Zealand residents who are 17 or older and want support to plan their career. You can also use this service if you are 16 years old and you’re not in school, training or work. It’s especially helpful if you’re: - unemployed - at risk of losing your job - looking for support to return to the workforce.

chunks.title: How to get started
chunks.text: Request an appointment by: - calling 0800 222 733 - emailing direct_careers@msd.govt.nz - asking your case manager or work broker. We will ask you some questions to check if you’re eligible. After this, we will pass on your details to a career practitioner, who will contact you to schedule an appointment. You can meet with a career practitioner: - in person at a Work and Income site - by phone - online through Zoom or other platforms. Find a service centre

chunks.title: How it works
chunks.text: During the appointment, the career practitioner will talk with you about your situation, skills, interests, and goals. Together, you will create a personalised career action plan, which can include advise and practical steps on: - planning and developing your career - study and training options - skills you can use in your career - job applications - understanding the labour market - understanding employment rights and conditions. You can talk to your career practitioner about what you would like your plan to look like. Your career practitioner may also book some future appointments to work with you on your progress. When you feel you no longer need their help, you can stop the service any time.

chunks.title: Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Disability Allowance is a weekly payment for people who have regular, ongoing costs because of a disability. These could be visits to the doctor or hospital, medicines, extra clothing or travel. You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for a Disability Allowance.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get a Disability Allowance if you: - have a disability that is likely to last at least 6 months - have regular, ongoing costs because of your disability that are not fully covered by another agency - aren't getting a Residential Care Subsidy - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. Residential Care Subsidy It also depends on how much you and your partner earn. The income limits for Disability Allowance are:

chunks.title: Your child has a disability
chunks.text: You can apply on behalf of a child if they're 18 or under and financially dependent on you. You may be able to get both the Disability Allowance and the Child Disability Allowance for the same child. Child Disability Allowance You can't get a Disability Allowance if you get Board payments from Oranga Tamariki for the child.

chunks.title: Check if you can get Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Find out if you might get this benefit, and what other financial assistance may be available to you. If you are a student, visit StudyLinkexternal. The information provided in this page is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: Types of costs that can be included
chunks.text: Regular, ongoing disability-related costs that can be included are: - Alternative treatment - Ambulance fees and subscriptions - Authorised consumables - Clothing - Counselling - Day care for the elderly disabled - Gardening, lawns and outside window cleaning - Gym and swimming pool fees - Medical alarms - MedicAlert costs - Medical fees - Nicotine replacement products - Prescription fees, subsidised and unsubsidised - Power, gas and heating - Rental equipment - Residential care services - Rest home costs for a private paying patient - Special foods - Phone - Travel to counselling - Travel because of your disability - Vitamins, supplements, herbal remedies and minerals. Your health practitioner must confirm you need these costs. You need to provide proof of your costs when you apply.

chunks.title: Types of costs that can be included
chunks.text: Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: You can get up to $82.85 a week for Disability Allowance. How much you get depends on the extra costs you have.. This payment is not taxed and you don’t have to pay it back.

chunks.title: How it's paid
chunks.text: The Disability Allowance is paid straight into your bank account, on the same day as any other payments you get from us.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: We can grant you the financial assistance you’re entitled to from the date you first contact us if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date.

chunks.title: Step 1: Fill in application form
chunks.text: What application form you fill out depends on whether you’re already getting payments from us. If you’re already getting payments from us, fill in the Disability Allowance application form: If you’re not getting payments from us, or only getting childcare payments You can either: - apply online through MyMSD, or - fill out a paper Extra Help application form. MyMSDexternal

chunks.title: Step 2: Visit your health practitioner
chunks.text: Ask your health practitioner (e.g. your doctor) to complete a Disability Certificate for you. This will confirm that the disability is ongoing and also verify what extra costs can be included. They will give this back to you, so you can bring it to us.

chunks.title: Step 3: Gather your proof of your costs
chunks.text: You need to provide proof of any costs you’re claiming for, so we know how much to pay you. This needs to show: - what it’s for and - how much it costs (or enough information that we can work this out ourselves). Some examples of you can provide are:

chunks.title: Proof you'll need to provide
chunks.text: Doctor's, specialist's and hospital fees (That aren't already subsidised) Receipts or print-outs from your medical practitioner showing the date, cost, and reason for your visit. Travel costs Prescription fees Your doctor needs to complete the 'Disability Allowance Medical Assessment for Medical Alarm' form. You'll also need to provide the contract or receipt for the installation/rental of the medical alarm. You, your doctor and counsellor also need to complete a Counselling form. Disability Certificate - Counselling formexternal Special food costs You can use the special foods information form to help you work out your extra costs. Disability Allowance – special foods information formexternal

chunks.title: Step 4: Get your documents to us
chunks.text: You can get your proof of costs and form (if you applied using a paper form) to us by either: - dropping it in to your nearest service centre - posting it to your nearest service centreexternal, or - uploading it to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre MyMSDexternal If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you’ll need to bring your ID and any other supporting documents listed in your application form, such as documents relating to your back account, income and residency into a service centre so we can check it.

chunks.title: Step 5: You may need an appointment
chunks.text: After you've applied we may ask you to call us to book an appointment. This could be a phone appointment or a face-to-face appointment.

chunks.title: If your costs or circumstances change
chunks.text: If you're getting Disability Allowance and your disability costs or circumstances change, let us know. This includes new, increased, stopped, or decreased costs. For any new or increased costs, you'll need to provide a medical certificate and proof of the costs. Tell us about your change of costsexternal If you're not sure what costs are included in your Disability Allowance, you can check MyMSD.

chunks.title: Renew your medical certificate
chunks.text: You may need to get your health practitioner to complete another Disability Certificate. We’ll let you know when you need to renew this. Renew your medical certificate or information

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: If you get a Disability Allowance, we will review your circumstances at least once every 52 weeks (one year) to make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. As part of this, we might ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Disability Allowance obligations
chunks.text: There are things you and your partner need to do when you're getting a Disability Allowance. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You and your partner must tell us (or your Youth Service Provider if you have one assigned to you) immediately if you: - have a change in work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - have a change to your disability costs - become self-employed or start a business - have changes to your income or financial circumstances - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have changes to your personal details, e.g: name address bank account number - name - address - bank account number - have changes to their living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children you support - have a change in accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other change that may affect your entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you or your partner can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. Contact us If you or your partner don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your payment entitlement, or rate, then: - your payment may be reviewed and cancelled - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you've received - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined and/or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text: If you or your partner intend to travel overseas and don't let us know before you leave New Zealand, your payment will be stopped the day after you leave New Zealand.

chunks.title: Other things we may ask you to do
chunks.text: We must review Disability Allowance payments regularly. This means we may also ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. This information helps us make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. If you don’t respond to the form before the due date, your Disability Allowance payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Doing seasonal work
chunks.text: You may be able to get help to pay for things like clothes, gear or temporarily moving home. There's also help if you can't work due to bad weather.

chunks.title: Who can get these
chunks.text: You need to have recently started a seasonal job and stopped your benefit.

chunks.title: When you start work
chunks.text: If you're starting seasonal horticulture or viticulture work, the New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme can help with: - costs like transport, gear and clothing - an accommodation costs payment - an incentive payment. Talk to us about New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme before you start the job. Find out the full details of who can get this and what you can get: New Zealand Seasonal Work Scheme

chunks.title: Can't work due to bad weather
chunks.text: Seasonal Work Assistance is a payment to help if you've: - lost wages because of work missed due to bad weather, and - stopped getting a benefit to do this job. Find out the full details of who can get this and what you can get: Seasonal Work Assistance

chunks.title: Planning your next job
chunks.text: Most seasonal jobs are temporary, so you need to plan what job you'll do next. Seasonal jobs are available all year in New Zealand. We have information about finding seasonal work and how to plan out where you can work and when: Finding seasonal work If you'd like to try a different type of job, or just want to see what's out there, you can see jobs available now: Where to look for jobs

chunks.title: When your seasonal work ends
chunks.text: When your contract ends we may be able to help with: - money while you look for work - finding a new job. Seasonal worker

chunks.title: Dress for Success
chunks.text: Support and practical help for women looking for work. You can get help to feel more confident when you're going to job interviews or starting a new job. Dress for Success is a worldwide organisation which supports women to find and keep work. They provide clothing suitable for your job interview and work, job-seeking advice and skills, and ongoing employment support.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To get the Dress for Success service you need to qualify for a Transition to Work Grant from us. This covers the cost of the service. Check the Transition to Work Grant page on our website to find out who can get this and how to apply: Transition to Work Grant

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Dress for Success offers: - clothing and styling services, and - careers services The costs are covered by Transition to Work Grant. You don't have to pay the money back. Transition to Work Grant

chunks.title: Clothing and Styling Services
chunks.text: You can get clothing suitable for an interview or work experience. They'll adjust the styling to the type of job you're applying for. You can then get a mix-and-match wardrobe once you're successful in finding a job. This will include shoes and other accessories.

chunks.title: Careers services
chunks.text: You can get practical skills and advice to improve your chances of getting and keeping a job. You'll get help to prepare your CV and job interview material, get more skilled in doing job interviews, and learn how to plan your career. These services might be one-on-one, or with a group of women in workshops and seminars.

chunks.title: Locations
chunks.text: These services can change depending on what the Dress for Success closest to you can offer, you can find their addresses on their websites: Auckland - Dress for Successexternal Bay of Plenty - Dress for Successexternal Christchurch - Dress for Successexternal Hamilton - Dress for Successexternal Hawkes Bay - Dress for Successexternal Northland - Dress for Successexternal Palmerston North - Dress for Successexternal Wellington - Dress for Successexternal

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 to apply for a Transition to Work Grant. We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Early Learning Payment
chunks.text: The Early Learning Payment helps pay the costs of Early Childhood Education for children aged 18 months to 3 years. These children need to be from families enrolled in selected Family Start or Early Start Programmes. If you're enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme, you'll be assigned a family/whānau worker who'll contact us for you.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get the Early Learning Payment if: - you're enrolled in a Family Start or Early Start programme - your child is aged 18 months to 3 years. This can be paid for your child to attend an approved early childhood service for up to 20 hours a week. Families getting Childcare Subsidy or Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment (GCAP) can't get Early Learning Payment for the same hours.

chunks.title: Leaving Family Start or Early Start
chunks.text: From 1 October 2017, if your family leaves Family Start or Early Start, you may be able to continue getting the payments. Your child must be: - the child that the Early Learning Payment was being paid for when your family left Family Start or Early Start - aged between 18 months to 3 years - a dependent child and - attending an approved early childhood service.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. You'll need to fill out the 'Early Learning Payment application form'. We'll discuss the best way to get the completed form to us.

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit
chunks.text: If you can't support yourself and don't qualify for any other payment, you may be able to get the Emergency Benefit. If you qualify for another payment, you need to apply for this instead of the Emergency Benefit. Other payments you may qualify for could be: - Jobseeker Support - Sole Parent Support - Supported Living Payment - New Zealand Superannuation To find out if you qualify for other benefits or payments, you can use our Check What You Might Get tool. It's a guide to help you find out the ways we can help you and your family.

chunks.title: Emergency Benefit obligations
chunks.text: There are things your partner needs to do when you're getting an Emergency Benefit. If they don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Overview of your obligations
chunks.text: - You have an obligation to tell us if something changes. - If you're taking care of dependent children, you have social obligations. - If we ask you to, you have an obligation to take part in a Work Ability Assessment or to work with a contracted service provider. You may also have an obligation to find or prepare for work. If so, your case manager would have discussed this with you when you applied for the benefit. These obligations are detailed on this page below. If you have a partner, there are things they'll need to do as well. Emergency Benefit obligations for partners

chunks.title: Obligations in detail
chunks.text: Select the relevant heading below to find out more about each obligation.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell us (or your Youth Service Provider if you have one assigned to you) immediately if you: - have a change in your work situation, e.g. starting part-time, casual or full-time work (paid or unpaid) - become self-employed or start a business - have changes to your income or financial circumstances - have a boarder or renter that moves in or out, or the payments you get from them change - plan to travel overseas - start or finish study - part-time or full-time - have changes to your personal details, e.g: name address bank account - name - address - bank account - have changes to your living situation, e.g: marriage or separation starting or ending a civil union starting or ending a de facto relationship change in the number of children you support

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: - marriage or separation - starting or ending a civil union - starting or ending a de facto relationship - change in the number of children you support - have a change in accommodation costs - are imprisoned or held in custody on remand - are admitted to or discharged from hospital - are granted an overseas pension - have any other changes that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: You’re expected to take reasonable steps to meet social obligations as a parent or a caregiver. These obligations are to help ensure children get a good start. You must ensure your dependent child(ren) (including any child you get Orphan’s or Unsupported Child’s Benefit for) are: - enrolled with a general practitioner (GP) or a medical practice that’s part of a Primary Health Organisation (PHO) - enrolled in and attending one of the following from the age of 3 until they start school: an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu – The Correspondence School, or another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: - an approved early childhood education programme, eg, Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus parenting and early childhood home education programmes kindergartens preschools childcare centres playcentres home-based care services, or - Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus - parenting and early childhood home education programmes - kindergartens - preschools - childcare centres - playcentres - home-based care services, or - Te Aho o Te Kura Pounamu – The Correspondence School, or - another approved parenting and early childhood home education programme - up to date with core Well Child/Tamariki Ora checks if aged under 5, at a Well Child/Tamariki Ora provider, eg: Plunket Maori health provider Pacific health provider

chunks.title: When taking care of dependent children (social obligations)
chunks.text: - Plunket - Maori health provider - Pacific health provider - enrolled in and attending school from the age of 5 or 6 (depending on when they start school). We understand there could be some situations outside of your control that mean you may not be able to meet an obligation right now. For example: - your child is on a waiting list for a GP, or - there aren’t any available places in your nearby childcare centre. You may be required to meet with us to discuss how you’re meeting your obligations as a parent or a caregiver.

chunks.title: Take part in Work Ability Assessments
chunks.text: When it has been agreed, you have an obligation to attend and participate in a Work Ability Assessment.

chunks.title: Take part in activities with our service providers
chunks.text: When it has been agreed that you will work with a Contracted Service Provider, you have an obligation to co-operate with them and to: - attend and participate in any interview with them - report to them on how you're meeting your obligations - complete assessments with them.

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: You'll generally be expected to look for work of at least 30 hours a week, unless you have a health condition or disability that means you can't work full-time. If you have full-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable job - take any offer of suitable full-time, part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with Work and Income as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities we refer you to that will improve your work readiness or help you get work, such as: job training courses work experience, or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment)

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: - job training courses - work experience, or - work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, you'll need to look for work of at least 15 hours a week. If you have part-time work obligations, you need to: - be available for and take reasonable steps to get a suitable part-time job - take any offer of suitable part-time or temporary work, or work that is seasonal or subsidised - attend and take part in any suitable job interviews we ask you to - take and pass any drug test potential employers or training providers require - attend and take part in interviews with us as required - work with us to plan how you'll find a suitable job - take part in any other activities that we refer you to, such as attend any job training courses, seminars, work experience or work assessments (including rehabilitation, but not medical treatment) that will improve your work readiness or help you get work

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: - let us know how you're meeting your work obligations as often as we reasonably require.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you're unable to work, or can only work fewer than 15 hours a week, you won't be asked to meet work obligations until your situation changes. In the meantime, you have the following work preparation obligations to: - take reasonable steps to prepare and plan for work - attend and take part in work preparation interviews, where we ask you to - attend and take part in work related activities or programmes such as a work assessment, a programme or seminar to increase particular skills or enhance motivation where we ask you to - attend and take part in any other activity that we require you to (including rehabilitation but not medical treatment, voluntary work or activity in the community).

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. If you don't meet your obligations without good and sufficient reason, your benefit could be reduced or stopped. Contact us To find out what happens if you don't meet your obligation for telling us if something changes, go to the 'When you don't meet your obligations' page. When you don't meet your obligations We have a traffic light colour system to help you stay on track with your work-related and social obligations (if you have these). It lets you know where you're at and what you need to do. Go to the 'Traffic light system' page to find out what happens if you don't meet the following obligations: - find or prepare for work

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: - take part in Work Ability Assessments - take part in activities with our service providers - social obligations (when taking care of dependent children). Traffic light system

chunks.title: Other things we may ask you to do
chunks.text: We must review Emergency Benefit payments regularly. This means we may also ask you to fill out a Confirming your Circumstances form. This information helps us make sure you are getting the correct assistance and amount. If you don't respond to the form before the due date, your Emergency Benefit payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Emergency housing
chunks.text: If you have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 nights, we may be able to pay for you to stay in emergency housing. Emergency housing is short-term accommodation for people who need it because: - they can’t stay where they are, and - they have nowhere else to go.

chunks.title: Who can get emergency housing
chunks.text: If you need emergency housing, you must meet certain criteria. Who can get emergency housing

chunks.title: Apply for emergency housing
chunks.text: Find out how to apply for emergency housing. Apply for emergency housing

chunks.title: Cost of emergency housing
chunks.text: In most cases we'll cover the cost of your accommodation for the first 7 nights if you qualify. Then you'll have to start paying for some of the accommodation costs. This is called an Emergency Housing Contribution. Cost of emergency housing

chunks.title: Security deposit
chunks.text: If you're going to stay in emergency housing, your housing supplier may ask for a security deposit. Security deposit for emergency housing

chunks.title: Staying in emergency housing
chunks.text: If you're staying in emergency housing, you can find information about: - your rights - what we expect you to do - your responsibilities - what to do if you have concerns or want to make a complaint - what to do when you leave. Staying in emergency housing

chunks.title: Employer help if you have a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text: Help from your employers because of a health condition, injury or disability doesn't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.

chunks.title: What is this?
chunks.text: This includes any payment or service you get so you can keep working eg transport to and from your job.

chunks.title: How it affects your benefit and allowances
chunks.text: You have to tell us about this payment if you: - get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Your employment plan
chunks.text: An employment plan is an easy way to see the activities you need to do to find and prepare for work. Some people who get Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support have an employment plan in MyMSD - we'll let you know if you have one. When you get Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support, one of your obligations is to find or prepare for work. To meet this obligation, there are activities you need to do by a certain date. An employment plan is an easy way to see these activities and the date you need to do them by. You'll get a notification on your MyMSD homepage when your activities are due within 7 days. If one of your activities is to apply for jobs, you can use MyMSD to: - let us know when you've applied for a job, by 'Adding a job search activity'

chunks.title: How to see your employment plan
chunks.text: If you have an employment plan in MyMSD, you can see it by going to 'My employment plan' on the home screen. MyMSD

chunks.title: Can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can’t use MyMSD, your case manager will print the plan with your activities and when they need to be done by.

chunks.title: Your activities
chunks.text: Your case manager will talk to you about your employment needs. They'll tailor the activities based on your conversations. Together you will agree on a due date for each activity. Activities could be things like: - creating a CV - updating your Jobseeker profile on MyMSD, or - applying for suitable jobs. You may have to apply for jobs as one of your activities. If you apply for a job, record this activity in your employment plan in MyMSD. You don't need to tell your case manager about it. When you complete any other activity, you need to contact your case manager. They can then mark that activity as complete in your plan. If there's any reason why you can't complete an activity by the due date, contact your case manager straight away.

chunks.title: Help with your activities
chunks.text: If you're unsure what you need to do or need help with your activities, the best thing to do is contact your case manager. They'll be able to talk you through it.

chunks.title: What happens if you don't complete your activities
chunks.text: These activities are part of your obligation to find or prepare for work. If you don’t do an activity, it means you’re not meeting your obligations. If you don't meet your obligations without good and sufficient reason, your benefit could be reduced or stopped. If there's any reason why you can't complete an activity by the due date, contact your case manager straight away. We have a traffic light colour system to help you stay on track with your work obligations. Traffic light system

chunks.title: Employment service for people with a disability or health condition
chunks.text: If you have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, you can get one-on-one help to find work, support during your first year of employment, and as needed while you're in employment. We have contracted experienced Employment Service providers who can work with you to prepare you for work, and help you find an ongoing job. The provider will also support you while you're in work. Our providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. They specialise in helping people who have a disability, health condition, mental health condition, or are neurodiverse move into work.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You can use Employment Service if: - you have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, and this is likely to continue for six months or more, and - your disability or health condition affects your ability to find work, and - you're ready to go into work, and - you're currently living in New Zealand, and - you're a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident, and - you're aged between 16 and 64, and - you've left school. You don't need to be getting a benefit to use Employment Service.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Employment Service providers can help with: - career planning - preparation for employment, e.g. help writing a CV, techniques for interviews, etc. - job searching and matching - employment placement - negotiations of any flexible working arrangements - talking with your employer about how they can best support you while you're working. Once you're in work, they can provide ongoing support to you and, if needed, your employer, for up to one year.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You'll need to contact an Employment Service provider. If you're getting a benefit from us, you may already have an Employment Service provider. If you don't already have a provider, you can choose from a list of providers in your area: Our Employment Service providers Your provider will let you know how they'll work with you and help you develop a plan for your employment future.

chunks.title: Employment service for secondary school students with a disability or health condition
chunks.text: Employment Service in Schools is for secondary school students who have a disability or health condition, including mental health condition or neurodiversity. This pilot service helps the students, their family or whānau, and school plan for their future and explore job and career opportunities. Working with the Ministry of Education, we have contracted providers in Otago-Southland, Canterbury, Wellington, Waikato, and parts of Auckland. These providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. Their focus is on preparing students for employment through skill development and work experience or job trials. This service is a pilot and will be available until 30 June 2026.

chunks.title: Who can take part
chunks.text: You can take part in Employment Service in Schools if you: - have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity, which: is likely to continue for six months or more, and may mean you have trouble getting into or finding work - is likely to continue for six months or more, and - may mean you have trouble getting into or finding work and you are: - a student aged 14 to 21 enrolled in English or Māori medium secondary school or kura, and you plan to leave school in the next two years, and - finding out what job or type of work you would like - living in Otago-Southland, Canterbury, Wellington, Waikato, or parts of Auckland, and - a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident.

chunks.title: Who can take part
chunks.text: You don't need to be getting a benefit to use Employment Service in Schools. You won't be able to take part in the service if you: - can get funding from ACC to transition from school, or - are currently getting funding from us through Transition Services. If you're already getting help through our Transition Service, and would like to move to Employment Service in Schools, please email us at Employment_Service_in_Schools@msd.govt.nz If you're not living in an area with Employment Service in Schools please see the information about other support available at the bottom of this page or you can email us at Employment_Service_in_Schools@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: With Employment Service in Schools, you'll work with a provider in your area to get ready for when you leave school and go into a job or training for a job. Our providers are experts in preparing people for work and finding job opportunities. You'll get help with things like: - identifying what types of jobs you could do when you leave school - finding information to help you make decisions - finding out what job of type of work you would like - creating your CV - getting ready for interviews - work experience - getting a part-time job while you're at school. Our providers specialise in helping people who have a disability or health condition, including a mental health condition or neurodiversity. They'll work with you, your family or whānau, school and other networks to help you plan your future.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Talk to your teacher, your teaching support, or your careers advisor about Employment Service in Schools. They'll let you know which providers are in your area, and help you and your family or whānau choose the right one. You'll need to complete the form (linked below) to apply, and get your parents/whānau, your school and the provider you've chosen to fill in the sections marked for them. Once you've completed this form give it to the provider you've chosen. There are several providers available in each region. You and your family or whānau can choose the provider you want to work with.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll process your application, this usually takes 2-3 working days. Your provider will tell you if your application is accepted or not. If your application is accepted, your provider will contact you to organise a meeting. This will be with you and your parents or whānau. You'll work together to find out what kind of employment future you'd like, and what needs to happen for this. You'll get Employment Service in Schools until you leave school or when the pilot ends (30 June 2026), even if you start a job while you're still at school.

chunks.title: Other support available
chunks.text: There's other support available if you're not able to get Employment Service in Schools, or if you were getting this and it's now finished. You can contact your school about these: - Transition Service, for students who are verified on the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme (ORS) and are in their last year of school. - Mana Whaikaha, a disability support system offering disabled people and whānau more choice and control over their supports. - Vocational support through your school, such as career support, Gateway or Vocational Pathways. - Funding for students with very high needs, who are verified on the Ongoing Resourcing Scheme, and are leaving school. Mana Whaikaha (Disability Support Services)external,

chunks.title: Other support available
chunks.text: We may also be able to help you with: - Employment Service, similar to Employment Service in Schools and available when you leave school. Employment Service - Mainstream programmes, to help you get paid work experience and a long-term job. Mainstream programmes

chunks.title: Employment Transition Assistance
chunks.text: Employment Transition Assistance is a weekly payment you can get if you've completed a Supported Living Payment Employment Trial.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get an Employment Transition Assistance if you: - have completed a Supported Living Payment Employment Trial - can no longer get a Supported Living Payment - are earning less than the Supported Living Payment after completing the trial - regularly work 15 hours or more per week (not in sheltered employment) - can’t carry on working these hours without this payment. It also depends on how much you and your partner earn.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on your living situation and age. You can see the rates for Employment Transition Assistance here: View our maximum current rates (Manuals and Procedures)external

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009. We'll book an appointment for you to meet with us. When you book the appointment, we'll let you know what information you need to provide.

chunks.title: Child turning 18
chunks.text: If a child in your care is turning 18 and there is a change in their circumstances, your payments can be affected. Find out what you need to do to keep getting the right support, and when you need to tell us you’re no longer supporting them.

chunks.title: When a child can stay included in your payments
chunks.text: When a child turns 18, we usually stop including them in payments. However, if the child in your care has their 18th birthday on or after 4 September 2026, they can continue to be included in your payments if they: - are enrolled and attending school or tertiary education, and - still depend on you for financial support.

chunks.title: Tell us before they turn 18
chunks.text: You need to tell us if the child in your care is still meeting these requirements to stay included in your payments before they turn 18. You can tell us through this form: Child turning 18external If you don't let us know, your payments may reduce. If a child in your care has finished or left education before they turn 18, but they are still financially dependent on you, they can be included in your payments until they turn 18. If the child in your care is no longer financially dependent on you, please contact us. Phone us If you are receiving one of these payments, you need to get in touch with us before your child turns 18 or your payments will stop: - Emergency Benefit - Emergency Maintenance Allowance

chunks.title: Tell us before they turn 18
chunks.text: - Jobseeker Support on ground of hardship - Jobseeker Support Student Hardship - Special Benefit - Community Costs.

chunks.title: No longer supporting your 16-17 year old
chunks.text: We can only include your 16 or 17 year old in your payments if you're supporting them. If you're not supporting them at the moment, you need to tell us. Supporting a child means you take the main responsibility for them, and: - they're part of your family - they depend on you financially - they're not in paid full time work (30 hours or more a week) - you're not getting payments from Oranga Tamariki on behalf of them. If you support your 16 or 17 year old at the moment, you don't need to do anything. Your payments will continue even if they are not in education.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: If you're not supporting your 16 or 17 year old at the moment, you need to contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll send you a letter to let you know if there are any changes to your payment.

chunks.title: Your child's studying
chunks.text: If your child wants to study next year, they may be able to get a Student Allowance from StudyLink. Student Allowanceexternal

chunks.title: Automated decision-making
chunks.text: Please let us know before a child in your care turns 18 if they are still financially dependent on you, and still attending either school or tertiary education. This is so that they can continue to be included in your benefit. If we do not hear from you, we will use automated decision-making to automatically remove them from your benefit from the beginning of the next pay period after their 18th birthday. This means your payments from us may change or stop. We’ll always let you know when we’ve used automated decision-making to make a decision that affects you. More information about how we use automated decision-making can be found here: Automated decision-making

chunks.title: Enhanced Taskforce Green
chunks.text: If there's been an emergency event that's caused significant damage, the Government may approve an Enhanced Taskforce Green (ETFG) work programme to help with clean-up and recovery. The Ministry of Social Development will work with a range of agencies in the impacted area to determine what support is needed. If required we will contract a local provider to employ workers to help with clean-up activities. These workers could be job seekers or workers at risk of losing their employment because of the emergency.

chunks.title: What costs will be covered by ETFG
chunks.text: ETFG assistance may cover the costs of: - wages for workers - wages for supervisors - purchasing personal safety gear - hiring light equipment and transport, for example: chainsaws vans four-wheel-drive vehicles - chainsaws - vans - four-wheel-drive vehicles - a start-up grant for local authorities to assist with administration costs. ETFG does not cover the cost of hiring heavy machinery.

chunks.title: Work and Income's role
chunks.text: Work and Income is responsible for: - liaising with affected councils and the Ministry for Primary Industries - contracting a suitably qualified provider to complete the clean-up work required - identifying suitable workers and profiling them to the provider - providing identified workers with financial assistance (including Working for Families Assistance information).

chunks.title: The contracted provider's role
chunks.text: The contracted provider will: - organise Site Safe Certificate training for each ETFG worker - pay ETFG workers and supervisors - purchase and/or hire safety gear and equipment, including: boots gloves overalls hi-visibility vests helmets earmuffs protective eye wear chaps wet weather gear - boots - gloves - overalls - hi-visibility vests - helmets - earmuffs - protective eye wear - chaps - wet weather gear - oversee the day-to-day management of the work programme - transport workers to and from the areas of work. Relevant programme costs will be covered by an upfront lump sum payment, by way of a contract with the Ministry of Social Development.

chunks.title: ETFG workers
chunks.text: Each ETFG work crew will be accompanied by a supervisor. Crews will assist with clean-up activities, for example: - fence clearance and repair - tree and debris removal on: farms marae orchards parks reserves. - farms - marae - orchards - parks - reserves. ETFG crew workers are paid the living wage for a 40 hour week. ETFG supervisors are paid at a higher hourly rate.

chunks.title: Employment disputes
chunks.text: Anyone who expresses concerns regarding the conduct of ETFG workers should be directed to their relevant council for resolution as the council is the employer.

chunks.title: Establishment Grant
chunks.text: The Establishment Grant is a one-off payment to carers of someone else's child to help with the costs when a child first comes into their care, eg a bed, bedding and clothing. You'll automatically receive an Establishment Grant when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You'll automatically receive an Establishment Grant when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. The Establishment Grant is not available to carers who: - applied for the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit before 13 January 2014. However, you'll be able to apply every year for the School and Year Start-up Payment to help with costs that come at the beginning of the year such as pre-school or school-related costs. - received (or have been approved to receive) an upfront payment for the child as part of the Child, Youth and Family Home for Life support package. School and Year Start-up Payment A carer will only be paid the Establishment Grant once for the child. If the child leaves the person's care (resulting in the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit being stopped) and then returns after a period of time, the Establishment Grant won't be paid to that carer again.

chunks.title: How much you get
chunks.text: You'll receive a one-off payment of $350 for each child. You won't be taxed on this money and you won't have to pay it back.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You'll automatically get this payment when you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. You don't have to apply for it. If you're granted the Orphan's or Unsupported Child's Benefit for more than one child on or after the 13 January 2014, you'll automatically get the Establishment Grant for each child.

chunks.title: Ex gratia and compensation payments
chunks.text: Most ex gratia and compensation payments are not considered as income or cash assets. You'll need to let us know if you get one of these payments, so we can check if it will affect your payments from us.

chunks.title: About these payments
chunks.text: You may get an ex gratia payment if you've been harmed in some way. An ex gratia payment means there's no legal requirement to pay you or accept blame. Compensation payments are also made because of harm done, or to settle a claim of harm. They are sometimes ordered by a court or tribunal, but can also be made through a settlement outside court.

chunks.title: Lake Alice payments
chunks.text: This includes: - ex gratia or compensation payments for people who were patients at the Lake Alice Hospital - ex gratia payments as part of the redress package for survivors of the Lake Alice Child and Adolescent Unit.

chunks.title: When these payments count as income or a cash asset
chunks.text: An ex gratia or compensation payment may not count as income and/or a cash asset if it is paid for a case of harm. These payments are usually made by: - the Government - agencies who provide services on behalf of the Government, or - charities, incorporated societies, and faith-based institutions such as churches. It can be counted as income or a cash asset if it's paid for other things like: - a loss e.g. involving money, land, an asset or goods and services you've provided - a personal grievance at work. Some ex gratia and compensation payments may not count as income or a cash asset for the first 12 months after they're paid. Others, e.g. Lake Alice payments, may not be counted as income or a cash asset permanently. The amount of time a payment is not counted as income or a cash asset depends on who makes the payment to you and why.

chunks.title: When these payments count as income or a cash asset
chunks.text: It's best to talk to us so we can make sure your payments are right.

chunks.title: How your payments from us could be affected
chunks.text: You need to tell us about any ex gratia or compensation payment you get. If we decide that an ex gratia or compensation payment does count as income or a cash asset, it may affect your payments from us if: - you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - you save or invest the payment and earn interest or other income from it.

chunks.title: What we expect you to do when in emergency housing
chunks.text: When you’re staying in emergency housing, there are things we expect you to do.

chunks.title: We expect you to:
chunks.text: - understand the security deposit responsibilities and conditions of payment - understand and follow the supplier's rules and not do anything that will result in being asked to leave - understand what will happen if you cause or contribute to your emergency housing need - be responsible for your actions and those of your guests. For example, if you or one of your guests has damaged property, you'll need to pay for it - accept offers of housing if it meets the needs of you and your whānau, including temporary options like transitional housing - let us know if things change, including if: you leave your emergency housing your or your partner's income changes the make-up of your household changes (for example, if your relationship changes or the number of children in your care changes)

chunks.title: We expect you to:
chunks.text: - you leave your emergency housing - your or your partner's income changes - the make-up of your household changes (for example, if your relationship changes or the number of children in your care changes) - do all you need to do to meet any benefit obligations you may have, such as searching for or getting ready to work.

chunks.title: Your responsibilities after 7 nights
chunks.text: If you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights, there are also responsibilities you have to meet from the 8th night. Find out what these are and what happens if you don't meet them. Your responsibilities in emergency housing

chunks.title: Extending childcare when your child turns 5
chunks.text: If your child's going to a school where children start when they turn 5, but they can't start straight away, we may be able to pay for an extra 4 weeks of childcare.

chunks.title: Who can extend their childcare payments
chunks.text: There could be a number of reasons why your child can't start school straight away, eg, the school's closed because it's the middle of the school/Christmas holidays. Whatever your situation, we may be able to pay an extra 4 weeks of childcare if: - you're getting Childcare Subsidy - your child's going to a school where children start when they turn 5, instead of a cohort entry school (where new entrants start after they turn 5) - your child can't start school straight away - you continue to meet the criteria for Childcare Subsidy until your child starts school. Childcare Subsidy

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 and tell us why your childcare payments need to be extended.

chunks.title: Getting Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: If you get Child Disability Allowance for your child and they're not starting school yet, we may be able to keep paying your childcare until they start - up until they turn 6. Call us on 0800 559 009 to discuss your situation.

chunks.title: Extraordinary Care Fund
chunks.text: You can apply if a child you care for shows promise in a skill or talent, or because they are experiencing difficulties and need extra support. To qualify you need to get the Orphan’s Benefit or Unsupported Child’s Benefit. You can apply for one grant of up to $2,000 each year. If you're caring for more than one child, you can apply for each child.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: The Extraordinary Care Fund helps pay for extra costs you have because a child you care for: - shows promise in an ability, skill, or talent, for example in school, sports, dance, or music - is experiencing difficulties that impact their development, for example learning or behavioural difficulties You can apply if you get the Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. Grants are made based on your child's needs and the documents that support this, not your family’s financial situation.

chunks.title: Showing promise
chunks.text: Examples of costs we can help with: - Participating in a national Kapa Haka competition - Attending a science academic programme or event - Competing in a national sports competition - Coaching, tutoring or mentoring - Private music lessons and instrument hire or purchase

chunks.title: Experiencing difficulties
chunks.text: Examples include: - courses or activities to: develop self-esteem, physical capability, or social skills for example YMCA programmes improve their ability to learn if they have learning difficulties swimming lessons (if they haven't learnt to swim at school) - develop self-esteem, physical capability, or social skills for example YMCA programmes - improve their ability to learn if they have learning difficulties - swimming lessons (if they haven't learnt to swim at school) - orthodontic work that isn’t funded by the Ministry of Health - counselling You can apply for other costs we haven't mentioned here.

chunks.title: We can’t help to pay for:
chunks.text: - costs covered by an Establishment Grant or School and Year Start-up Payment - health and medical costs, for example: doctor's visits medication - doctor's visits - medication - everyday costs, for example: school trips vehicles (this includes any repairs, warrants, registration, and any fuel costs to and from events) legal costs childcare - school trips - vehicles (this includes any repairs, warrants, registration, and any fuel costs to and from events) - legal costs - childcare - overseas travel and related costs, for example: hotels overseas courses - hotels - overseas courses - teacher aides - school uniforms.

chunks.title: How much can you get
chunks.text: Between 1 July to 30 June each year you can get one grant of up to $2,000 for each child you care for. This table is a guide to how much we can help with: Cost type Technology: LaptopsTablets/iPads Secondary school level: up to $1,400 Intermediate school level: up to $1,200 Primary school level: up to $750 Primary school level to secondary school level all $600 Under 5 years: $600 by exception only You can apply for help with technology every two years unless there are exceptional circumstances. Counselling Psychological fees/services Development programmes e.g. Speech development, YMCA programmes Initial assessment $125 to $180 per hour. $45 to $130 per session

chunks.title: Step 1: Fill out an application form
chunks.text: Print and fill out the Extraordinary Care Fund Grant application form. If you can't print the form, call us and we'll post one to you. Phone us

chunks.title: Step 2: Gather your documents
chunks.text: You'll need to provide: - Proof of the cost you're applying for, for example: A quote The receipt A letter from an organiser asking for payment. - A quote - The receipt - A letter from an organiser asking for payment. - Letters of support. There may be other documents you need to provide if you're applying for help with technology, costs over $2000, orthodontic treatment, extra tuition or eyewear.

chunks.title: Letters of support
chunks.text: A letter of support explains how your child is showing promise or how they're experiencing difficulty. If you're applying for a cost that's: - under $500, you need one letter of support - $500 or more, you need 2 letters of support The letter needs to be from an independent person, for example: - A teacher - Coach - Other person of standing in the community

chunks.title: Technology
chunks.text: If you're applying for help with technology, you need to provide documents: - from the school with their recommended item, especially if they have a 'bring your own device' (BYOD) programme - for anything that's significantly more expensive than what the school recommends, your letter of support will need to outline why it's needed. You can apply for help with tablets/iPads/laptops every two years unless there are exceptional circumstances.

chunks.title: Applying for costs over $2,000
chunks.text: If you're applying for a cost that's more than $2,000, you need to confirm how you can pay for the rest of the cost.

chunks.title: Orthodontic treatment
chunks.text: If you're applying for help with orthodontic treatment, for example braces, you need to provide documents from the orthodontist with: - the proposed treatment - how long the treatment will take - confirmation of any payments made so far and the balance owing.

chunks.title: Progress report for extra tuition
chunks.text: If you're applying for extra tuition, you need to provide a progress report for your 2nd application, and any further applications after this. The report must detail how your child has progressed with their extra tuition over the previous 12 months.

chunks.title: Eyewear over $300
chunks.text: If you're applying for eyewear that costs more than $300, you need to provide documents from an optometrist which specify that the child needs specialised lenses or frames.

chunks.title: Step 3: Submit your application
chunks.text: You can get your completed form and documents to us by either: - dropping these into your nearest service centre - posting these to your nearest service centre. Find a service centre

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Our panel assesses each application. They meet 4 times a year, but you can apply at any time. We'll send you a letter telling you the outcome of your application. If you apply before: You will hear back from us after: 24 July 2026 By 16 September 2026 23 October 2026 By 16 December 2026 4 February 2027 By 24 March 2027 20 April 2027 By 23 June 2027

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you get the Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit, you can apply for the School and Year Start-up Payment. This payment helps you with the costs that are mostly at the start of the year. These costs are usually things children need for school or pre-school, like pre-school and school-related costs such as clothing, school fees and stationery. School and Year Start-up Payments

chunks.title: Family breakdown
chunks.text: If you're under 19 and have had a family breakdown, we may be able to help.

chunks.title: Who can get help
chunks.text: If you're under 19 and can't live with your parents or guardians, we may be able to help. You may be in one of these situations: - you've left the care of Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children, or an agency approved by Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children, eg, Iwi Social Services or Cultural Social Services - your relationship with your parents or guardians has broken down and they're not prepared to financially support you - your parents or guardians can't support you financially, eg: they've gone to prison they've moved overseas they're in hospital long term they've died. - they've gone to prison - they've moved overseas - they're in hospital long term - they've died.

chunks.title: Under 16
chunks.text: If you're under 16, your guardian should talk to us about what help is available. They can call us on 0800 559 009
If you're 16 or 17 and your relationship with your parents or guardians has broken down and they can't support you, you may be able to get a Youth Payment. Youth Payment

chunks.title: Teen parent
chunks.text: If you're a 16-19 year old parent, you may be able to get a Young Parent Payment. Young Parent Payment

chunks.title: Getting Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment
chunks.text: If you get Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, a Youth Service provider will work with you to: - get the correct financial support - ensure you're in either education training or work-based learning - manage your money well, including helping you with budgeting - make sure you are living somewhere reasonable and affordable - talk about other services you might need. Youth Serviceexternal
If you're 18 years or older, we may be able to help in a number of ways. Use "Check what you might get" to find out what help you could qualify for.

chunks.title: Call us
chunks.text: Call us if you're unsure of what you can get and you want to discuss your situation. Phone us

chunks.title: Housing when escaping family violence
chunks.text: If you need to leave home because of family violence, we may be able to help you find somewhere to go. If you're in immediate danger, dial 111 and ask for the Police.

chunks.title: Women's Refuge
chunks.text: If you’re a woman in a family violence situation, call the Women’s Refuge free Crisisline on 0800 733 843 (0800 REFUGE). There are many ways they can help, including a safe house if you need accommodation urgently. Their safe houses are in secret locations and you can come to them in a crisis, day or night. Women's Refugeexternal

chunks.title: Family violence information and services
chunks.text: The 'Are You Ok' website has information for people experiencing family violence: www.areyouok.org.nzexternal You can also call the 24/7 helpline on 0800 456 450. Trained counsellors can provide support and connect you with support services in your area.

chunks.text: If you have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 days, you may be able to apply for emergency housing. Emergency housing

chunks.title: FamilyBoost payment
chunks.text: If you get a FamilyBoost payment from Inland Revenue, it is not counted as income. If you keep it (or part of it) for 12 months or more, or get interest from the payment, you need to tell us.

chunks.title: About FamilyBoost
chunks.text: FamilyBoost is a childcare payment to help households pay for the cost of early childhood education (ECE). It's administered by Inland Revenue. FamilyBoost (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: How it affects your payments from us
chunks.text: You have to tell us if you: - keep the money you get (or part of it) for 12 months or more - this will be counted as a cash asset - get interest from the payment - the interest will be counted as income. If you're applying for a one-off hardship payment (e.g. food), we’ll consider FamilyBoost payments as part of your available resources.

chunks.title: Feeling anxious about work
chunks.text: Getting a job and going to work doesn't have to be hard. These services can make life easier and give you confidence. These support services are designed to help you mentally prepare yourself to get into work. They can help you with: - building your confidence - working through your worries - overcoming obstacles. All these services are free.

chunks.title: Te Heke Mai
chunks.text: An app to help when you're looking for work or starting training or a new job. Te Heke Mai offers: - a digital coach and real-life mentors - personalised support and feedback - quick and easy chats. It's open to anyone in New Zealand. Te Heke Maiexternal

chunks.title: Here Toitū
chunks.text: Get a dedicated support team working with you and your health provider. They'll help you set goals and plan how to reach them. You can get this if you: - get a main benefit (e.g. Supported Living Payment or Jobseeker Support), or - have a job but can't work right now due to a health condition, injury or disability. Your doctor must also be registered with either: - THINK Hauora in MidCentral - Pegasus Health in Christchurch - ProCare in Auckland - National Hauora Coalition in Auckland. To join Here Toitū, contact one of these health providers, or talk to your doctor.

chunks.title: Individual Placement and Support
chunks.text: You can get this if you get mental health support from Te Whatu Ora (Health New Zealand) in: - Auckland, - Counties Manukau, or - Waitematā. You'll get an employment consultant, who will work with you and your mental health support team. Together you'll make a plan to help you get a job. Contact your Mental Health Key Worker to apply for this.

chunks.title: E Ara E
chunks.text: A counselling and mental health service helping young Aucklanders with work or study. It's run by Odyssey Auckland. You can join if you're 18-24, getting a benefit, and live in Auckland region. Visit the E Ara E page on the Odyssey website or talk to a case manager. Work and study support for ages 18-24 (Odyssey)external

chunks.title: Take Charge
chunks.text: A counselling and mental health service for young people in Canterbury. You can get help to work or study, and manage your wellbeing. It's run by Odyssey House. You can join if you're 18-24, getting a benefit, and live in Canterbury. Visit the Take Charge page on the Odyssey House website, or talk to a case manager. Supporting youth mental health and employment (Odyssey)external
