chunks.title: Final work payments
chunks.text: We’ve found an error in the way we treated some payments people received at the end of their employment. This meant the start date of benefit payments was incorrect and we owe some people money.

chunks.title: Who's affected by this error
chunks.text: You may be affected if you: - received payments, such as holiday pay or pay in lieu of notice, at the end of your employment, and - your benefit was granted on or after 23 March 2020, but before 8 June 2020.

chunks.title: Check if you or someone else is owed money
chunks.text: We’re contacting and paying all our current clients affected by this error. If you used to get payments from us, you can use the ‘Payment errors enquiry’ form to check if you’re owed money. Our staff can’t tell you if you’re owed money or how much it is. You can also use the ‘Payment errors enquiry’ form to enquire for someone else if: - they’re not a current client with us - a person has died. The form will check if you (or the person you’re enquiring for) are owed money. It won’t say how much you’re owed, we’ll send you a letter to let you know this. Payment errors enquiry form external

chunks.title: Using the enquiry form overseas
chunks.text: At this stage the enquiry tool can only be assessed from Australia and New Zealand.

chunks.title: Checking payment errors for someone else
chunks.text: You can also use the payment errors enquiry form to check to see if we owe someone else money when: - they're not a current client - a person has died. Information to make an enquiry for someone else The form will tell you if the person you're making an enquiry for is on the list of clients who may be affected and you can apply for them. It won't say how much they may be owed.

chunks.title: How this payment affects your benefit or allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or allowance from us, it won't be affected for 12 months from when we pay you the money we owe. If you: - still have this money after 12 months, you'll need to tell us and it will be counted for any benefits or payments that are asset tested - invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months you'll need to tell us and this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Review rights
chunks.text: If you don't understand or agree with a decision we've made, please talk with us so we can explain it. You have the right to ask us to review a decision you think is wrong. You can use the application form on our website, or write to us. We need to get your request within three months. If you have a good reason why you can't ask us to review a decision within three months, get in touch. We may still be able to review the decision. You can find out more on the review of a decision page of our website, or you can give us a call on 0800 559 009. Get a decision reviewed

chunks.text: If you need to find a place to live, we may be able to help. You may be able to apply for public (social) housing or get some ideas on where to look for private housing. chunks.text: If you can't afford a private rental, you may be able to live in a public house where the Government pays part of the rent. These are houses that are rented out by Kāinga Ora (used to be Housing New Zealand) and other Community Housing Providers. You need to meet certain criteria to qualify for public housing. If you apply, you may have to wait for a while until a suitable property becomes available. - Who can get public housing Find out if you can get public housing.

chunks.title: Finding seasonal work
chunks.text: Seasonal jobs are available all year, in places like orchards, farms, forests, or tourist hotspots. Doing a seasonal job can help you: - learn new skills and get work experience - earn good money, sometimes more than $700 a week - be active and fit - meet new people - gain confidence. Seasonal jobs can last from a few weeks up to 6 months. You may be offered a permanent job, or you can use your new skills and experience for a similar job.

chunks.title: How much it pays
chunks.text: Employers rely on seasonal workers and will pay good money for a good worker. For example, if you worked 30 hours a week picking fruit or vegetables you could earn around $700 before tax a week, or more. Exactly how much depends on the employer and the job. Some jobs are paid by the hour and others by a contract rate, e.g. if you’re picking apples you might get a set amount for each bin you fill.

chunks.title: Finding seasonal work
chunks.text: Pick NZ specialises in seasonal jobs: Pick NZexternal

chunks.text: The work changes with the seasons, so the type of jobs needed and available change too. You can use this table to see what type of work is available, and when, so you can plan ahead. chunks.title: Fire or theft
chunks.text: If you need help replacing essential items after a fire or theft and can't pay for these any other way, we may be able to help. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You may have to pay the money back depending your situation.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: We may be able to help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - have urgent and necessary costs - have no other way to meet these costs - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Youth Servicesexternal Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We may be able to pay up to $1000 to help with costs such as: - whiteware (e.g., fridge, freezer, washing machine) - bed - couch.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. You may need to send us a police or fire report.

chunks.title: Fired for misconduct or left voluntarily
chunks.text: If you've been fired for misconduct or left your job without a good reason there may be a number of ways we can help you, but you won't be paid right away. It's important you contact us right away as you may need to wait up to 13 weeks before your payments start. It depends on why you've been fired or left your job. How payments work and when your payments start

chunks.title: Stopped working during a trial period of up to 90 days
chunks.text: If you've stopped working during, or at the end of, a trial period of up to 90 days, you may be able to apply for Jobseeker Support. You may have a shorter stand-down period if you're in this situation. Jobseeker Support Information about trial periodsexternal When you apply for Jobseeker Support, there may be some things you need to do before you can get it. The online application process

chunks.text: You're looking for full-time work and need help with day-to-day expenses. Jobseeker Support When you apply for Jobseeker Support, there may be some things you need to do before you can get it. The online application process

chunks.title: Ability to work affected because of a health condition or disability
chunks.text: You have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work. This means that you have to reduce your hours or stop work for a while. We may still be able to help if you have a job to go back to. You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner, eg, your doctor, to tell us how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work. Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: How Flexi-wage can help
chunks.text: There's a wage contribution to help employers pay wages, as well as training and ongoing support for employees if it's needed. Find out more below. - Employers

chunks.title: Flexi-wage – job seeker information
chunks.text: Flexi-wage is one of the ways we're supporting more New Zealanders into work, by helping you get the skills you need for the job, and supporting more employers to hire staff. Flexi-wage can support you if you need some extra help to get started and learn the skills you need for a job.

chunks.title: What's Flexi-wage
chunks.text: Flexi-wage can help you get the skills you need to meet the entry-level requirements for a job. You can get training and ongoing support if you need it, and your employer can get a wage contribution to help them pay your wages. The job must continue after the Flexi-wage has finished.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get Flexi-wage if you: - are likely to need a benefit for a long time if you don’t get this assistance, and - haven't worked for a long time, and - need training to meet the entry-level requirements for the job and/or - have difficulty getting or keeping a job. For example, you might have barriers to finding a job because you need education or training, or your current job may be at risk. Flexi-wage can help you get the skills you need to do a job, which might be with: - an employer who wants to hire you, or - an employer you're already working for who needs to move you into a different role that requires further training and more hours, rather than making you redundant.The employer also needs to meet the 'Who can get it' criteria outlined in Flexi-wage - employer information.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: Flexi-wage - employer information The job must: - pay at least the minimum wage - have the minimum number of hours to meet any work obligations Work obligations and be either: - ongoing, continuing after Flexi-wage has finished, or - a fixed-term project that benefits the community or environment and will help you gain the skills needed to get into work once it's finished.

chunks.title: What support you can get
chunks.text: Support from us can include: - a contribution to your wages - we'll pay this to your employer - training - ongoing support. We'll talk to your employer about what you need and how we can help.

chunks.title: How to find out more
chunks.text: If you're already talking to us about finding or getting ready for work, ask about Flexi-wage. Otherwise, call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment to talk about Flexi-wage and how we can help you into work. You’ll need a client number to book an appointment – if you don’t already have one, you can request a client number here. How to get a client number

chunks.title: Flexi-wage for self-employment
chunks.text: Flexi-wage is one of the ways we're supporting more New Zealanders into work. We may be able to help you start your own business and help with costs while you get started.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To get Flexi-wage self-employment there's basic criteria you and your intended business need to meet. Additional criteria will also apply - we can talk to you about this when you contact us to find out more about Flexi-wage self-employment.

chunks.title: Criteria your business needs to meet
chunks.text: You need: - to be in the early stages of developing a business and unable to be self-sufficient - an in-depth understanding of all aspects of your proposed business idea - a business plan – find out how to write this here: How to write a business plan (Business.govt.nz)external We must be satisfied your business idea is viable before we can consider any assistance.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet:
chunks.text: You need to be: - out of work, and - 18 years or older and not able to get NZ Super, and - having difficulty getting or keeping a job (for example you might have barriers to finding a job because you need training, or your current job may be at risk). You must also be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: - a New Zealand citizen, or - a resident with a residence class visa, or - recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet:
chunks.text: - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can't get it
chunks.text: You can't get Flexi-wage for self-employment if you're: - re-starting a business that you've owned before, or - already running an established business that is struggling financially, or - currently bankrupt.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can only get Flexi-Wage for self-employment if you meet the eligibility criteria and we are convinced your business idea is viable. To do this, we'll meet with you and get you to give us details of your business idea so we can assess it in detail.

chunks.title: Step 1: Appointment for initial eligibility
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment. At the appointment we will: - check if you and your business meet the eligibility criteria - discuss how your job search is going - talk about your business idea, your needs and what type of help we may be able to offer. We may ask if you have a business plan, and if you're already operating any other businesses.

chunks.title: Step 2: Give us details of your business
chunks.text: After your appointment you need to give details of your business idea. This includes details about: - your business plan - any relevant skills and experience - market research - marketing and competition - finance and operations - compliance and risk planning. We'll tell you how you can send this information to us. We may also ask for your findings and proof of research for these things.

chunks.title: Step 3: Appointment for business plan
chunks.text: If we're satisfied with the information you have provided, we'll book an appointment with you go through your business details and discuss your business idea in full. We'll also talk about developing your business plan, and whether a Business Training and Advice Grant could help.

chunks.title: Step 4: Assessing your business idea
chunks.text: To make sure your business idea is viable, we'll send your business plan to be independently assessed. If it's approved you'll be granted Flexi-Wage for self-employment. We'll then send you a contract, which you need to complete and email back to us with evidence of your bank account number.

chunks.title: If you get the subsidy
chunks.text: We'll: - contact you regularly to see how things are going - send you 4-weekly claim forms for the Flexi-wage subsidy over the period of the contract. We'll make sure you know how to make a claim every 4 weeks.

chunks.title: Mid-project financial report
chunks.text: You'll need to provide a mid-project financial report within the first 12-20 weeks. The report needs to outline things like: - productivity levels (for example, the amount of work or items manufactured) - actual cash flow - a comparison of performance against the original business plan - cash flow expectations for at least the next 6 months. We'll let you know when we need this and who to send it to. The report will be reviewed by an independent person, and we'll let you know the outcome of this review.

chunks.title: Business Training and Advice Grant
chunks.text: You may be able to get up to $5,000 to help you develop a business plan and/or train in business skills, advice and project reports. Business Training and Advice Grant

chunks.title: Self-Employment start up payment
chunks.text: You may also be able to get help with essential start-up costs, for example furniture or the first lot of stock. Self-Employment start up payment

chunks.title: Flexible Childcare Assistance
chunks.text: We may be able to help with the costs of informal childcare e.g. a babysitter, if you can't access formal childcare programmes while you're at work or in employment-related study or training.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get Flexible Childcare Assistance if you: - are the principal caregiver of a dependent child or young person - have informal childcare costs because you’re unable to access formal childcare - are in or starting an employment-related activity and need childcare because of this - likely to need a benefit for a long time if you don’t get this assistance, and - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident (you may be able to get this payment if you have a temporary entry class visa that allows you to work in New Zealand). Principal caregiver

chunks.title: Employment-related activity
chunks.text: You need to be participating in the employment-related activity for at least 3 hours a week, during times you need informal childcare. This can include: - paid employment - employment-related study, or - employment-related training. If you're working and won't be getting a main benefit, your job must be expected to last at least 13 weeks. Main benefit If you're in training or study, you must be doing a specific type of course, and it will depend on how long you’ll be taking part. If your course is: - 12 weeks or less, the course can be at any level and does not need to be NZQA certified - 13 weeks or more, the course must be Level 3 or below on the NZQA framework, which means it is certificate level study.

chunks.title: The child or young person
chunks.text: The child or young person must be: - 13 years or younger, or - 14 to 18 years but can’t safely be left home alone, e.g. because they need special help.

chunks.title: Income and asset limits
chunks.text: There is no income or asset limit for this payment.

chunks.title: Other parent or caregiver
chunks.text: You may not be able to get this payment if the child's other parent or caregiver can take care of them.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can get a weekly rate of: - $64.02 for one child - $32.01 for each additional child. The maximum amount you can get is $192.06 a week. You can get the payment for up to 52 weeks. The payment is to help pay for your informal childcare costs, e.g: - paying the person who’s caring for your child, which could be a: family member trusted friend neighbour child-minder - family member - trusted friend - neighbour - child-minder - food - activities - travel. You need to pay the person caring for the child or young person yourself.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment. In most cases, we’ll need you to come in for a face-to-face appointment. However, there may be times we’ll be able to support you over the phone. Find a service centre The information we need from you is listed in our pdf form. You can print and fill out the form yourself, or we can help you fill it in at your appointment. We’ll also need you to provide documents showing your: - employment details e.g. name of the company, your position, and start date - employment-related training details, or - employment-related education details. Types of documents we accept If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you need to bring your original government-issued ID into a service centre so we can check it.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Verify your identity at a service centre

chunks.title: Organising childcare
chunks.text: You’re responsible for choosing and organising appropriate care for your children. When you’re looking at options for childcare, there are a number of things you may like to consider or do, so that you know your children will be safe and well cared for. These could include: - asking the person for references, then contacting their referees and talking to them - asking to see a copy of the person’s criminal record they can get this from the Ministry of Justice - they can get this from the Ministry of Justice - thinking about the environment where your children will be cared for, e.g: fencing for pools and balconies who else will be there safety around animals - fencing for pools and balconies - who else will be there

chunks.title: Organising childcare
chunks.text: - safety around animals - checking if the child will be travelling in the person’s car, e.g: do they have a driver licence is the vehicle safe do they need car seats - do they have a driver licence - is the vehicle safe - do they need car seats - talking to the person about how you want your child looked after, e.g: types of food and activities behaviour expectations special needs or medication they need to be aware of. - types of food and activities - behaviour expectations - special needs or medication they need to be aware of. You can leave a child under 14 at home or in another place if you’ve made reasonable provisions to have them supervised and cared for safely, and they’re not left for a long time.

chunks.title: Reviews and changes
chunks.text: You must also tell us straight away about any changes in your circumstances that could affect your payments, e.g. if your child leaves your care. Phone us

chunks.title: Paying for formal childcare
chunks.text: If you get Flexible Childcare Assistance, you can still apply for OSCAR or Childcare subsidy to help with childcare costs during the times you're able to access formal childcare programmes. OSCAR or Childcare subsidy

chunks.title: Food
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay for food if you’re on a low income or a benefit. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You could find yourself in a situation where you've had to pay for an essential cost that means you don’t have enough money to pay for food. Maybe you’ve paid for: - doctors visits - dental treatment - clothing for a job interview - school clothes or materials for your child. You may also find that you have less income this week because: - you’ve been off work due to sickness but you’re not eligible for sick pay - your hours are reduced unexpectedly. Whatever your situation, we may be able to help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) Youth Servicesexternal - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: - have an urgent and immediate need to buy food - have no other way to pay for food (e.g., no money in the bank and no other cash assets). Definition of cash assets It also depends on how much you and your partner if you have one) earn. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income limits usually apply:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation. You can only use the money for food and essential grocery items, e.g., toiletries. You can’t buy other things, e.g., alcohol, cigarettes, gift cards, vouchers, etc.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: If you are a current client, you may be able to apply using MyMSD. If you are a new client or unable to use MyMSD, you’ll need to call us. We’ll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help, and let you know if you need to do anything else. Phone us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we’ll give you a payment card (if you don’t already have one) and load the money onto it. We’ll talk to you about how we'll get this card to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires. A payment card is like an Eftpos card and you can use it at any supermarket or store that accepts them. Find out where payment cards are acceptedexternal You can also login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Once you've used your payment card, keep it. You can use it again if you need help from us in the future.

chunks.title: Fraud and investigations
chunks.text: Information about fraud, how to avoid it, our fraud investigations and your rights. Fraud is where you have intentionally misled us to receive money you are not entitled to. It's not fraud if you have received money from us that you were not entitled to, but did not intentionally mislead us.

chunks.title: Talk to us
chunks.text: You need to tell us everything about your situation so we can work out the correct amount you're entitled to. It's important to tell us about changes that affect your entitlement. If you don't, you could find yourself in the situation of being investigated for fraud. Don't take the risk. Call us if there's anything you'd like to know more about. We're always happy to answer your questions and there is no need to identify who you are. You can call us free on 0800 559 009 or if you are a student call 0800 889 900 Your obligations while getting payments from us

chunks.title: How we find fraud
chunks.text: We find benefit fraud in lots of different ways, including: - through members of the public - sharing information with other government agencies - our own internal sources, and - regular entitlement reviews. Sharing your information Report a suspected fraud

chunks.title: How we investigate fraud
chunks.text: If we have information that suggests you may be involved in benefit or housing fraud, our investigators need to gather evidence. Evidence helps us determine if you: - received money you weren't entitled to, and - misled us to receive it. Our investigators will talk to you as well as other people. They'll decide on a case-by-case basis whether to talk to you first or go to a third party. They will also make sure the right amount of information is collected.

chunks.title: We will talk to you in most cases
chunks.text: In most cases our investigators will contact you first to request more information about your situation and talk to you about our concerns. If they want to talk to you about your entitlement or an investigation, they'll meet you at a time that suits you. You can choose whether or not you want to be interviewed. You can also get legal advice if you want to. You may wish to seek advice about this from an advocate or legal representative. If you want legal advice and don’t already have a lawyer, you can contact: - your local Community Law Centre, or - Citizens Advice Bureau. Community Lawexternal Citizens Advice Bureauexternal If you choose to be interviewed, they'll give you an opportunity to tell us:

chunks.title: We will talk to you in most cases
chunks.text: - your side of the story, and - about any changes in your circumstances. They'll also go through the information we have and there'll be opportunities for you to ask questions. If you need to, they can make a further appointment to discuss your entitlement in more detail. You can bring a support person or advocate with you to the interview. For example, you could bring a lawyer, family member, friend, an interpreter or benefit advocate. Please tell us if you want an interpreter and we can arrange one for you. Having someone act on your behalf What you say in an interview can be used as evidence in a criminal prosecution. Because of this, you have rights which we'll remind you of at the interview. - You don't have to answer all our questions and you can stop the interview at any time

chunks.title: We will talk to you in most cases
chunks.text: - You can leave the interview at any time - You can speak with a lawyer or support person at any time in private.

chunks.title: We may talk to a third party
chunks.text: Our investigators may request information from others before they talk with you. This can include: - financial institutions - employers - property managers, and - other government agencies. They may also contact other organisations or talk to people in the community. When we have to approach others for information directly, we can use powers under the Social Security Act 2018 and the Public and Community Housing Management Act 1992. These powers to collect information are controlled by Codes of Conduct with rules about what information we can request and the process we must follow. Read the Codes of Conductexternal We'll only gather information that is relevant and necessary for our investigation.

chunks.title: We may use publicly available information
chunks.text: We may also access information that's publicly available, including: - newspapers and media - using internet search engines - looking up public lists and registers, and - social media (we won't interact with you or private groups you're part of). We have a policy that allows us to use publicly available information for this purpose.

chunks.title: How to make a complaint about the investigation
chunks.text: If you believe we have collected information we weren't entitled to, or breached the Codes of Conduct, you can email our privacy team. They will look into your complaint and be in touch with you as soon as they can. Email the Privacy Team

chunks.title: Complaint to Privacy Commissioner
chunks.text: If you're not happy with our response, you can also make a complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner. Make a complaint to the Office of the Privacy Commissionerexternal

chunks.title: Formal review
chunks.text: If you believe there was a breach of your privacy that affected a decision we made on your entitlements, you can ask for a formal review. You can use the review of decision form on our website or you can write to us. You need to do this within 3 months. If it’s after that, please get in touch anyway. If you have a good reason why you couldn’t ask us earlier, we may still be able to review the decision for you. Visit our 'Review of decision' page for more information. Review of a decision

chunks.title: Legal advice
chunks.text: You may wish to seek advice about this from an advocate or legal representative. If you want legal advice and don’t already have a lawyer, you can contact: - your local Community Law Centre, or - Citizens Advice Bureau. Community Lawexternal Citizens Advice Bureauexternal

chunks.title: Accessing information about the investigation
chunks.text: To protect your privacy, only authorised people can access detailed information about our benefit and housing fraud investigations. This includes only a few MSD people who need it for their work. Case managers, contact centres and most other people working at MSD don’t have access to this level of detail. However they may be able to see some information, such as letters we’ve sent to you. If you want a copy of your records that we hold, you can ask us for this. Request a copy of your recordsexternal If you have any questions about the information in your file, or want to correct something, we can work with you to do this.

chunks.title: If you were investigated before 2018
chunks.text: If you were investigated before 2018 and want to know more about the information gathered about you, email privacyofficer@msd.govt.nz. We'll get back to you as soon as we can.

chunks.title: What happens if you're found to have committed fraud
chunks.text: Fraud is taken very seriously and can have severe consequences, e.g. you may: - be restricted from using our phone and online channels - have a decrease in the amount you get from us - have to pay back any money you weren’t entitled to - face criminal prosecution – this can mean a fine or being sentenced to community service, home detention or imprisonment (on top of having to pay back any money you owe us). A conviction for fraud is very serious and can affect your: - job or future job prospects - ability to travel overseas, and - ability to get a loan, credit or insurance.

chunks.title: Privacy Commissioner's 2019 inquiry
chunks.text: From 2012 until 2018, for the most serious fraud allegations, we went to third parties for information without going to the client first. In 2019, an Office of the Privacy Commissioner inquiry found we had been acting inconsistently with our legal obligations for some fraud investigations.

chunks.title: We accepted this finding
chunks.text: We accepted all 5 recommendations made by the Privacy Commissioner and made changes to the way we do investigations. We also undertook an independent review of our fraud investigation practices and policies and made more improvements in line with that. Our investigators now decide on a case-by-case basis whether to go first to the client, or third party, and to make sure the right amount of information is collected. MSD accepts Privacy Commissioner's recommendations (Ministry of Social Development)external

chunks.title: If you were investigated before 2018
chunks.text: If you were investigated before 2018 and want to know more about the information gathered about you, email privacyofficer@msd.govt.nz We'll get back to you as soon as we can.

chunks.title: Funeral Grant
chunks.text: A Funeral Grant can help with some of the funeral costs of someone who has died. A Funeral Grant can only be used towards reasonable funeral expenses. Some examples of reasonable funeral expenses are: - any professional services fees charged by a funeral director - the cost of a casket - death certificate - newspaper notice costs - hearse fees - burial costs (including plot and interment) - cremation fees - venue hire - food and catering including kai for a tangihanga - flowers - celebrant, minister or clergy fees - a slideshow or photo tribute. You do not have to pay back a Funeral Grant if all the criteria are met (under 'Who can get it'). If we can't confirm income or asset amounts when you apply, we may still pay a Funeral Grant and confirm the amounts later. If the income or asset criteria is not met later, you will have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Funeral Grant if the person who's died is: - your partner - your parent or guardian - your child (if they're under 18), or - someone over 18 and single (with or without children) who you're arranging a funeral for. In all cases, the person who died must have normally lived in New Zealand. If the person who's died is your partner or child, it will also depend on your income. We'll also make sure the reasonable funeral expenses cannot be met by: - the assets of the deceased person, and - your assets, if the person who died was your partner or child.

chunks.title: Income limits
chunks.text: If the person who's died is your partner or child, your income needs to be under a certain limit. Definition of Income (MAP)external

chunks.title: When you can't get a Funeral Grant
chunks.text: If there's other help with costs available to you, you may not be able to get a Funeral Grant. Other help could be that funeral costs are covered by: - another organisation, e.g. ACC or Veteran's Affairs - prepaid funeral cover. ACCexternal Veteran's Affairsexternal

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: The most you can be paid is $2,697.43.

chunks.title: If the person who died is not your partner or child
chunks.text: If the person who died has assets, we'll count the total amount of their assets. We'll then deduct this from the total funeral expenses. We'll then pay the lesser amount of either the: - maximum Funeral Grant, or - balance of the reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: What's counted as assets
chunks.text: Find out what's counted as assets (Manuals and Procedures)external If we've kept their payments going for 28 days, this is also counted as an asset. Payments when a client dies

chunks.title: If the person who died is your partner or child
chunks.text: We'll count: - some of your assets (we won't count the first $2,351.46 of your assets), and - the total amount of the deceased person's assets. We'll deduct the total amount of assets from the total amount of reasonable funeral expenses. We'll then pay the lesser amount of either the: - maximum Funeral Grant, or - balance of the reasonable funeral expenses.

chunks.title: What's counted as assets
chunks.text: Find out what's counted as assets (Manuals and Procedures)external If we've kept their payments going for 28 days, this is also counted as an asset. Payments when a client dies

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: The person applying for a Funeral Grant must be able to provide estate details or other information about the person who has died (including details about any children they are responsible for).

chunks.title: Step 1: Complete the form
chunks.text: You need to complete an application form to apply for a Funeral Grant.

chunks.title: Step 2: Gather your documents
chunks.text: You will need to provide: - confirmation of death (if you don’t have this, please tell us as we may be able to get this information), for example: a death certificate (you can order this online here) funeral director confirmation, or a newspaper death notice. - a death certificate (you can order this online here) - funeral director confirmation, or - a newspaper death notice. - details of the funeral expenses: the itemised funeral account, and if it's already paid, the original receipt and proof of a bank account number for the person who paid it. - the itemised funeral account, and - if it's already paid, the original receipt and proof of a bank account number for the person who paid it. - proof of who you are, for example your: driver's licence passport, or business card if you're applying on behalf of a funeral home.

chunks.title: Step 2: Gather your documents
chunks.text: - driver's licence - passport, or - business card if you're applying on behalf of a funeral home. Order certificates (NZ Government)external You may also need to provide details about assets and income.

chunks.title: Step 3: Send in your documents
chunks.text: Drop the completed form and your documents off at one of our service centres, or you can post it in to us. Find your nearest service centre

chunks.title: Getting a payment card
chunks.text: Payment cards are used to buy one-off costs, for example food, groceries, glasses or dental treatment. Find out how we can help with these costs, how to apply and how to get a payment card. You must have set a personalised PIN on your payment card before you can use it. Setting your PIN If you're a young person in Youth Service getting payments, there are a few differences in getting and using your payment card. Find out more on the Youth Service website: Payments (Youth Service)external

chunks.title: How to apply for help with a cost
chunks.text: If you need help with an urgent, unexpected or one-off essential cost, you can find out how we can help here: Urgent or unexpected costs Help with living expenses The links above will also tell you how to apply for these costs. If your application is approved, we'll check how we can pay this. Some costs will not need a payment card – we'll let you know if this is the case. If we need to put this onto a payment card for you, we'll check if you already have a card. If you don't, you'll need to pick up a card from your local service centre - see below to find out how to do this.

chunks.title: Step 1:
chunks.text: Once your application is approved, pick up a payment card from any of our service centres. There's a list of their locations here: Find a service centre

chunks.title: Step 2:
chunks.text: Go to reception and ask for a payment card. You need to have: - your client number - a government issued identity document (for example a driver licence, birth certificate, or passport). You don't need an appointment for this.

chunks.title: Step 3:
chunks.text: Our staff will finish your application and load the money onto your card. They will tell you: - how much money is on the card - you can also check this online in MyMSDexternal - which shops you can use it at - what you can buy with it - how long the money will stay on the card for.

chunks.title: Step 4:
chunks.text: You need to set a PIN on your card before you can use it. The easiest way is to do it online: - Log in to MyMSDexternal. - Go to 'My payment cards'. - Select the card you want to add a PIN for. - Enter a 4-digit PIN - don't use a PIN that is consecutive, easily associated with you (like birthdays), or the numbers on your card. - Re-enter your PIN to confirm. - Done! Your PIN is now ready to go. Other ways to set your PIN: - call us and say "set my card PIN" - register your voice so you can set your PIN by calling us at any time without waiting to talk to a person - our staff in our service centres can help set your PIN in MyMSD - we have other ways you can contact us if you're deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment.

chunks.title: Step 5:
chunks.text: Sign the back of your card. When you use the card you will need to sign your receipt, and the shop staff will check this matches the signature on your card. Keep your payment card in a safe place. If you need further payments, we can load them onto this card, so you don't need to go to a service centre to get another one.

chunks.title: Getting a Notice of Credit letter instead of a payment card
chunks.text: There are times when we need to give you a Notice of Credit letter instead of a payment card. This can happen when: - the EFTPOS network or our internal systems are down - there's a state of emergency or natural disaster - you're unable to use a payment card. When you call us to apply, we'll talk about whether you need this letter.

chunks.title: Getting a Support Person or Job Coach
chunks.text: Job and Training Support Funds can help you pay for a support person or job coach. Find out how you can get someone to help you at work or training. Before you get a support person or job coach, you need to have an assessment done. This will identify the level of support you need. You can request this assessment when you apply for Job or Training Support Funds. You can also email us at support_funds@msd.govt.nz or call us on 0800 551 001.

chunks.title: Choosing a support person or job coach
chunks.text: It's your choice who you would like to be your support person or job coach. They can be someone you know, or a person found through an agency. When you hire a job coach you should talk to your employer before making your choice. This will help you find someone suitable to help with your job. Once you have chosen someone you should discuss with them: - the tasks they will do - their hours and pay rate - signing an agreement between you as confirmation. It's up to you to manage your relationship with your support person or job coach. This includes making sure the support you get meets your needs.

chunks.title: What a support person does
chunks.text: A support person is someone you who will help you at work or during training. This could include a: - reader/writer - New Zealand Sign-language interpreter - driver. You may be able to get funding for more than one support person if they're doing different tasks, e.g. a driver and a New Zealand Sign-language interpreter. You can't get funding for 100% of your working hours. If your support person is driving you, they must have a full New Zealand drivers licence. Your employer or training provider may be a Contracted Supported Employment provider with us. If they are, they may already provide some of the support you would get from a support person. When you apply we'll work with you to understand if you need any extra support on top of this, and if we can cover it.

chunks.title: What a job coach does
chunks.text: A job coach is someone who gives you short-term coaching to help you if: - you start a new job - your job description changes - your job requires new or different skills - your disability changes, which affects your ability to do your normal job. You can get help to pay for a job coach for up to 6 weeks. You can't get help to pay for a job coach if: - your employer already provides employment coaching for you - you're getting help to pay for training through Skills for Industry. When you apply you'll need to tell us how many hours you'll need the job coach for, and what tasks they'll need to do.

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: You must record and send us the information we need to make sure your support person or job coach gets paid. This information includes: - a supplier registration form - timesheets and invoices. This must be done by you and your support person or job coach.

chunks.title: Supplier registration
chunks.text: Your support person or job coach needs to register as a supplier with us. To do this they must print and fill in a Retailer/Supplier/Payee Details PDF form: Once they've completed the form, they need to scan or take a photo of it and email this to support_funds@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: Timesheets and invoices
chunks.text: Your support person or job coach must give you a timesheet and invoice every 2 weeks. This shows the hours they have worked. Make sure the invoice is not more than the number of hours we have agreed to fund. You both need to agree to and sign the timesheet. Email the signed timesheet and your invoice to us at support_funds@msd.govt.nz. We will use these to pay the support person or job coach their approved hours on your behalf. There's more information about invoices on Inland Revenue's website: How taxable supply information for GST work (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Other things you need to do
chunks.text: You and your support person or job coach also need to take care of your other obligations. These includes things like income tax, GST, ACC levies and other legal matters.

chunks.title: Gifts - one-off
chunks.text: We don't treat one-off gifts as income but if you earn interest, dividends or rent from the gift, you will need to tell us about it. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about the gift.

chunks.title: What is this?
chunks.text: A one-off gift of cash, rental property or personal property won't affect your benefit.

chunks.title: Example
chunks.text: You get some cash and vouchers for your birthday. You usually don't need to tell us about them.

chunks.title: How it affects your benefit and allowances
chunks.text: You have to tell us about this payment if you: - get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - invest the money you get and earn interest, dividends or rent, this will be counted as income. You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Gifts that provide a regular income
chunks.text: If you get regular payments from money or assets you've received as a gift you need to let us know. The amount you get will affect your benefit. If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back.

chunks.title: Payment details
chunks.text: A one-off gift of cash, rental property or personal property won't affect your benefit. But if you get regular gifts of cash, goods or services then we'll treat this as income and your benefit will be affected.

chunks.title: Example
chunks.text: You are given $100 a week by a family member to help out with food and bills. As this is a regular payment you need to tell us about it. If you hold onto the cash gift and you are getting extra help from us, this may be affected. Extra help includes: - Accommodation Supplement - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit. If you invest the money and earn interest, this will be counted as income and you have to tell us about it.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to contact us Phone us

chunks.title: How your benefit will be affected
chunks.text: You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Glasses
chunks.text: If you're on a low income or benefit we may be able to help you with the cost of eye tests and glasses. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You'll have to pay the money back. - You don't have to get a quote before you see us.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We can pay $280 for: - an eye test - lenses, including: single vision bifocals, or standard progressives - single vision - bifocals, or - standard progressives - frames - prescription sunglasses, if they're part of an in-store special that includes glasses and sunglasses for under $280 - a fitting service - repairs - a cleaning cloth and case - a 2 year warranty on defective parts. You'll have to pay this money back.

chunks.title: What's not included
chunks.text: We don't pay for: - high end, expensive frames - extras you may want, eg tinting - lens coatings or glasses specifically for Irlen Syndrome. You also can't 'top up' or 'up-grade' with your own money so you can obtain costlier items or extras.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us. Phone us We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Choose a supplier
chunks.text: We'll ask you what supplier you want to use. We have an arrangement with certain optometrists and opticians to provide optical services. Here's a list of our preferred suppliers for glasses in your area. You can choose which one to go to. Preferred suppliers for glasses If there's no preferred supplier in your area, we may still be able to help. Talk to us about your situation.

chunks.title: Step 1 - We'll give you a payment card
chunks.text: If your application's approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about the best way to get this to you. You'll pay the supplier with your payment card (much like an Eftpos card). You have 21 days to spend the money before it expires.

chunks.title: Step 2 - Book an appointment with the supplier
chunks.text: You need to book an appointment with the optometrist or optician that you've chosen. Take your payment card to the appointment. They'll give you an eye examination and then advise you what you'll need. Use your payment card to pay for the frames you choose.

chunks.title: Assessed as having high clinical needs
chunks.text: We may be able to pay more than $280 if the optometrist or optician assesses you as having high clinical needs. If this happens, you need to get evidence of the amount you need to pay and call us. Phone us

chunks.title: Repairs
chunks.text: Your glasses are covered by a 2 year warranty. If they're faulty, contact the optometrist or optician and they will exchange or repair them. If you break your glasses, the optometrist or optician won't replace them or refund money to you. If you need another pair of glasses you'll need to apply for hardship assistance again.

chunks.text: The following pages list the preferred suppliers for glasses in each region. Use them to find a supplier near you. chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Greece
chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Greece to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Greek payments (paid by the Greek Social Security Institute). NZ payments covered by this agreement are: - New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) - Veteran's Pension - Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability - Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers - Orphan's Benefit - Funeral Grant. Greek payments covered by this agreement are: - Old Age Benefit - Invalidity Benefit - Survivors Benefit - Funeral Grants. It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment
chunks.text: If you're under 20 and in full-time education, training or work-based learning, you may be able to get the Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment (GCAP) to assist with the cost of childcare.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get GCAP if you're: - getting a Young Parent Payment (or 16–19 and included as a partner of a specified beneficiary) Specified beneficiary - in full-time education, training or work-based learning - the main caregiver for a child aged either: under 5, or over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. - under 5, or - over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday. Or, if you're not on a benefit, and: - under 18 - attending secondary school full-time - the main caregiver for a child aged either: under 5, or over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: - under 5, or - over 5 if the school has advised they can't start until the beginning of the term straight after their fifth birthday - either living with, and supported by your parents or guardian, or married or in a civil union or de facto relationship. If you have a partner, in order to receive GCAP there needs to be a good reason why your partner can’t provide childcare. For example, your partner is studying, working or actively seeking work.

chunks.title: Approved programmes
chunks.text: Approved programmes include licensed early childhood education and care services, eg: - kindergartens and preschools - childcare centres and creches - playcentres and playgroups - Kohanga Reo, Punanga Reo, Aoga and other programmes with a language and culture focus - approved home-based care.

chunks.title: Check if you can get GCAP
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Guaranteed Childcare Assistance Payment and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: GCAP covers the actual childcare service costs, up to $6.38 an hour and up to 50 hours a week for each child and can be paid for the hours you're: - in full-time education, training or work-based learning (including travel time) - working part-time (for up to 15 hours a week) - meeting your youth activity obligations, if you have them (eg attending a parenting course). Young Parent Payment activity obligationsexternal GCAP is usually paid straight to the early childhood centre or service. You can't get both GCAP and the Childcare Subsidy for the same child. GCAP can't be paid for an informal carer. If you need help with the costs of informal childcare, check to see if you can get Flexible Childcare Assistance:

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Flexible Childcare Assistance

chunks.title: 20 Hours Early Childhood Education
chunks.text: You can only get GCAP for the same hours you're getting 20 Hours Early Childhood Education (ECE) if: - your child is at a home-based educator, and - the home-based educator is charging a top up payment for the same hours as 20 Hours ECE. Home-based educators may charge you a top up payment to cover the difference between their normal hourly rate and the 20 Hours ECE. 20 Hours ECE - Ministry of Educationexternal

chunks.title: Optional charges and donations
chunks.text: You can’t get GCAP for optional charges and donations requested by your childcare provider.

chunks.title: Term breaks (including Christmas holidays)
chunks.text: If you are still eligible for GCAP after a term break, it can be paid to ensure your child retains their place at the childcare centre.

chunks.title: Absences
chunks.text: GCAP will continue to be paid (if an absence fee is charged) if you or your child is temporarily sick or away.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: How you apply depends on what payments you’re already getting from us. If you need help, talk to your Youth Service provider if you have one, or contact us. Find a Youth Service providerexternal Contact us We can grant you the financial assistance you’re entitled to from the date you first contact us if you complete your application within 20 working days of that date.

chunks.title: You’re not getting any payments from us
chunks.text: If you're not getting any payments from us, you can either: - apply online through MyMSD, or - fill out a paper application form.

chunks.title: Apply online
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us based on the answers you give in your application. Apply online

chunks.title: Fill out paper application form
chunks.text: If you can’t print out the form we can send one to you, or you can complete it when you come in to see us. You can get your application form and supporting documents to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). Find a service centre Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Already getting payments from us
chunks.text: If you're already getting payments from us, eg, Young Parent Payment, you can complete a paper application form. If you can’t print out the form we can send one to you, or you can complete it when you come in to see us. You can get your application form and supporting documents to us by either: - dropping them in to your nearest service centre - posting them to your nearest service centre, or - uploading them to MyMSD (you'll need to call us first). chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Guernsey to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Guernsey payments (paid by the Guernsey Social Security Department). NZ payments covered by this agreement are: - New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) - Veteran's Pension - Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability - Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers. Guernsey payments covered by this agreement are: - Old Age Pension - Sickness Benefit - Bereavement Allowance (formerly Widow's Benefit) - Industrial Injury Benefit - Industrial Disablement Benefit - Invalidity Benefit. It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Having another child
chunks.text: If you have another child or another child comes into your care, you must tell us as soon as possible as it could affect how much we pay for your childcare

chunks.title: If you're getting childcare only
chunks.text: You need to send the original or certified true copy of your child's birth certificate to your local service centre, or drop it off at one of our service centres. This will be returned to you once we've scanned and saved it to your record. Documents to provide when you apply Find a service centre

chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 to tell us if you've had another child, or a child has come into your care. We may book you an appointment to come in and see us. If we book you an appointment, we'll let you know what you need to bring.

chunks.title: Unsure of what payments you're getting?

chunks.title: Having a baby
chunks.text: We may be able to help during your pregnancy and after your baby is born.

chunks.title: Pregnant
chunks.text: Go online with SmartStart and get step-by-step information and support to help you access the right services for you and your baby. SmartStartexternal If you're pregnant, it's important that you get a midwife and access maternity services. Talk to your doctor, or the local hospital maternity services, to find out what's available in your area.

chunks.title: Getting a benefit
chunks.text: If you're pregnant and getting a benefit, you may have a change in obligations. Having a baby while you're on a benefit

chunks.title: Unable to work
chunks.text: You may be able to get Jobseeker Support if your health practitioner (eg, your midwife or doctor) says you're unable to work because of your pregnancy. You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner. Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Getting a benefit
chunks.text: Having a baby while you're on a benefit If you're having a baby and getting a benefit, you may have a change in obligations or your payments could be affected. There are also other types of support that you may be able to get.

chunks.title: Working for families
chunks.text: Best Start tax credit (BSTC) is a payment to help families with costs in a child's first 3 years. If you're getting a Work and Income benefit, we'll pay you the Best Start tax credit with your payments. You'll need to apply through Inland Revenue (IR) if you don't get a benefit from Work and Income. It is also available to caregivers getting either: - Orphan's Benefit - Unsupported Child's Benefit, or - Foster Care Allowance. Eligibility and how to apply for the Best Start tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: Paid parental leave
chunks.text: If you're getting paid parental leave, you can't get the Best Start tax credit until your paid parental leave ends.

chunks.title: Helping with living costs
chunks.text: Help with living expenses If you're struggling financially or have had an unexpected bill, we might be able to help you, even if you're working.

chunks.title: Help with costs for the baby
chunks.text: We may be able to help with costs for the baby if it's an essential or emergency cost you can't pay for another way, eg: - car seats - cots - buggies - clothes. Advance Payment of Benefit If you're getting a benefit, we may be able to help with an advance payment. Recoverable Assistance Payment If you're not getting a benefit, we may be able to help with a recoverable payment.

chunks.title: Breast pumps
chunks.text: Special Needs Grant Help with a breast pump if you can't breastfeed because you or your baby have health issues. Finding or starting work – help with costs Help with a breast pump if you can't breastfeed because you're returning to work. Disability Allowance Help with a breast pump if you or your baby have an ongoing disability.

chunks.title: Childcare
chunks.text: Childcare We may be able to help with childcare costs, depending on your circumstances.

chunks.title: Sole parent support
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support You might be able to get Sole Parent Support, a payment that will help you get ready for future work and supports you to find part or full-time work.

chunks.title: Teen parent
chunks.text: Young Parent Payment If you're 16-19, you might be able to get a Young Parent Payment from us.

chunks.title: Multiple birth - Need help
chunks.text: Home Help We may be able to help you with the cost of home help when you've had a multiple birth.

chunks.title: Your baby is sick and needs ongoing medical care

chunks.title: Having a baby while you're on a benefit
chunks.text: If you're having a baby while you're on a benefit, you need to let us know as it could affect your payments and whether you need to look for work.

chunks.title: Unable to work
chunks.text: You may be getting a benefit that requires you to look for work. If your health practitioner, eg, your doctor or midwife, says you're unable to work because of your pregnancy, we may be able to help. We'll need to see a medical certificate from your health practitioner. Some health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate. If they don't send your medical certificate electronically, or you want to send something else as proof, call us to talk about how to get this information to us. Phone us

chunks.title: 27 weeks pregnant
chunks.text: You may be getting a benefit that requires you to look for work. You don't have to meet this requirement if you're at least 27 weeks pregnant. We'll need to see proof of your child's expected date of birth (eg. a medical certificate). Your health practitioner or midwife can complete a medical certificate for you. Most health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate. If they don't send your medical certificate electronically, or you want to send something else as proof, call us to talk about how to get this information to us. Phone us

chunks.title: Tell us once you have the baby
chunks.text: If you've had a baby you need to tell us right away. You may also need to apply for child support. We'll talk to you about this when you come to see us. To tell us you can either: - Register the birth with SmartStartwhen you register your child's birth with Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), using SmartStart, agree to share this information with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD). You won't have to purchase a physical birth certificate. SmartStartexternal We'll then: - work out if the change affects what you're getting from us - send you a letter to let you know the outcome. If you need to do anything else, we'll book a phone appointment for you and include the details in your letter. or - Call us to book an appointmentYou need to call us on 0800 559 009. We'll let you know what information we'll need from you.

chunks.title: Having another child and your work obligations
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit which requires you to look or prepare for work and you have a child, you will be expected to prepare for work until your youngest child turns 3 years old. If your youngest child is: - between 3 and 13, you'll be expected to actively seek part-time work of at least 20 hours a week and accept any suitable job - 14 or older, you'll be expected to actively seek full-time work of at least 30 hours a week and accept any suitable job.

chunks.title: Helping you get back into work
chunks.text: We can help you access training and a range of other support to help you get ready to move into work. You may be able to get assistance with the cost of childcare while you're working, attending training or doing some other activity that will help you move into work. The Childcare Subsidy is for preschool children and the Out of School Care and Recreation (OSCAR) Subsidy is for before and after school care and holiday programmes for children aged 5-13. For more information, read: Childcare Work This information is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Phone us

chunks.title: Having someone act on your behalf
chunks.text: You can choose to have someone else act on your behalf in your dealings with us. We call them an agent. You may be able to verbally agree to have an agent for one meeting, or you can fill out a form to have an agent for longer. In most cases, we'll only let someone represent you if you agree to it. Agents must always act in the best interests of the person they represent and treat our staff respectfully.

chunks.title: Why have an agent
chunks.text: You can have an agent for any reason. This may be because: - you're overseas - you have mobility issues that makes it physically hard to go to our offices - you're sick or unwell - you're living in residential care or an institution - you want help or advice with a decision we've made - you've been served a trespass notice which says you cannot enter our offices. If you're having difficulty communicating in English, you can talk to us in another language using our free translation services. You can still use these services with or without appointing an agent. We speak other languages

chunks.title: Who can be your agent
chunks.text: Your agent can be a person or an organisation. They generally need to be 18 or older. They may be able to be an agent if they're under 18, e.g. if they're your partner. You can give your agent a lot of power over your affairs. You can also give them a lot of access to your personal information. It is important to be careful who you choose as an agent and what you allow them to do. Your agent should be someone you trust. They can be someone like: - a family member - a person or an organisation that cares for you (but not your Youth Service provider if you have one) - a lawyer - an advocate.

chunks.title: How to find an advocate
chunks.text: There are advocate groups who may be able to help you with an independent advocate who has experience in dealing with us. A good advocate can: - help you if you don't understand or disagree with a decision we made - work with us to make sure you get all the support you're entitled to - help explain your situation in meetings with us or in a review or appeal process. You can find an advocate through the Citizens Advice Bureau or Community Law. Citizens Advice Bureauexternal Community Lawexternal

chunks.title: When an agent is appointed for you
chunks.text: There may be cases where an agent is appointed for you, for example: - a court may appoint someone as your agent. The court will state what rights and responsibilities they have. - if someone has your power of attorney or enduring power of attorney. If the court has appointed someone to help you, usually you cannot change or cancel their authorisation. Only the court can do that. You can change or cancel someone's power of attorney but not someone's enduring power of attorney. In exceptional circumstances, we may allow someone to act as your agent without any legal document. For example this might be if you're in a coma and need help from us and there isn't time to get a court order. We would normally need proof that you cannot act for yourself temporarily, e.g. a medical certificate.

chunks.title: What your agent can do
chunks.text: You're responsible for deciding what your agent can and cannot do. You can allow your agent to do things like: - get personal information we hold about you - tell us information on your behalf, e.g. change of address or income - get your mail from us - complete and sign application forms on your behalf - have authority over your affairs, as granted by a current Power of Attorney - be paid part or all of your benefit on your behalf if there's a good reason, e.g. you're sick or unwell and cannot physically withdraw money or manage your finances you're living in residential care or an institution you're misusing your benefit payment and the wellbeing of your family is put at risk. - you're sick or unwell and cannot physically withdraw money or manage your finances

chunks.title: What your agent can do
chunks.text: - you're living in residential care or an institution - you're misusing your benefit payment and the wellbeing of your family is put at risk. You can have more than one agent and they can do different things. For example, you may have: - a family member who fills in forms for you, and - an advocate who represents you in a dispute with us. Agents cannot access or use your MyMSD account. You can still talk to us and act for yourself when you have an agent. You can choose to remove your agent or change what they're allowed to do at any time.

chunks.title: Court Order or Power of Attorney
chunks.text: If your agent has been appointed by a court order, the court determines what they can and cannot do on your behalf. If your agent holds an Enduring Power of Attorney, they will have authority over your affairs.

chunks.title: How to appoint an agent
chunks.text: You can verbally agree for someone to act on your behalf when you meet with us or call us, which will only last for that meeting. If you want someone to be your agent for longer, you'll need to fill out an 'Appointment of Agent' form. You can use the form below or you can have one sent to you by calling 0800 559 009. This will: - name you and your agent - show exactly what rights and responsibilities you want your agent to have - be signed by both you and your agent. Please complete this form if you would like an agent to act on your behalf. You or your agent can bring the completed form into a service centre. You can just drop it off, you don't need an appointment. Your agent needs to bring their original government-issued identity document (ID) with them.

chunks.title: How to appoint an agent
chunks.text: Find a service centre If you or your agent can’t bring the form into a service centre, call us to find out how to get it to us. Phone us If this is your first time applying for a benefit or ongoing payment, you or your agent needs to bring your original government-issued ID into a service centre so we can check it. Checking ID in person helps us make sure we give support to the right person and protect your identity. Types of documents we accept

chunks.title: Paying your benefit to an agent
chunks.text: If you want your payments to go to your agent, you'll also need to fill in a 'Redirection of benefit payment' form with them. - why you need your payments to go to your agent - what other ways you've tried to organise your payments - how much of your payments you want to go to your agent. Your agent will need to show us proof of their bank account details, e.g. a bank statement or a deposit slip. Complete this form if you want part or all of your payments to be paid to another person or organisation. Or you can ask for a form to be sent to you by calling 0800 559 009. Requests for a redirection will only be approved in special circumstances and for good reason.

chunks.title: Change or remove an agent
chunks.text: If you want to change or remove your agent, you can contact us and let us know. You should also tell your agent what changes you've made. Your agent can decide to stop representing you, but they need to contact us and let us know. Contact us We can refuse to deal with an agent if we have good reason, for example if we do not think they will always act in your best interest.

chunks.title: Stopping work because of health condition or disability
chunks.text: If you have to stop work because of a health condition, injury or disability we may be able to help you.

chunks.title: Talk to your health practitioner
chunks.text: You'll need a medical certificate from your health practitioner, eg your doctor, to tell us how your health condition or disability affects your ability to work. Some health practitioners send us medical certificates electronically. If you already have a Work and Income client number, make sure they include that on the certificate. If your health practitioner doesn't send your medical certificate electronically, you'll need to send it to us.

chunks.title: Have to stop work for a while or reduce hours
chunks.text: You have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work. This means that you have to reduce your hours or stop work for a while. We may still be able to help if you have a job to go back to. Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Sole parent
chunks.text: You're a sole parent with children under 14 and have a health condition or disability that affects your ability to work. Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Permanently unable to work
chunks.text: You're permanently and severely restricted in your ability to work because of a health condition, injury or disability, or are legally blind. Supported Living Payment

chunks.title: You've had to stop work and your partner is working
chunks.text: You're down to one wage and you need help to pay day-to-day expenses while you look for work.

chunks.title: Working and have no sick leave or paid leave
chunks.text: You're not on a benefit anymore and you can't work because of sickness or a breakdown in childcare arrangements. You don't have any sick leave or paid leave available. New Employment Transition Grant You can't work for a while because you have a health condition or disability which affects your ability to work, and you have no sick pay available. Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Hearing aids
chunks.text: If you're on a low income or benefit you may be able to get help with the cost of hearing aids.

chunks.title: Funding from Disability Support Services
chunks.text: Disability Support Services may be able to help you pay for hearing aids. This funding is free - you don’t have to pay it back. Find out who can get this and how to apply on their website: Deaf or hearing loss equipment for adults (Disability Support Services)external

chunks.title: Help you may be able to get from us
chunks.text: If you can't get funding from Disability Support Services, or need extra help, Work and Income may be able to help. You don't have to be on a benefit to apply for this. You will have to pay the money back. If you’re getting a benefit, you can apply for an Advance Payment of Benefit. Advance Payment of Benefit If you’re not getting a benefit, you can apply for a Recoverable Assistance Payment. Recoverable Assistance Payment

chunks.title: Contact us
chunks.text: If you're not sure what help you can get, call us and we can talk through your options with you. Phone us
