chunks.title: Power, gas, water bills or heating
chunks.text: We may be able to help you with an urgent power, gas or water bill, heating costs or water tank refill if you have no other way to pay. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You may have to pay the money back depending on your situation.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You could find yourself in a situation where you have an outstanding power, gas or water bill that you can't pay. You need to talk to the power or water company first to see if you can make a payment arrangement with them. If this is not possible, we may be able to help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate and essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Generally, we can pay up to $200 to help with: - an outstanding power, gas or water bill - reconnecting your electricity, gas or water supply.

chunks.title: Water tank refill
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay to get your personal water tank refilled and delivered. You need to be living in either: - a property you own - a property you're renting and you're responsible for refilling the water tank. You can get up to $500 to pay for refill and delivery. You can generally get one payment for water tank refill every 12 months.

chunks.title: Help to keep your family warm
chunks.text: We may be able to help you with the cost of bedding, blankets, curtains or heaters, depending on your circumstances. It may be that: - your children are unwell - you can't keep warm in your home - there is wear and tear to your bedding because of long-term sickness or disability in the family - a new child has come into the family. Call us to discuss your situation. Phone us

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Help to get a driver licence
chunks.text: Need help to get your driver licence? We can help you get the support you need.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We have providers across New Zealand who can help you get your driver licence. They can help you with things like: - studying for the learner licence test - professional driving lessons for the restricted or full licence test - paying the test fees - a vehicle to take the test in.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You don't have to be getting a benefit. There are lots of ways we can help. We'll talk to you about getting your licence, and we'll check what help is available.

chunks.title: Get in touch
chunks.text: If you're a client with us, call us on 0800 559 009 to book an appointment, or ask your case manager. We'll help you find a provider in your area and make a referral for you. If you're not a client with us, use the Family Services Directory to find a provider near you, and contact them about help to get your driver licence: Learning to drive (Family Services Directory)external

chunks.title: Help while you're working
chunks.text: We may be able to help you pay living expenses, an unexpected cost, or get your finances sorted, even if you've got a job. You don't need to be getting a benefit to get this help.

chunks.title: Living expenses
chunks.text: You may be able to get ongoing help with everyday living expenses. This could be things like: - rent, mortgage or board - childcare - doctor's appointments - public transport fares. What you can get depends on how much income you get (and your partner, if you have one), any savings or cash assets you have, and what your expenses are. You can use our 'Check What You Might Get' tool to see what payments you might be able to get. Check what you might getexternal

chunks.title: Urgent or unexpected costs
chunks.text: We can help pay for one-off urgent or unexpected costs. These could be costs like: - food - power - an unexpectedly high bill - home repairs - whiteware. What you can get depends on how much income you get (and your partner, if you have one), any savings or cash assets you have, and what costs you need help with. Urgent or unexpected costs

chunks.title: Managing your money
chunks.text: Find organisations that can help you manage your money and deal with debt. We can also provide support and practical information to help you budget. Managing your money Budgeting

chunks.title: Debt with us
chunks.text: If you owe us money, we can help with: - a breakdown of your debt - debt repayments - what to do if you don't agree with your debt, and - support for managing your debt. Your debt with us

chunks.title: Holiday and Birthday Allowance
chunks.text: You automatically get the Holiday and Birthday Allowance if you already get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas. If you get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit for a child you’re caring for, use the Holiday and Birthday Allowance to help pay for the costs of making the child feel special. Celebrating important events in a child’s life helps them feel valued, part of the family and more secure and happy. Being the centre of an enjoyable event helps the child’s emotional and mental health. You get this payment two times each year. If you don’t celebrate birthdays or Christmas, use the money to do something fun that makes the child feel special.

chunks.title: Holiday and Birthday Allowance
chunks.text: Holiday and Birthday Allowance payments don’t: - affect other payments you may get from us - count as income for tax purposes.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You automatically get the Birthday and Holiday Allowance if you get Unsupported Child’s Benefit or Orphan’s Benefit.

chunks.title: How much you get
chunks.text: How much money you get depends on the age of the child you're looking after. You don't have to let us know when the child's age changes. We update the payment automatically.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You don't need to apply for the Holiday and Birthday Allowance. You get this payment automatically when you get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit.

chunks.title: How you’re paid
chunks.text: We pay you the Holiday and Birthday Allowance with your Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. Each year, you get the: - Birthday Allowance around 2 weeks before the child’s birthday - Holiday Allowance around 2 weeks before 25 December. When you stop getting Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit, the allowance also stops.

chunks.title: Home equity conversion scheme lump sum
chunks.text: Lump sum payments from a home equity conversion scheme don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.

chunks.title: What is this?
chunks.text: A one-off payment (also known as a reverse mortgage) that lets you borrow against your home to pay for major expenses, for example: - a new car - house repairs or maintenance - a holiday - a medical operation.

chunks.title: How it affects your benefit and allowances
chunks.text: You have to tell us about this payment if you: - get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income - don't use the payment for major expenses, but everyday goods and services - get regular home equity conversion payments.

chunks.text: If you need more information or want to discuss this in more detail contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: Home Help
chunks.text: If you're a parent or carer we may be able to help you with the cost of home help to complete household tasks or training in parenting skills.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get Home Help if: - you're either a: New Zealand citizen permanent resident - New Zealand citizen - permanent resident - you normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - you either have a multiple birth from the same pregnancy adopt 2 or more children from the same pregnancy have a domestic emergency (a sudden change of circumstances that creates a crisis situation) need domestic support. - have a multiple birth from the same pregnancy - adopt 2 or more children from the same pregnancy - have a domestic emergency (a sudden change of circumstances that creates a crisis situation) - need domestic support. If you have or adopt twins, you must already have another child under 5.

chunks.title: Domestic emergencies and Home Help
chunks.text: You can get Home Help for a domestic emergency, but you must have: - no immediate family or anyone else living with you who can help - a current Community Services Card, or your partner must have one. Domestic emergency Home Help is also based on any money or assets you and your partner have.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on your current circumstances. View our maximum current hourly rates (Map)external

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009. We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. We'll ask you to complete a 'Home Help Payments' form and discuss the best way to get this to us.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application's approved, you and your home helper need to complete a timesheet for each week you get the home help. There's a section on the timesheet for you to fill in and a section for your home helper to fill in. Both of you will need to sign and date the timesheet. Call us to talk about the best way to get the completed timesheet to us. Phone us

chunks.title: Going into or leaving hospital
chunks.text: If you're going into hospital or have just left, you need to tell us.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to contact us as soon as you can. If you don't tell us we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll have to pay the debt back. Phone us

chunks.title: Payments may be affected
chunks.text: Your benefit or payment will keep being paid for the first 13 weeks you're in hospital. Then your payments will change to our hospital rate of $58.34 a week (after tax), unless you either: - have a partner and a child, or - are a veteran. The hospital rate covers the cost of personal items you need to get while you're in hospital.

chunks.title: Get Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: You may get the Supported Living Payment because you're caring for someone. If you, or the person you're caring for, is in hospital, your benefit will keep being paid for the first 4 weeks. Then it will stop. If you're in hospital for longer than 4 weeks, we'll need to check if there are other payments you could qualify for.

chunks.title: You have a partner and no child
chunks.text: Once you get the hospital rate, we'll review any benefit or payment your partner gets from us. This is so we can make sure they're getting all the help they qualify for while you're in hospital. They may also be able to get a Special Disability Allowance to help cover the costs of visiting you in hospital. If they qualify for this, we'll pay it to them automatically once you start getting the hospital rate.

chunks.title: Hospital rate won't cover costs
chunks.text: If the hospital rate isn't enough to cover your costs, we may be able to pay more. This will depend on what expenses and income you have while you're in hospital.

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: You need to fill out an 'Increased payment while you're in hospital' form. You can drop it off to one of our service centres, or post it to us. Find a service centre If you can't download and print the form, ask the hospital. They may have some on site. The hospital staff may also be able to help you fill it out and send it.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once we've processed your form, we'll send you a letter and give you a call to let you know if it's approved.

chunks.title: Home repairs and maintenance
chunks.text: If you need money for essential repairs or maintenance for your home and you're on a benefit, we may be able to help. You may have to pay the money back depending on your situation.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get help if: - you’re receiving a benefit, pension or NZ Superannuation - you have an immediate and essential need - the repairs or maintenance are needed to keep your home to a reasonable living standard - you’ve been to your bank or another provider but they weren’t able to help you. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits usually apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: Not on a benefit
chunks.text: If you’re not on a benefit and need help urgently, e.g., with a sewage treatment system, we may still be able to help. Call us on 0800 559 009 to discuss your situation.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Generally you can get up to $1,000 depending on your situation.

chunks.title: What you get it for
chunks.text: You can get help with essential repairs and maintenance for your home, e.g.: - roof - hot water cylinder - paths - fences - retaining walls. You may also be able to get help with essential services such as: - sewerage (e.g., sinks, toilet, shower, drains) - water - electricity connection.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us to book an appointment with us. Our phone numbers During your appointment, we’ll need to understand your situation and how we can help, and let you know what information you need to provide. This will include: - evidence that you own your home (or have joint ownership) - evidence that you live in your home - evidence that you went to your bank or another provider for help but your application was unsuccessful - evidence of the costs you're applying for, e.g., quotes or a link to a cost on the supplier's website. You'll need to check with the store or supplier to see if they can accept our payment.

chunks.title: House Modification Funding
chunks.text: House Modification Funding is a payment which helps someone pay for changes to their home because they or their child have a disability.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You can only get House Modification Funding if you are assessed as needing the house modification. The Ministry of Health makes this decision. This information is a guide only. Contact us to talk about your individual circumstances. Contact us

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on: - the cost of the house modification - your living costs and expenses - how much you and your spouse or partner earn - any money or assets you and your spouse or partner have.

chunks.title: For more information
chunks.text: For more detail go to our: House Modification Funding (Manuals and Procedures)external

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: For a needs assessment contact: Enable NZexternal

chunks.title: Housing costs
chunks.text: If you need help to pay rent or other accommodation costs, or support to stay in your home, we may be able to help.

chunks.title: On-going costs of rent, board or owning a home
chunks.text: If you need help to pay your on-going costs of rent, board or the costs of owning a home, you may be able to get an Accommodation Supplement. You don't have to be on a benefit to get this payment. If you live in public housing, you won't qualify for this payment. Accommodation Supplement

chunks.title: Falling behind in accommodation costs
chunks.text: You may be worried you'll lose your housing because you owe accommodation costs, e.g. rent, board or cabin hire. If so, you may be able to get an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. You need to talk to your accommodation supplier first, e.g. your landlord or head tenant. Check if you can make a payment arrangement with them. If you can't make a payment arrangement, see if you qualify for an Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant. Accommodation Costs Arrears Grant

chunks.title: Spending rent money on other bills
chunks.text: If you've had to spend your rent money on other bills, like food or power, we may be able to help with these bills. This is so you can still pay your rent. Help with urgent or unexpected costs

chunks.title: Renting
chunks.text: If you're renting, it's the landlord’s responsibility to repair and maintain the house. So, if something breaks down or goes wrong, tell the landlord straight away. Key rights and responsibilities (Tenancy)external If you live in public housing, you can request maintenance and view maintenance jobs through MyKāingaOra. This is an online way for public housing tenants to check their accounts, rent balances, maintenance requests and much more. MyKāingaOraexternal

chunks.title: Own your own home
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit and own your own home and need money for essential repairs or maintenance, we may be able to help. Home repairs and maintenance

chunks.title: Help with heating costs
chunks.text: We may be able to help you with the costs of: - an urgent power, gas, or water bill - bedding - blankets - curtains - heaters. Power, gas, water bills or heating

chunks.title: Extra heating if you have a disability
chunks.text: If you have extra power, gas or heating costs because of your disability or health condition, we may be able to help you pay this as part of a Disability Allowance. Power, gas and heating if you have a disability

chunks.title: Costs to end your tenancy early, or sublet or assign your tenancy
chunks.text: If your landlord charges you costs to end your tenancy early, or to sublet or assign your tenancy to someone else, we may be able to help. Your landlord must give you an itemised account of the actual costs, e.g: - cost of advertising - credit checks, or - money to cover rent while another tenant is found. We need to see this account.

chunks.title: If you're not on a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Recoverable Assistance Payment up to $200, or more in exceptional circumstances. You'll need to pay it back. Recoverable Assistance Payment

chunks.title: If you're on a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get an Advance Payment of Benefit up to $200, or more in some circumstances. You'll need to pay it back. Advance Payment of Benefit

chunks.title: Rates rebate
chunks.text: A rates rebate is a partial rebate for eligible, low-income ratepayers who pay rates on their home to the council. You need to apply to your local council for the rebate. You'll need to provide proof of your income to your local council. If you're getting a benefit or payment from us, call us and ask for a rates rebate income statement. Getting a rates rebate (New Zealand Government)external

chunks.title: Make your home accessible
chunks.text: If you need to make changes to your home because you or your child has a disability, you may be able to get House Modification Funding. House Modification funding

chunks.title: Parent or carer
chunks.text: If you're a parent or carer we may be able to help you with the cost of home help to complete household tasks or training in parenting skills. Home help

chunks.title: Injury covered by ACC
chunks.text: If you've had an injury that ACC cover and you need help at home afterwards, ACC may be able to help. Help at home after an injury (ACC)external

chunks.title: Support services
chunks.text: CCS Disability Actionexternal CCS Disability Action offers a broad range of support services for disabled people, family and whanau. Home and Community Support Services (Ministry of Health)external If you need support in your home, there are Home and Community Services funded by the Ministry of Health. They can help with both household management and personal care. Nurse Maudeexternal Nurse Maude provides nursing and home support services to more than 400,000 people. RDNS New Zealandexternal Royal District Nursing Service (RDNS) New Zealand is a leading provider of home-based healthcare solutions for people living in their own homes across the Southland, Otago and Auckland Districts.

chunks.title: Getting older
chunks.text: If you’re getting older, you may be finding it harder to cope on your own. There are support services that help you to stay in your home for as long as you can. Services for older people (Health New Zealand)external

chunks.title: How board and rent affect your payments
chunks.text: You need to tell us if you're getting board or rent payments or paying board or rent to someone else. Board or rent payments you get may affect how much help you get for accommodation costs, how much Income Related Rent you pay, and they may count as income. You need to tell us about any board and rent payments you get or pay. This is part of meeting your obligations when you get payments from us. Your obligations while getting payments from us

chunks.title: What is board
chunks.text: A boarder is someone who pays for accommodation and food in another person's home, and their food costs can't be easily separated out from the amount they pay. Their board payment may also cover other service costs, e.g. internet or power. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will be considered a boarder. If you're getting payments from a boarder, it can affect: - any housing subsidies (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support) for your own accommodation costs - how much Income Related Rent you pay if you're living in public housing - income-tested payments from us in some cases. If you're paying board to someone, we will ask for details of who you're paying this to and how much.

chunks.title: What is board
chunks.text: If you're flatting, and all household members share the responsibility to cover the accommodation cost for the property, you do not need to declare your flatmates as boarders or renters. The amount you pay as a flatmate is usually considered rent.

chunks.title: What is rent
chunks.text: A renter is someone whose accommodation costs cover the room or property they stay in. This may also include service costs (e.g. gardening). If you're getting payments from a renter, it can affect: - any housing subsidies you get (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Temporary Additional Support) for your own accommodation costs - any income-tested payments from us in some cases. If you're paying rent to someone, we will ask for details of who you're paying this to and how much. If you're flatting, and all household members share the responsibility to cover the accommodation cost for the property, you do not need to declare your flatmates as boarders or renters. The amount you pay as a flatmate is usually considered rent.

chunks.title: How board or rent affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: Housing subsidies include: - Accommodation Supplement - Temporary Additional Support and Special Benefit - Away from Home Allowance. How much housing subsidy you can get depends on how much your accommodation costs are.

chunks.title: How board affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: If you're getting board payments, some of those payments will already cover part of your accommodation costs. To work out how much your accommodation costs are, we: - look at how much board you are paid - work out 62% of this, which is the accommodation portion of the board (the other 38% is for food and other services) - reduce your accommodation costs by that amount. Your total accommodation costs are used to work out how much housing subsidy we will pay you.

chunks.title: How rent affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: How much housing subsidy you can get depends on how much your accommodation costs are and whether you live in the same property as your renter. If you're getting rent payments for part of the same property you live in, those payments will not be included in your personal accommodation costs. This includes when you rent out: - a self-contained portion of the property (e.g. granny flat), - non-accommodation rentals (e.g. garage being used as storage). For these types of rent payments, we work out the portion/percentage of the property you live in, not including the area used by someone else. The non-accommodation rental payments are treated as income, but will not affect your accommodation costs for a housing subsidy.

chunks.title: How rent affects housing subsidies
chunks.text: If you're paid rent by someone who doesn't live with you (e.g. they live in a separate property), we treat the whole payment you get from them as income, but it will not affect your accommodation costs for a housing subsidy. To work out how much your accommodation costs are, we: - look at how much rent you are paid - reduce your accommodation costs by the full rent payment amount. If you rent out a self-contained portion of your home, we work out your personal accommodation costs based on the portion/percentage of the property you live in - this does not include the area used by someone else.

chunks.title: How board affects Income Related Rent
chunks.text: If you live in public housing, Income Related Rent is the amount of rent you pay. When we calculate your Income Related Rent, we add on 62% of any board payments you get. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will always be considered a boarder. You can read about the full calculation here: Calculating your rent payments This change took effect on 2 March 2026. This means 62% of the board payments will be added to your Income Related Rent rate from: - your next annual rent review, or - when you next tell us about a change in circumstances.

chunks.title: How board and rent payments affect income-tested payments
chunks.text: The money you get from board or rent can affect other payments you get from us, so you need to tell us if you're getting board or rent payments. Not all the money you get from board or rent payments counts as income – only the amount that is more than either: - your accommodation costs, or - the market rent for your home if you're living in public housing, or - the full amount of the rent payment if they don't live on the same property as you. To work out how much of your board or rent payments count as income, we: - calculate how much of the payment we need to count – for board this is 62%, and for rent 100% - then we compare this amount to your accommodation costs, or market rent if you're in public housing.

chunks.title: How board and rent payments affect income-tested payments
chunks.text: If this amount is higher than your accommodation costs or market rent, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income. If this amount is lower than your accommodation costs or market rent, your board or rent payments do not count as income. You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: How to tell us you're getting board or rent payments
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us is online in MyMSD. Once you’ve logged in, select 'Declare boarders and renters'. You need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you board or rent - how much the board or rent is - when you get paid, and how often. We will continue to use this amount every week, so make sure you let us know if it stops or changes. If you can't use MyMSD, you can also fill out our PDF form: You need to print this form, complete it, and either post it to us or bring it into one of our services centres. You can also pick one up from any of our service centres. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Checking your board or rent details
chunks.text: When people tell us about their accommodation costs, we ask them: - if they pay board or rent, or get paid board or rent - who they pay it to, or are paid by - how much and how often those payments are. If both the boarder/renter and the person they pay board or rent to (e.g. their landlord or the head tenant) are getting either a housing subsidy or are living in public housing, we need to independently check this information with each of them. If it doesn't match, we need to contact both these people to get the correct details. This is part of meeting their obligations. We'll try calling them first. If we can't contact them by phone, we'll send them a letter giving them 10 working days to confirm the correct details. We'll also send them a MyMSD notification, where they can confirm the details.

chunks.title: Checking your board or rent details
chunks.text: - If they don't confirm or still don't agree, after the 10 working days: - if they get a housing subsidy, this will stop on day 11 - if they are a public housing tenant, we will notify the housing provider and their rent may go up to market rent.

chunks.title: How income affects your payments
chunks.text: Getting a job doesn't always mean your payments will stop. We're still here to help even when you're working. Your payments may be able to continue, and there may be other ways we can help out too.

chunks.title: Let us know you’re starting a job
chunks.text: Starting a new job is a great achievement, but it can be scary. We want to help you as much as we can, and make it easy for you to get off to a great start. Get in touch with us before you start your new job. We'll sort out your payments from us and make sure you're getting everything you're entitled to. We'll also check if there's anything else we can do to help while you're starting out. Call us on 0800 559 009 before you start your new job.

chunks.title: How much you can earn
chunks.text: You may be able to keep getting your benefit or payment even if you're working. This depends on: - which benefit or payment you're getting, and - how much you get paid for your job. Our income deduction tables show how much income you can get before your benefit is affected: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Declare your income while you’re working
chunks.text: If you're getting payments from us while you're working, you need to declare your income so we can pay you the correct amount. We need to know by Friday 6pm the week you earn the money (not the week you've been paid). If you're working the weekend, include the hours you think you’ll work. You can change it later if your hours change. If your income and hours are the same every week, you only need to tell us once. The amount you declare will continue every week until you let us know it has stopped or changed. The easiest way to tell us your income is through MyMSD: Find out more about declaring wages, how to do this, and what happens after you've declared them: Wages

chunks.title: If you can't use MyMSD
chunks.text: If you can't use MyMSD you can call us or come into one of our service centres. If you’re declaring income from self-employment, make sure you mention you're self-employed. Phone usFind a service centre

chunks.title: Help while you're working
chunks.text: As well as checking whether your existing payments can continue, we may also be able to help with: - paying for work costs like training or equipment - managing your money - budgeting - managing your debt with us.

chunks.title: How much you can get for NZ Super
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. How much you get depends on your situation and what tax code you use. Payment rates may be different if: - you live overseas, or - your partner is included in your payment. You live overseas Your partner is included in your payment If you get an overseas pension, this could affect your NZ Super payments. Talk to us about how this could affect your payments. Overseas pensions Phone us If you or your partner get other income as well as NZ Super, it may change the tax code you use. This means you could get less for your NZ Super payments, it depends what tax code you're on.

chunks.title: Increases to NZ Super
chunks.text: NZ Super rates increase every year on 1 April to adjust to changes in the average wage. Any information about this increase, or any other changes to our payment rates, will always be communicated here on the Work and Income website.

chunks.title: Your tax code
chunks.text: NZ Super is a taxable payment. The amount of tax you pay depends on the tax code you use. If you only get NZ Super, your tax code will probably be 'M'. If you get other income as well, it may be a different tax code. If you need help working out what tax code you should use, go to the Inland Revenue website to look at what tax code you should use. What tax code should I use? (Inland Revenue)external If you've changed your tax code, you need to let us know. You can do this by filling out our 'Change tax code' form online. Change of tax code form

chunks.title: Payment rate if you're single
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your living situation and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Live alone or with a dependent child Live with someone who's either: - 18 or older (unless they're a dependent child who's 18), or - visiting and staying more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period. Definition of dependent child

chunks.title: Payment rate if you have a partner
chunks.text: How much you get depends on who meets the criteria for NZ Super and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Both you and your partner meet the criteria for NZ Super If you don't see your situation in the table, there are non-standard rates under the heading 'NZ Super and Veteran's Pension' on our page: Benefit rates at 1 April 2026

chunks.title: Increases to Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Your tax code

If you get other income as well, it may be a different tax code. If you need help working out what tax code you should use, go to the Inland Revenue website to look at what tax code you should use. chunks.title: Payment rate if you're single
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your living situation and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Live with someone who's either: - 18 or older (unless they're a dependent child who's 18), or - visiting and staying more than 13 weeks in any 26 week period. Definition of dependent child

chunks.title: Payment rate if you have a partner
chunks.text: How much you get depends on who meets the criteria for Veteran's Pension and what tax code you use. Payments are fortnightly. Who can get Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: If you get other income
chunks.text: If you get other income, it will affect your Veteran's Pension payments if: - you're under 65 - you were getting a Veteran's Pension on 7 December 2014, when the War Pensions Act 1954 was replaced by the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - you've chosen to get Veteran's Pension instead of weekly income compensation from Veteran's Affairs. Other income will also affect your Veteran's Pension when: - you're 65 or older, and - you have included your partner in your Veteran's Pension payments.

chunks.title: How other income will affect your payment
chunks.text: You and your partner can earn up to $160 a week (before tax) in total before it affects your payment.

chunks.title: Then, if you're under 65
chunks.text: Once you and your partner earn over $160 (before tax) a week: - any income you get between $160 and $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your payment by 30 cents for each $1 of income - any income you get over $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your payment by 70 cents for every $1 of income.

chunks.title: Or, if you're 65 or older
chunks.text: Once you and your partner earn over $160 (before tax), your payment reduces by 70 cents for every extra $1 of income you earn.

chunks.title: How payments work
chunks.text: Information about when your payments start, pay days and when you get your first and last payment.

chunks.title: When your payments start
chunks.text: If you've applied for a benefit, you may have a stand-down of 1 or 2 weeks. Your payments will start after your stand-down finishes. If you've been working recently, your payments may take longer to start. Stand-down periods

chunks.title: You've been working recently
chunks.text: Your payments can take up to 3 months (13 weeks) to start if you've recently been in work and: - left your job without a good reason, or - lost your job because of misconduct

chunks.title: Other payments you get from work
chunks.text: You may get other payments from work, eg: - holiday pay - sick pay - pay in lieu of notice - retirement payments If you get one of these, your payments from us will start once they're finished. For example, you get 3 weeks worth of holiday pay. This means your payments from us will start 3 weeks after your stand-down finishes.

chunks.title: Redundancy pay
chunks.text: If you’re made redundant and get redundancy pay, you’ll have a stand-down of 1 or 2 weeks. It depends how much your redundancy pay is. The stand-down period for redundancy pay has changed over time. If you’ve had a redundancy payment, you can ask us to check if we treated this correctly when working out your stand-down period.

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: Once your payments start, you won't get any money in the first week. This is because we pay you for the week that's just been. This means you're on a benefit for one week and get paid for that benefit in the next week. This is also called arrears. For example: - Your payments start on Monday - you won't get any money in this week - Your first weekly payment is paid in the next week, on your pay day

chunks.title: Approved part-way through the week
chunks.text: If your payments start part-way through the week, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get. For example: - Your payments start on Wednesday - Your first weekly payment: is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and will be for 5 days (Wednesday - Sunday). - is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and - will be for 5 days (Wednesday - Sunday).

chunks.title: NZ Super and Veteran's payments
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. These are set pay dates. NZ Super payment dates Once your payments start, you'll get your first payment of NZ Super or Veteran's Pension on the next set pay date. In most cases if you apply: - before your 65th birthday, your payments will start from your birthday - after your 65th birthday, your payments will start from the date you apply. These payments are paid in arrears, so it includes the previous 13 days and the pay day. For example, the pay day Tuesday 25 June will cover the period from Wednesday 12 June to (and including) Tuesday 25 June. If your payments start part-way through the pay period, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get.

chunks.title: NZ Super and Veteran's payments
chunks.text: Examples Your application is approved on Friday 12 January 2018, your first payment: - is paid on Tuesday 23 January - will be for 12 days (Friday 12 January - Tuesday 23 January). Your application is approved on Friday 26 October 2018, your first payment: - is paid on Tuesday 30 October - will be for 5 days (Friday 26 October - Tuesday 30 October)

chunks.title: Child Disability Allowance
chunks.text: Child Disability Allowance is paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. These are set pay dates (the opposite fortnights to NZ Super and Veteran's Pension payments). Once your application is approved, you'll get your first payment of Child Disability Allowance on the next set pay date. If your application is approved part-way through the pay period, your first payment will be less than what you would normally get.

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: Most benefits and payments are paid weekly. If you get a weekly payment, your official pay day is either: - Tuesday - Wednesday, or - Thursday Once you have a pay day, it will never change. Even if you get another benefit or payment from us later on. You might see your payment in your account the night before, it depends on who you bank with.

chunks.title: Fortnightly payments
chunks.text: There are 3 payments that are paid fortnightly. These are: - New Zealand Superannuation - Veteran's Pension - Child Disability Allowance New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension are paid every fortnight on a Tuesday. If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, most other payments you get from us, eg Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance, will also be paid fortnightly. Child Disability Allowance is paid every fortnight on a Tuesday (the opposite fortnight to NZ Super and Veteran's Pension). You might see your payment in your account the night before, it depends on who you bank with. NZ Super payment dates

chunks.title: Find out your pay day
chunks.text: Once your application is approved, we'll send you a letter letting you know the date of your first payment. You can also check what your pay day is in MyMSD. Find out more about MyMSD

chunks.title: Weekly payments
chunks.text: If your benefit or payment stops, you'll get your last payment a week after the date it stops. This is because we pay you for the week that's just been. This means you're on a benefit for one week and get paid for that benefit in the next week. This is also called arrears.

chunks.title: Stops part-way through the week
chunks.text: If your benefit or payment stops part-way through the week, your last payment will be less than what you would normally get. For example: - Your benefit stops on Wednesday - Your last weekly payment: is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and will be for 2 days (Monday - Tuesday) - is paid in the next week, on your pay day, and - will be for 2 days (Monday - Tuesday)

chunks.title: Pay days on public holidays
chunks.text: Sometimes your regular pay day will fall on a public holiday. When this happens, we'll always make sure you get your payments either the day before or on your regular pay day. For example, if you're usually paid on Wednesdays, and Wednesday is a public holiday, your payment will be available from Tuesday.

chunks.title: Regional anniversary holidays
chunks.text: If your regular pay day falls on a regional anniversary (eg Wellington or Auckland anniversary), you will still be paid on your usual pay day. This is because pay dates only change when there is a national holiday for the whole country.

chunks.title: How to choose the right job
chunks.text: Tools and experts to help you find out what you're good at and what job suits you. Knowing what kind of job you want will make searching and applying for jobs easier. You can do this by figuring out your skills, planning your career and finding a job that fits your life.

chunks.title: Discover your skills
chunks.text: Explore job ideas and find out what you might be good.

chunks.title: Discover your skills and what employers value
chunks.text: Use Tahatū’s resources to learn about your skills, what matters to you at work, and explore career ideas. Know your skills (Tahatu Career Navigator)external

chunks.title: Not sure what you're good at
chunks.text: The Interest quiz suggests job ideas matched to your interests. You can also learn about the pay, skills and qualifications for your job matches. Interest quiz (Tahatu Career Navigator)external

chunks.title: Flexi-wage
chunks.text: Help to get started and learn the skills you need for a job. We'll find you a job where you can get paid while you learn, with an employer who will help you towards long-term work. You'll also get ongoing support from us and your employer. Flexi-wage - job seeker information

chunks.text: Get paid while you train towards a career you love. We'll find a job for you in an industry that interests you. You'll get started on an apprenticeship or industry qualification. Mana in Mahi - Strength in work

chunks.title: Community Job Coaching
chunks.text: A job coach can help you prepare for and find work. This is for 18 to 24 year olds in some regions, who have been getting Jobseeker Support for at least 3 months. Community Job Coaching

chunks.title: Family-friendly jobs
chunks.text: The Jobs for Mums website lists jobs in 30+ career fields that meet the needs of families. They have flexible job opportunities in your area or remote work. Jobs for Mumsexternal

chunks.title: If you're disabled or have a health condition
chunks.text: We can help you get a job and set up your career if you're disabled or have a health condition. This includes mental health conditions or neurodiversity. - Employment Service: Get an employment provider who will help you prepare for work, find a job that's right for you and make sure you have everything you need. Employment service for people with a disability or health condition - Employment Service in Schools: For secondary school students. An employment provider will work with you, your family and your school to help you plan your future and explore job and career opportunities. Employment Service in Schools - Mainstream Programmes: Get a work placement, on-the-job training, and a long-term job. There's different programmes for your situation and goals.

chunks.text: If you've come off your benefit to start work, we can offer ongoing support and advice to help you manage any challenges that come up. chunks.title: Income from boarders
chunks.text: If you have other people sharing your home and paying you to live there, you need to tell us about it as it could affect your payments.

chunks.title: What is board
chunks.text: Board is the amount paid by someone (called a boarder) who pays for accommodation and food in another person's home, and their food costs can't be easily separated out from the amount they pay. Their board payment may also cover other service costs, e.g. internet or power. If you're living in public housing, and the person living with you is not on the tenancy agreement, they will be considered a boarder.

chunks.title: How board payments can affect payments from us
chunks.text: The money you get from your boarders can affect any income-tested payments you get from us. You need to tell us if you're getting board payments. Not all the money you get from board payments counts as income – only the amount that is more than either: - your accommodation costs, or - the market rent for your home if you're living in public housing. To work out how much of your board payments count as income, we: - look at how much board you are paid and work out 62% of this - compare this amount to your accommodation costs, or market rent if you're in public housing. If the 62% is lower than your accommodation costs or market rent, your board payments do not count as income. However, it will affect the amount of housing subsidy you can get from us.

chunks.title: How board payments can affect payments from us
chunks.text: If the 62% is higher than your accommodation costs or market rent, we work out the difference – that difference counts as income. You can check how this affects your payments using the income deduction tables: Income deduction tables

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: The easiest way to tell us is online in MyMSD. Once you’ve logged in, select ‘Declare boarders and renters’. You need to tell us: - the address - details of the person paying you board - how much the board is - when you get paid, and how often. We will continue to use this amount every week, so make sure you let us know if it stops or changes. If you can't use MyMSD, you can also fill out our PDF form: You need to print this form, complete it, and either post it to us or bring it into one of our services centres. You can also pick one up from any of our service centres. Find a service centre

chunks.title: Income Related Rent reassessment issue
chunks.text: We've found we incorrectly reassessed some people's Income Related Rent. This only affects you if you have an Income Related Rent debt because you were investigated for benefit fraud. The investigation must have happened between 14 April 2014 and 21 December 2016. All Income Related Rent debt established since then has been calculated correctly. We'll contact you to let you know if you're affected. You don't need to do anything. If you are affected, your Income Related Rent debt will decrease. This means your overall debt with us will also decrease.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Income Relief Payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Income Relief Payment was a temporary, short-term payment for people who lost their jobs from 1 March 2020 to 30 October 2020 because of COVID-19. Applications were open from 8 June 2020 to 14 November 2020. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Income Relief Payment was up to 12 weeks of payments. It was available for people who: - lost their jobs due to COVID-19 - normally worked 15 hours or more a week (for 12 weeks or more) - were normally living in New Zealand when they lost their job - were a New Zealand citizen or a resident with a residence class visa - were 18 years old or over, or a financially independent 16- or 17-year-old. A person’s partner could also qualify if they met the criteria and earned less than $2,000 in wages or salary each week, before tax.

chunks.title: Payment rates
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Income Relief Payment was paid for up to 12 weeks. It stopped after 12 weeks, or if the person no longer qualified. The payment was paid at either: - $490 a week for people previously working 30 hours or more a week - $250 a week for people previously working 15 hours to 29 hours a week. Tax did not have to be paid on this payment.

chunks.title: Declarations
chunks.text: The declarations contain the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Income Relief Payment, for recipients and their partners. Applicant declaration for Income Relief PaymentPartner declaration for Income Relief Payment

chunks.title: Information for parents/caregivers of applicants for Youth benefits
chunks.text: If your dependent child applies for Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment, you may need to talk with someone. If someone else is caring for your child and applies for Unsupported Child's Benefit, you may need to go to a meeting.

chunks.title: Youth Payment
chunks.text: If your child meets the criteria, they might be able to apply for Youth Payment. Youth Payment

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: If your child applies for this benefit, we may ask an Independent Assessment Provider to contact you. This depends on why your child has applied for Youth Payment, eg if there's been a family breakdown. They won't contact you if there are any concerns about the safety or care and protection for your child. For example, your child has left the care of Oranga Tamariki. The Independent Assessment Provider will talk with you to get a better understanding of your child's situation. They'll also ask if there are any other options available to your child, eg if someone else could support them. They'll give us a report which will include their conversation with you. This will help us make a decision about whether to approve your child's benefit.

chunks.title: Young Parent Payment
chunks.text: If your child meets the criteria, they might be able to apply for Young Parent Payment. Young Parent Payment

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: If your child applies for this benefit, we may ask an Independent Assessment Provider to contact you. This depends on why your child has applied for Young Parent Payment, eg if there's been a family breakdown. There are some situations when they won't contact you, eg your child is: - married, in a de-facto relationship or civil union - 18 or older. The Independent Assessment Provider will talk with you to get a better understanding of your child's situation. They'll also ask if there are any other options available to your child, eg if someone else could support them. They'll give us a report based on their conversation with you. This will help us make a decision about whether to approve your child's benefit.

chunks.title: Unsupported Child's Benefit
chunks.text: If another person is caring for your child, they may be able to apply for an Unsupported Child's Benefit. To get this benefit, the carer and your child will need to meet certain criteria. Unsupported Child's Benefit

chunks.title: What you need to do
chunks.text: If the carer applies for this benefit, we'll call you to let you know. We'll also send you a letter. We may ask you to go to a Family Group meeting with the carer and your child (if they're 14 or older). You won't need to go to the meeting if you've already been to a family group conference with Oranga Tamariki. The Family Group meeting is held by Barnardos, an Independent Assessment Advisor. They'll talk with you to get a better understanding of the situation and why your child can't live with you.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If we approve the benefit, you may need to pay child support. The carer will apply for this through Inland Revenue. Inland Revenue will let you know if you need to pay this and how much you need to pay.

chunks.title: Insurance payments
chunks.text: Not all insurance payments affect your benefit. It depends on what you are getting the insurance for and what benefit or help you are getting from us.

chunks.title: When you need to tell us
chunks.text: You need to tell us if you get an insurance payment for any of the following: - income replacement insurance - whether you are paid this weekly or as a lump sum. If you invest the money and earn interest, this will be counted as income and you have to tell us about it - mortgage protection - only if you get Accommodation Supplement - health and disability - only payments for general expenses while in hospital, not for medical expenses - debt insurance - only if you get for Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - loan protection insurance - only if payments are taken directly from your bank account (you don't get to make payments) or if you get Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit

chunks.title: When you need to tell us
chunks.text: - life insurance - only if you invest the money (includes a bonus or if you give up policy early) - fire and general protection policies - only if you invest the money and earn interest, this will be counted as income and you have to tell us about it - after a severe weather event – you need to tell us these payments, but it may not affect your payment from us for 12 months, find out more about payments relating to a severe weather event. chunks.title: International Custody Dispute Payment
chunks.text: If you're a parent involved in an international custody or access dispute over the care of your child or children, and you have limited financial support, we may be able to help you. The International Custody Dispute Payment is a non-recoverable weekly payment that is made on the grounds of hardship.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get the International Custody Dispute Payment if you: - are the main carer of a dependent child or children - are finding it hard financially - have no other financial support reasonably available to you. You must also be: - in New Zealand under a temporary or limited purpose residency permit with a child to resolve a custody and access dispute, or - a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident who is in another country because of a Hague convention application or a Hague Convention order to resolve a custody dispute.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on your circumstances. This payment will start from the date you apply and can continue until you: - start work - can support yourself financially some other way (eg, payments from an overseas government) - leave the country or can't stay in the country - resolve the custody dispute (including any rights of appeal) - no longer require an order relating to possession and care because the child reaches an age where they don't need this.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 If you're overseas, call us on +64 9 913 0300 We'll: - talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help - let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us - ask you to complete an International Custody Dispute Payment form and discuss the best way to get this to us. Please only send certified copies to us (not original documents). They can be certified by a: - lawyer - notary public - Justice of the Peace, or - court official.

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Ireland
chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with Ireland to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Irish payments (paid by the Department of Social Protection). NZ payments covered by this agreement are: - New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) - Veteran's Pension - Supported Living Payment, where you have a health condition, injury or disability - Sole Parent Support for widows and widowers - Orphan's Benefit. Irish payments covered by this agreement are: - State Pension (Contributory) - State Pension (Transition) - Invalidity Pension - Widow's or Widower's (Contributory) Pension - Orphan's Contributory Allowance - Bereavement Grant

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with Ireland
chunks.text: - Guardian's Payment (Contributory). It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Job and Training Support Funds
chunks.text: We may be able to help if you're disabled or have a health condition and need training or have extra costs to do your job. The information on this page is also available in alternative formats and languages at the bottom of this page. Alternative formats and te reo Māori

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can get either Job Support or Training Support, depending on what you need help with.

chunks.title: Job Support
chunks.text: Job Support is funding to help pay for certain things related to your health condition or disability that you need to get a job or stay in a job. You can also apply if you're self-employed. Job Support funding can cover: - Equipment: Specialist disability office furniture or adaptive software. - Workplace modification: Money to help your employer make your workplace suitable for you. - New Zealand Sign Language and other interpreters: To interpret work meetings, documents about your job (e.g. your contract), and interpret some professional development. - Support person: Someone you hire to help you at work, such as a reader/writer or driver. - Parking: To cover costs of parking during your working hours.

chunks.title: Job Support
chunks.text: - Transport: To get to and from your work if you can't access public transport. - Productivity allowance: A wage subsidy paid to your employer while you learn skills and set up workplace supports. - Job coach: A short-term coach to help you if you start a new job, your job description changes, or you have a change in your disability which affects your job. If you're not sure what you need funding for, or how much, you can have an assessment done. This will help you find out what you need for your job.

chunks.title: Training Support Funds
chunks.text: Training Support funding can help you pay for extra costs relating to training if you have a disability or health condition. This is to help you get or stay in a job, including self-employment. Training Support funding can cover: - Equipment: Specialist disability furniture or adaptive software. - New Zealand Sign Language and other interpreters: To interpret classes, presentations and some documents. - Support person: Someone you hire to help you with your training, such as a reader/writer or driver. - Transport: To get to and from your training course if you can't access. If you're not sure what you need funding for, or how much, you can have an assessment done. This will help you find out what you need for your training.

chunks.title: What it doesn’t pay for
chunks.text: Job Support and Training Support can’t be used to pay for: - costs you’ve already paid for - anything your employer or training provider must provide to enable someone to do the job or training, for example a standard desk and chair - training course fees.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To apply for either Job Support or Training Support you must: - have a disability or a health condition that is likely to last longer than 6 months - need to pay for extra support to do a job or training because of your health condition or disability, these should be costs a non-disabled person would not have if they do the same job or training - be aged 16 to 64 years old (we may be able to keep paying if you keep working after you turn 65) - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand Ordinarily resident - be either a: New Zealand citizen residence class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand recognised refugee or protected person temporary class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand, and you're either waiting for the outcome of your claim to be recognised as a refugee or protected person, or you're applying for a residence class visa and must stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: - New Zealand citizen - residence class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand - recognised refugee or protected person - temporary class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand, and you're either waiting for the outcome of your claim to be recognised as a refugee or protected person, or you're applying for a residence class visa and must stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. If you're applying for Job Support, the job must: - pay at least minimum wage - this also applies if you're paid by commission - pay a similar rate that a non-disabled person doing the same job would get - not be a job reserved for disabled people only. If you're self-employed - you must work at least 15 hours a week and the business must be viable.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: If you're applying for Training Support, the training must be related to work. This can be either training to help you get a job in future, or for a job you already have.

chunks.title: Who can't get it
chunks.text: You can't get Job Support or Training Support if ACC or the Ministry of Health are already covering your job or training costs.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: If you qualify, you may get: - one-off costs, paid as a lump sum - ongoing costs, paid in instalments. How much you can get depends on your needs. We try to cover as much of the cost as possible. When you apply, we check what you need and tell you what costs we'll cover and how it will be paid. We can't reimburse you for costs you've already paid for. If you hire a support person or job coach, they must be paid at least the minimum wage.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can apply yourself, or have someone act on your behalf. Having someone act on your behalf

chunks.title: Step 1: Fill in the application form
chunks.text: Download and fill in the form for Job Support or Training Support (you can apply for both): You can either print the form and fill it in by hand, or fill in your answers online and save them as a PDF. If you're not able to fill in this form, contact us so we can fill it in on your behalf. You can contact us by: - email us at Support_Funds@msd.govt.nz - call us on 0800 551 001 - using our contact services if you're deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment. Deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment

chunks.title: Step 2: Evidence of your health condition or disability
chunks.text: You need to show us evidence of your disability or health condition. This can be either a: - Medical certificate or letter from your health practitioner (e.g. a doctor) - Report from an occupational therapist - Report from a psychologist - Document from ACC (e.g. a letter) - Evidence of on-going literacy or learning disabilities (e.g. a SPELD assessment). You may not need to do this again if you have already shown us evidence of your disability or health condition.

chunks.title: Step 3: Gather your documents
chunks.text: You need documents to show: - what you're applying for and how much it costs (e.g. quotes or contracts) - evidence of who you are (find out what documents we need for this). If you're already a client with us, you may not need to do this - details of your job or training, e.g. your employment contract, a letter from your employer, registration for your training, evidence of your self-employment. What to provide when you apply for a benefit

chunks.title: Step 4: Send us your application
chunks.text: Send us your completed application form and documents. You can do this by either: - scanning and emailing them to Support_Funds@msd.govt.nz - handing your form into one of our service centres, and we'll scan the documents while you're there - posting them to Ministry of Social Development, PO Box 1556, Wellington 6140, Attention: Support Funds. If you're sending us identity documents, you'll need to post certified copies to us. Please do not post your original identity documents.

chunks.title: After you've applied
chunks.text: Once we get your application, we will contact you within 5 working days. We'll send you a letter to let you know if your application has been accepted. If it is we'll contact you about the costs you have and how we can help with these. We'll pay the costs directly to the business providing the service or item.

chunks.title: If you need a support person or job coach
chunks.text: If you applied for someone to help you with your work or training, you need to: - have an assessment done to identify how much support you need - chose a support person or job coach - make sure they're registered with us. Find out more about what you need to do: Getting a support person or job coach

chunks.title: While you're getting Job or Training Support Funds
chunks.text: If anything changes that might affect your funding, please let us know straight away. You can tell us about a change by filling in a Support Funds Review Form, which you can download here: You can let us know by either: - calling us on 0800 551 001 - emailing us at Support_Funds@msd.govt.nz - find out how to contact us if you’re deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment. Deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment

chunks.text: 00:02:07 This is to help you get or stay in a job, including self-employment. Training support can cover 00:02:12 One, equipment, specialist disability furniture or adaptive software 00:02:18 Two, New Zealand Sign Language interpreters. 00:02:22 Support for you to employ an NZSL interpreter to interpret classes, presentations, and course documents. 00:02:28 Three, support person, someone you pay for yourself to help you at work, such as a reader, writer or driver. 00:02:35 And four, transport to get to and from your training course if you can't access public transport. 00:02:43 If you are not sure what you need funding for or how much, please talk to us about having an assessment done. 00:02:49 This will help you find out what you need for your training.

chunks.title: Alternative formats and te reo Māori
chunks.text: 00:02:53 What it doesn't pay for 00:02:55 Job support and training support can't be used to pay for 00:02:59 One, costs you've already paid for. 00:03:02 Two, anything your employer or training provider must provide to enable someone to do the job or training. For example, a standard desk and chair. 00:03:10 And three, training course fees. 00:03:13 Who can get it? 00:03:15 To apply for either job support or training support, you must 00:03:19 One, have a disability or a health condition that is likely to last longer than six months. 00:03:25 Two, have costs for extra support to do a job or training because of your health condition or disability. These should be costs a non-disabled person would not have if they do the same job or training.

chunks.title: Alternative formats and te reo Māori
chunks.text: 00:03:38 Three, be aged 16 to 64 years old. We may be able to keep paying if you keep working after you turn 65. 00:03:46 And four, be ordinarily resident in New Zealand. Find out what ordinarily resident means also at https://tinyurl.com/bddw2s2 00:04:00 Five, be either a New Zealand citizen, or a resident class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand, or recognised refugee or protected person, or 00:04:14 temporary class visa holder with the right to work in New Zealand and you're either waiting for the outcome of your claim to be recognised as a refugee or protected person, or you're applying for a residence class visa and must stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. 00:04:31

chunks.title: Alternative formats and te reo Māori
chunks.text: If you're applying for job support, the job must 00:04:33 One, pay at least minimum wage. This also applies if you're paid by commission. 00:04:40 Two, pay a similar rate that a non-disabled person doing the same job would get 00:04:44 And three, not be a job reserved for disabled people only. 00:04:50 If you're self-employed, you must work at least 15 hours a week, and the business must be viable. 00:04:56 If you're applying for training support, the training must be related to work. This can be either training to help you get a job in future, or for a job you already have. 00:05:07 Who can't get it? 00:05:08 You can't get job support or training support if ACC or the Ministry of Health are already covering your job or training costs.

This can be either a 00:07:08 One, medical certificate or letter from your health practitioner, for example a doctor. 00:07:12 Two, report from an occupational therapist. 00:07:18 Three, report from a psychologist. 00:07:21 Four, document from ACC, for example a letter. 00:07:25 And five, evidence of ongoing literacy or learning disabilities, eg a SPELD assessment. 00:07:34 You may not need to do this again if you have already shown us evidence of your disability or health condition.

chunks.title: Alternative formats and te reo Māori

For example, quotes or contracts. 00:07:51 Two, evidence of who you are. Find out what documents we need for this. If you're already a client with us, you may not need to do this. 00:08:00 And three, details of your employment or training. For example, your employment contract, a letter from your employer, registration for your training or study, evidence of self-employment. 00:08:13 Step 4. Send us your application. 00:08:15 Send us your completed application form and documents. You can do this by either 00:08:20 One, scanning and emailing them to Support_Funds@msd.govt.nz

chunks.title: Alternative formats and te reo Māori
chunks.text: 00:08:28 Or two, handing your form into one of our service centres and we'll scan the documents while you're there. 00:08:34 Or three, posting them to Ministry of Social Development, PO Box 1556, Wellington 6140, attention, support funds. 00:08:44 If you're sending us identity documents, you'll need to have certified copies to post to us.
