chunks.title: Self-employment start up payment
chunks.text: If you're starting a business and need help with essential start up costs, eg furniture or the first lot of stock, we may be able to help. If you don't have a business planexternal, we can talk with you about how to create one. We need to make sure that your business is viable before we can approve the payment.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Self-employment start up payment if you’re: - out of work, and - aged 16 or older and not qualified to receive NZ Super, and - disadvantaged in the local labour market, and - at risk of likelihood of long-term benefit dependency (this usually means you are getting a benefit or you qualify for one), and - able to meet the residency criteria. To meet the residency criteria you need to be ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: - a New Zealand citizen - a resident with a residence class visa - recognised as a refugee or protected person, or - have a temporary visa that allows you to work in New Zealand and either: have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: - have applied to be recognised as a refugee or protected person and are waiting on the outcome, or - have applied for a residence class visa and are compelled to stay in New Zealand because of unforeseen circumstances. Disadvantaged in the labour market means you have, or are expected to have, difficulty in getting or keeping a job. For example, you might have barriers to employment such as lack of education and training. You also need to: - be starting a new business and - have essential start-up costs that you need help with.

chunks.title: Who can't get it
chunks.text: You can't get the Self-employment start up payment if: - you're currently bankrupt - you're re-starting a business you've owned before.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation. We can pay for things like: - equipment required for the business - initial start-up stock for the business - materials required to produce goods for the business - renovation of premises to facilitate start of business or - one-off start-up costs, for example: connection fees, such as power, phone or internet first month's lease and bond legal costs associated with establishing the business insurance start-up costs for advertising/marketing printing business cards or flyers - connection fees, such as power, phone or internet - first month's lease and bond - legal costs associated with establishing the business - insurance - start-up costs for advertising/marketing

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: - printing business cards or flyers - setting up a basic website.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009. We'll: - ask you about your business - talk with you about: your business plan, if you already have one how to create a business plan, if you don't already have one a Business Training and Advice Grant and how this may be able to help. - your business plan, if you already have one - how to create a business plan, if you don't already have one - a Business Training and Advice Grant and how this may be able to help. Business Training and Advice Grant You'll need to send your business plan to us and we'll send it away to be independently assessed to make sure it's viable.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your business plan is viable, we can approve the payment.

chunks.title: COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment was to help businesses pay their employees while they waited for PCR test results. It was available between 9 February 2021 and 17 October 2022. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: This payment was available to help businesses pay employees waiting for a COVID-19 PCR test result. The application for the person who took the COVID-19 PCR test must have been for either: - an employee - someone who was a dependant of an employee, or - someone who was self-employed. They must have been unable to work from home while they waited for the results. Also, during the period applied for: - the business must have been registered with the New Zealand Companies Office (except for self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand. - self-employed people must have been physically located and legally working in New Zealand, along with other requirements, e.g. having an IRD number. - State Sector organisations were generally not eligible for COVID-19 payments, however some may have been granted an exception. This could be because they had an exception for a previous COVID-19 payment, or the organisation was a State-Owned Enterprise or Mixed Ownership Model company.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: The full eligibility criteria is listed in the declarations.

chunks.title: Payment amount
chunks.text: The payment amount was a one-off payment of $359 for each eligible employee. This was regardless of whether they were working full or part-time.

chunks.title: Declarations
chunks.text: There are different declarations depending on when you applied for the COVID-19 Short-Term Absence Payment. Your obligations and repayment responsibilities are in the declaration you agreed to when you applied. Short-Term Absence Payment declaration (12am 10 Aug 2022 to 11.59pm 17 Oct 2022)Short-Term Absence Payment declaration(12.01am 16 Mar 2022 to11.59pm 9 Aug 2022)Short-Term Absence Payment declaration (4pm 12 Mar 2021 to 12am 16 Mar 2022)Short-Term Absence Payment declaration (9am 9 Feb 2021 to 3:59pm 12 Mar 2021)

chunks.title: Skills for Industry
chunks.text: You may be able to get short-term job-focused training to help you get a job. Skills for Industry programmes are entry-level industry training programmes to help you get and keep a job. We've partnered with employers and training providers to create these. Programmes usually include: - entry-level training, e.g. workplace safety training - industry-specific training - help to get a job - on-the-job training once you start work - help to get a qualification to advance in the industry. Skills for Industry programmes are available in industries offering entry-level employment with a career pathway. Their goal is to help you find meaningful work. If there’s an industry you’d like to work in, ask your local Work and Income service centre staff about Skills for Industry, or call us on 0800 559 009.

chunks.text: Social Rehabilitation Assistance is a payment which helps people who are in a residential social rehabilitation programme and their benefit isn't enough to meet the fees. Payments are made directly to the programme provider.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get Social Rehabilitation Assistance if you are in an approved social rehabilitation programme and getting a benefit. If you are getting New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension it also depends on how much you and your spouse or partner earn. If you are going into a social rehabilitation programme but are not getting a benefit, contact us to find out if you qualify for one.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: This depends on the area where the social rehabilitation programme is. View our current payments (Map)external

Contact International Services for more information. These guides give details on how to get New Zealand benefits or pensions if you've resided in countries that have social security agreements or special agreements with New Zealand. If you're using another country to meet the residence criteria for a NZ benefit or pension, apply as early as you can. It will take time to get information we need from Immigration and other countries.

chunks.title: Reapply for Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: If you're getting Sole Parent Support and you still need it after 52 weeks, you have to reapply. The easiest way to do this is online.

chunks.title: How to reapply
chunks.text: You'll get a letter and notification in MyMSD 4 weeks before you need to reapply for Sole Parent Support. You need to: - log in to MyMSD - select the notification - complete the online reapplication form. You may need to talk with us. MyMSD will let you know if you need to do this. MyMSDlogin If you can't use MyMSD, call us and we'll: - book an appointment for you - complete the reapplication form with you at your appointment - let you know if there are any other documents you need to provide. Call us

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once you submit your form, you'll get a page that confirms your reapplication has been submitted successfully. It also tells you: - to book an appointment, if you haven't already - what supporting documents you'll need to provide. If we need any supporting documents, e.g. proof of your income, you'll need to either: - drop them off to your local service centre, or - upload or email them, contact us to find out how to do this, or - bring them with you to your appointment, if it's at a service centre. Local service centre Contact us

chunks.title: Your appointment
chunks.text: During your appointment we'll talk with you about: - work you've done before what you enjoyed what you didn't enjoy - what you enjoyed - what you didn't enjoy - the types of jobs or training you're interested in - other skills or experience you have - what you've done to look for work - how we can help you look for work.

chunks.title: Sole parent support - deduction tables
chunks.text: Use this table to estimate how much will be deducted from your Sole Parent Support benefit payment if you earn income.

chunks.title: Your deductions
chunks.text: If you're a sole parent, you can earn up to $160 a week (before tax), before your benefit is affected. Once you earn over $160 a week (before tax): - any income you get between $160 and $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your benefit by 30 cents for each $1 of income - any income you get over $250 a week (before tax) will reduce your benefit by 70 cents for every $1 of income. We calculate this by: - We take the income you get between $160 and $250 (maximum will be $90) and multiply by 0.3. - If your income is over $250, we take your total income and minus $250, then multiply by 0.7. - Then we add these two amounts together. If you're paying for childcare, you may be able to earn up to $180 a week (before tax), before your payment is affected. This depends on the amount you're paying for childcare while you're working. It can include private childcare arrangements and childcare costs not covered by a Childcare or OSCAR Subsidy.

chunks.title: Your deductions
chunks.text: Any other payments you get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement, may also be affected. If you earn over a certain amount, you won't qualify for Sole Parent Support. We call this the 'Gross weekly income cut-out point'. Sole Parent Support cut-out pointsexternal

chunks.title: Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support is a weekly payment that helps single parents find part-time work or get ready for future work. This benefit: - helps you get ready for future work (if your youngest child is under 3) - supports you to find part-time work (if your youngest child is aged 3-13) - may mean you can get help with education and training. Only one parent or caregiver can get Sole Parent Support. Shared care of your child could affect your payments.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get Sole Parent Support if you: - are aged 20 or older (if you're 19 or younger, you may be able to get a Young Parent Payment) - are a single parent or caregiver - have one or more dependent children under 14 - are not in a relationship, and - do not have adequate financial support. Young Parent Payment You also need to: - be either: a New Zealand citizen a permanent resident, or have a residence visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - a New Zealand citizen - a permanent resident, or - have a residence visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - have lived continuously in NZ for at least 2 years since either: becoming a NZ citizen becoming a permanent resident, or getting a residence class visa - becoming a NZ citizen

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: - becoming a permanent resident, or - getting a residence class visa - be ordinarily resident in NZ, and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when you apply. Ordinarily resident If you meet all the above criteria except for the one about how long you've lived in New Zealand, talk to us. Phone us This information is a guide only. For more detail about who can get it, read: Sole Parent Support qualification criteria (Manuals and Procedures)external

chunks.title: Check if you can get Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Sole Parent Support and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Sole Parent Support is paid weekly. How much you get depends on your situation and how much you earn. Sole Parent Support rates and income limits (Map)external Income deduction tables If you get Sole Parent Support, you'll also automatically get a Winter Energy Payment. This is paid during the Winter months. Winter Energy Paymentexternal

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us, based on the answers you give in your application. If you want to get child support through Inland Revenue, you can apply through us when you complete your online application. Or you can apply through Inland Revenue. Any child support payments you get will be counted as income for your benefit. Apply online Child support

chunks.title: Complete your next steps in MyMSD
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, you need to complete your next steps in MyMSD. - Complete a Jobseeker profile. - Read and agree to your obligations. - Provide your documents. - Verify your identity. - Book an appointment. Apply online - Complete your next steps in MyMSD

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, we'll call you if there's anything else you need to do.

chunks.title: If your application's approved
chunks.text: - We'll let you know when your payments will start. - We'll send you a Community Services Card to help with the costs of healthcare and public transport. - You may get a family tax credit. This can be paid with your benefit or from Inland Revenue (it depends what option you chose when you applied for your benefit). Community Services Card Family tax credit (Inland Revenue)external

chunks.title: While you're getting Sole Parent Support
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting a Sole Parent Support benefit. If you don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop. This includes things like: - telling us if something changes - finding or preparing for work - taking part in work ability assessments. Sole Parent Support obligations

chunks.title: Getting Sole Parent Support for more than 12 months
chunks.text: If you're getting Sole Parent Support and you still need it after a year, you have to re-apply. Re-apply for Sole Parent Support

chunks.title: Once your youngest child turns 14
chunks.text: Once your youngest child turns 14, you are no longer able to get Sole Parent Support. We may transfer you from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support. Find out when you'll transfer and what you'll need to do differently when you're on Jobseeker Support. Transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: When someone getting Veteran's Pension dies
chunks.text: If someone getting Veteran's Pension dies, the surviving partner or dependent child may be able to get extra help from us. You need to let us know they've passed away. You can do this by completing our online form. Register a senior's death with usexternal We'll contact you to discuss what extra help you may be able to get.

chunks.title: Lump sum payment
chunks.text: There are 2 lump sum payments available. Which payment you may be able to get depends on whether the person who's died is a veteran or not.

chunks.title: Person who died is a veteran
chunks.text: If you're the surviving partner or dependent child of a veteran who's died, you may be able to get a lump sum payment. This is $7,580.60 and not taxed. It's to help with funeral costs. You may be able to get this lump sum payment if the veteran who died: - was getting Veteran's Pension when they died - had either a war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, or disablement pension of 52% or more under the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - war disablement pension of 70% or more under the War Pensions Act 1954, or - disablement pension of 52% or more under the Veterans' Support Act 2014, and - was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died. The surviving partner will get the full amount of the lump sum payment. If there is no surviving partner, the lump sum payment will be split between any dependent children.

chunks.title: Person who died is not a veteran
chunks.text: If your partner dies, you may be able to get a lump sum payment of $5,780.43. This is not taxed and is to help with funeral costs. You can get this lump sum payment if your partner: - was getting Veteran's Pension when they died, and - was ordinarily resident in New Zealand when they died.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension payments continue for 28 days
chunks.text: As well as a lump sum payment, we may also be able to keep payments going for 28 days into the person's account who's died. Or pay it into the surviving partner's account instead. If this happens, the amount we pay over 28 days will be deducted from any lump sum payment you receive.

chunks.title: Ongoing payments
chunks.text: What type of ongoing payments you can get from us depends on whether you're the surviving partner or dependent child.

chunks.title: Surviving partner
chunks.text: If you're the surviving partner of a veteran who's died, we'll look to see if you: - meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension, or - were included as a partner in their Veteran's Pension payments. If you meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension, we'll reassess your Veteran's Pension payment. This is so we can make sure you're now getting the correct amount. You may be better off getting a different payment from us, for example NZ Super. We'll contact you to discuss your options. If you were included as a partner in their Veteran's Pension payments, your Veteran's Pension payments may stop. It depends on your situation. We'll contact you to discuss your options.

chunks.title: Surviving dependent child
chunks.text: There may be a surviving dependent child of a veteran who's died, who's going to be cared for by a person who's not their parent. If so, the caregiver may be able to get Orphan's Benefit or Unsupported Child's Benefit. Orphan's Benefit Unsupported Child's Benefit The dependent child may also qualify for a Children's Pension from Veteran's Affairs. Veterans' Affairs websiteexternal

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: While you're living in public (social) housing, you need to let us know straight away about any changes in your or your partner's situation You need to tell us no matter how much rent you pay. This could be changes to: - income - assets - people moving in or out of the property - children in your care, for example having a child or changing custody arrangements. Changes may affect: - the amount of rent you pay - whether you still qualify for public housing, or - whether the property you're in is still suitable for you. If you don't let us know, you could end up paying the wrong amount of rent and may have a debt to pay back. Or you may only get a few weeks' notice before your rent goes up.

chunks.title: If you get child support through Inland Revenue
chunks.text: Inland Revenue (IR) will share your child support payment information with us every time they pay you child support. We'll use the shared information from IR and treat this as income if you get one of these payments from us: - a main benefit, e.g. Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension and you have a partner who doesn't qualify for this but is included in your payments - Veteran's Pension and you're under 65 - Accommodation Supplement - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support - Special Benefit - Childcare Subsidy - OSCAR Subsidy, or - Employment Transition Assistance. If you get one of these payments from us, you don't need to tell us about most types of IR child support payments. The only type you need to tell us about is if you're getting Court Ordered lump sum child support payments.

chunks.title: If you get child support through Inland Revenue
chunks.text: If you don't get one of the payments in the above bulleted list, you need to tell us about your IR child support payments. You also need to tell us about any other child support payments you get.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to call us. Who you call depends on your situation. If you get: - a benefit or extra help payments from us, call us on 0800 559 009 - NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, call Senior Services on 0800 552 002 - no payments from us or Senior Services, call Housing Unit on 0800 673 468.

chunks.title: Tenancy reviews
chunks.text: As well as telling us about any changes, your tenancy may be reviewed from time to time. Tenancy reviews

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with South Korea
chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with South Korea to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or South Korean payments (paid by the South Korean National Pension Service). NZ payments covered by this agreement are: - New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) - Veteran's Pension The only South Korean payment covered by this agreement is the Old-age Pension. It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text: If you get an overseas pension and a payment from us, you may be able to use the Special Banking Option. There are 2 methods of payment for overseas pensions: - Direct Payment Option, and - Special Banking Option. Your overseas pension will be paid using the Direct Payment Option unless you tell us you want the Special Banking Option.

chunks.title: Direct Payment Option
chunks.text: Usually when you get an overseas pension, the overseas agency pays this directly into your bank account. This means: - you'll get separate payments: your overseas pension from the overseas agency and your NZ payment from us - your overseas pension from the overseas agency and - your NZ payment from us - your NZ payment will be reduced dollar-for-dollar by the amount of your overseas pension - your NZ payment and overseas pension payments will vary as the exchange rates go up and down - you're responsible for paying tax on your overseas pension.

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text: In some cases, you can choose to have the overseas agency pay your overseas pension into a Special Banking Option bank account in NZ. This bank account is in your name but can only be accessed by Work and Income. The account doesn't incur bank fees and it doesn't earn any interest. Using the Special Banking Option (SBO) means: - you'll get a payment from Work and Income that is your NZ payment - any payments paid into the SBO account will not be passed on to you, except in specific circumstances. If the payment is passed on to you, it may affect your NZ payment amount. If the payment is not passed on to you, your NZ payment won't be affected (including when the exchange rate for the overseas payment changes)

chunks.title: Special Banking Option
chunks.text: - If the payment is passed on to you, it may affect your NZ payment amount. - If the payment is not passed on to you, your NZ payment won't be affected (including when the exchange rate for the overseas payment changes) - you don't need to pay NZ tax on payments that are in the SBO account, unless they are passed onto you. If the payment in the SBO account is passed on to you, we'll let you know. If the total amount of your overseas pensions is more than your NZ payment, you may be better off using the Direct Payment Option.

chunks.title: If you get a Netherlands pension
chunks.text: If your Netherlands pension is paid into the SBO account, we'll pay your holiday pay to you shortly after it's received. You may have paid voluntary contributions towards your Netherlands pension. If you did, and your pension is paid into the SBO account, we'll pay the voluntary portion to you shortly after it's received. This means you'll get an extra: - monthly payment from us with your voluntary portion of your Netherlands payment - yearly payment (in June) from us with your holiday pay portion. You may have to pay tax on these payments.

chunks.title: Who can use the Special Banking Option
chunks.text: You can choose to use the Special Banking Option if: - you get an overseas pension from either: Australia Guernsey Ireland Jersey the Netherlands, or United Kingdom, and - Australia - Guernsey - Ireland - Jersey - the Netherlands, or - United Kingdom, and - you don't have a non-deductible component in your pension (e.g. voluntary contributions), except if it's a Netherlands pension. If you choose to use the Special Banking Option and have a partner who also gets an overseas pension from the same country, they must choose the Special Banking Option as well. Once you've chosen the Special Banking Option, you can switch to the Direct Payment Option. But you can't switch back to the Special Banking Option again.

chunks.title: When you can't use it
chunks.text: You can't use the Special Banking Option when: - you're going overseas for more than 26 weeks - you're un-discharged bankrupt - you have an overseas pension debt with the overseas agency - you have more than one overseas pension and you can't get a NZ payment because one of your pensions is too much - you have a voluntary or non-deductible component to your overseas pension (except if it's a Netherlands pension).

chunks.title: Apply for Special Banking Option
chunks.text: To apply for the Special Banking Option, you need to complete 3 forms: - Information release form - Bank account application form, and - Special Banking Option Offer form. To find the forms you need, select the country you get your overseas pensions from below. Once you've filled the forms out, you can either: - scan and email them to us at international_services@msd.govt.nz - drop them off to one of our service centres or - post them to our International Services team.

chunks.title: Special Benefit issue
chunks.text: We found some people would have been better off financially if they'd moved from Special Benefit to Temporary Additional Support after 1 April 2006. We thought Special Benefit clients couldn't move to Temporary Additional Support. We got this wrong. We're sorry for this and we're fixing it. We want all our clients to get all the help they need.

chunks.title: Who's affected by the Special Benefit issue
chunks.text: You may be affected if you got Special Benefit after 1 April 2006.

chunks.title: If you're still getting Special Benefit
chunks.text: We'll arrange to meet with you if you're still getting Special Benefit and might be better off moving to Temporary Additional Support. We'll talk about your situation and help you work out what's best for you. You can bring a family member, friend or advocate with you, and take some time before you decide if you want to stay on Special benefit or move to Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: If you used to get Special Benefit check if you're owed money
chunks.text: If you used to get Special Benefit, you can use the payment errors enquiry form to see if you're owed money. It won't say how much you're owed. If you're owed money you can use the form to submit your enquiry. We can process it and pay the money we owe you. Unfortunately, our staff can't tell you if you're owed money or how much it is. Payment errors enquiry form The payment errors enquiry form will tell you if you're owed money - it won't say how much you're owed. We'll write to you to confirm your payment. The payment errors enquiry form will also let you know if we owe you money for the Accommodation Supplement error. More information on errors with Accommodation Supplement areasMore information on errors with Accommodation Supplement accommodation types

chunks.title: Checking payment errors for someone else
chunks.text: You can also use the payment errors enquiry form to check to see if we owe someone else money when: - they're not a current client - a person has died. Information to make an enquiry for someone elseInformation to make an enquiry for someone who has died The form will tell you if the person you're making an enquiry for is on the list of clients who may be affected and you can apply for them. It won't say how much they may be owed.

chunks.title: How payments may affect your benefit or allowance
chunks.text: If you're getting a benefit or allowance from us, it won't be affected for 12 months from the date we make any payment to you because of the Special Benefit issue. If you: - still have this money after 12 months, you'll need to tell us and it will be counted for any benefits or payments that are asset tested - invest the money you get and earn interest, after 12 months you'll need to tell us and this will be counted as income.

chunks.title: Working for Families and Special Benefit payment
chunks.text: Your payment won't affect your Working for Families payment because Special Benefit payments aren't counted as income for Working for Families.

chunks.title: Impact on your taxes
chunks.text: You won't have to pay tax on this payment because Special Benefit payments aren't taxable. Any income you earn on it (for example interest) will be taxable.

chunks.title: Review rights
chunks.text: If you don't understand or agree with a decision we've made, please talk with us so we can explain it. You have the right to ask us to review a decision you think is wrong. You can use the application form on our website, or write to us. We need to get your request within three months. If you have a good reason why you can't ask us to review a decision within three months, get in touch. We may still be able to review the decision. You can find out more on the review of a decision page of our website, or you can give us a call on 0800 559 009. Get a decision reviewed

chunks.title: Income rules for Special Benefit
chunks.text: If you're getting Special Benefit you have to tell us about any income, one-off payments or assets you, or your partner, get.

chunks.title: How it works
chunks.text: If you get Special Benefit as part of the benefits you're paid you have to tell us about any other regular payments, assets or one-off payments you, or your partner, get. Declare income

chunks.title: Changes to your other payments
chunks.text: If your other payments from us change, it could affect how much you get for your Special benefit. This includes main benefits (e.g. Jobseeker Support or Supported Living Payment), and extra help payments (e.g. Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance). If your main benefit payment goes up, your Special Benefit payment may go down. If your main benefit goes down, your Special Benefit may go up. Main benefits are reviewed every year on 1 April, and they usually go up from this date. If you're getting extra help, your Special Benefit may change if your extra help payment changes. If your costs go down (e.g. your prescriptions), your Special Benefit payment may go down, because you're paying less. If your costs go up (e.g. your rent), your Special benefit may go up, because you're paying more.

chunks.text: Special Disability Allowance is a weekly payment for people who have a spouse or partner who is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks. chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get a Special Disability Allowance if: - you are getting a benefit or pension - your spouse or partner is in residential care, or has been in a public hospital for over 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Special Needs Grant
chunks.text: A Special Needs Grant is a one-off payment to help you pay an essential or emergency cost if you can't pay it another way.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a Special Needs Grant if you: - have a cost you cannot pay for that's either: immediate and essential, or an emergency - immediate and essential, or - an emergency - have no other way to pay for this cost - either: are a New Zealand citizen are a permanent resident, or have a residence class visa - are a New Zealand citizen - are a permanent resident, or - have a residence class visa - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here. When you have an emergency cost, we'll also look at: - whether you knew the cost was going to come up - whether you could have covered the cost yourself - how the Special Needs Grant will help your situation. There may also be extra criteria you need to meet depending on the essential or emergency cost you apply for.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: It may also depend on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or cash assets you and your partner have. Cash assets The following income and cash asset limits apply :

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: Food
chunks.text: We may be able to help you if you have no other way to pay for food eg, no money in the bank and no cash assets. Cash assets Food

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on your situation and what you need help with. Essential costs could include things like: - driver licence - bedding - dental treatment - food - health travel costs - effluent treatment system maintenance and repair - laser therapy to remove birthmarks - vasectomies - wigs and hairpieces - breast pump if you can't breastfeed because you or your baby have health issues. Emergency costs could include things like: - ambulance fees - medical treatment - medical equipment - water tank refill.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll give you a payment card (if you don't already have one) and load the money onto it. We'll talk to you about how to get this to you. You have 7 days to spend the money before it expires.

chunks.title: Using your payment card
chunks.text: A payment card is like an Eftpos card and you can use it at any supermarket or store that accepts them. You can login to MyMSD to see how much you have left on your payment card and when it expires. Find out more about MyMSD Once you've used your payment card, keep it. You can use it again if you need help from us in the future.

chunks.title: Special portability of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Special Portability enables you to continue to have your New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension (New Zealand pension) paid to you when you move to a Pacific country. Special Portability enables you to continue to have your New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension (New Zealand pension) paid to you when you move to one of the following Pacific countries. - American Samoa - Cook Islands - Federated States of Micronesia - Fiji - French Polynesia - Guam - Kiribati - Marshall Islands - Nauru - New Caledonia - Niue - Northern Mariana Islands - Palau - Papua New Guinea - Pitcairn Island - Samoa - Solomon Islands - Tokelau - Tonga - Tuvalu - Vanuatu - Wallis and Fortuna To be able to receive your New Zealand pension in one of these Pacific countries you must:

chunks.title: Special portability of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: - be entitled to receive the New Zealand pension before leaving New Zealand, and - be entitled to the New Zealand pension in your own right. Non-qualified partners (eg those under 65 years) have no entitlement overseas, and - be going to live in one of these Pacific countries for more than 52 weeks, and - be resident in one of these Pacific countries when each payment is made to you, and - be residing in and present in New Zealand on the date of application for special portability Your payment rate will be: Extra assistance you may get in New Zealand cannot be paid overseas, including living alone allowances, disability allowances or accommodation supplements. If you are receiving an overseas benefit or pension the basic rate payable will be adjusted first, then payment will be calculated according to the table above.

chunks.title: Special portability of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Tax is not deducted in New Zealand before payments are made overseas. You may have to pay tax on your payments in the country you have moved to. Please contact the tax authority in the country you are moving to for more information. Please tell us about any changes that could affect your payments, such as changes to: - your personal details, eg your name or address - your living situation, for instance if you begin living with a partner - if you or your partner move to another country - if you or your partner begin to receive an overseas pension. Life Certificates will be sent out to you regularly to complete and return to ensure your details and entitlements are kept up to date. Please also tell us if you return to live in New Zealand.

chunks.title: Special portability of New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Contact us before you go overseas for any reason or any length of time. This will ensure that you continue to receive the correct entitlement. Contact us For further information on special portability please contact International Services. International Services

chunks.title: Transfer from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support
chunks.text: Once your youngest child turns 14, we may transfer you from Sole Parent Support to Jobseeker Support. Find out when you'll transfer and what you'll need to do differently when you're on Jobseeker Support. Once your youngest child turns 14, you are no longer able to get Sole Parent Support. You will then transfer to Jobseeker Support if you meet the criteria. If you don't meet the criteria (e.g. you're working 30 hours or more a week or studying full-time), you may be able to get other payments instead. Use our Check What You Might Get tool to find out what payments you could get. Check what you might getexternal

chunks.title: We'll let you know about the transfer
chunks.text: If we transfer you to Jobseeker Support, it will happen automatically. You don't need to do anything. We'll send you a letter 4 weeks before your youngest child turns 14 to let you know if you'll transfer to Jobseeker Support. - If you can transfer, we'll let you know when this will happen. - If you can't transfer, we'll let you know when your Sole Parent Support payments will stop.

chunks.title: What will change for you
chunks.text: Once you transfer to Jobseeker Support: - your work obligations may change - you'll need to reapply every 26 weeks (6 months), and - we'll assess your income differently. You'll have a weekly income assessment, so you'll have to tell us about your income as you earn it and it may affect your benefit payment. Your payment rate won't change when you transfer to Jobseeker Support. Read more about these changes below.

chunks.title: Work obligations
chunks.text: On Sole Parent Support, you have an obligation to either: - look for part-time work, if your youngest child is aged 3-13, or - prepare for work, if your youngest child is under 3 or you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can’t work. Once you transfer to Jobseeker Support, you have an obligation to: - look for full-time work, or - look for part-time work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can only work part-time, or - prepare for work, if you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can’t work or can only work less than 15 hours a week. While you're on Jobseeker Support we may ask you to meet with us or take part in activities that will help you meet these obligations. This could include attending a Kōrero Mahi work seminar or meeting with us in person.

chunks.title: Work obligations
chunks.text: Kōrero Mahi work seminar Jobseeker Support obligations

chunks.title: Reapply for your benefit
chunks.text: On Sole Parent Support you reapply every 52 weeks (1 year). Once you transfer to Jobseeker Support, you have to reapply every 26 weeks (or 6 months). Reapply for Jobseeker Support

chunks.title: Income assessment
chunks.text: On Sole Parent Support, you have an annual income assessment. This means we assess your income over 52 weeks. Once you transfer to Jobseeker Support, you have a weekly income assessment. This means: - you have to tell us about your income as you earn it, and - the amount you earn may affect your benefit payment. If you don't tell us about income you earn, we may not pay you enough. Or we may pay you too much and you'll get a debt which you'll have to pay back. Declare income

chunks.title: Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super and Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: You need to have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time to get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension. If you haven't, you may be able to use a Social Security Agreement (SSA) country to meet this criteria.

chunks.title: Residence criteria
chunks.text: You must have lived in NZ for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. The total number of years you need is based on your date of birth when you apply. If you're a refugee or protected person, this may be different depending on the age you started living in NZ. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive. Work out how many years you need

chunks.title: Using an SSA country to meet residence criteria
chunks.text: If you haven't lived in NZ for the required number of years, you may be able to include time you've spent: - living in a country that NZ has a SSA with, and/or - contributing to a SSA country's pensions scheme. You can only include time from one of the SSA countries. You cannot combine time across multiple SSA countries. If you're ordinarily resident in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, you usually cannot include time from an SSA country. You may be able to use time from some SSA countries (Australia, Canada, Denmark, Ireland, Malta and the Netherlands) if you meet certain criteria. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. International Services

chunks.title: How to include time from an SSA country
chunks.text: Some agreements have certain criteria you have to meet if you want to include time from their country. If you meet the criteria, you can add together your time: - in NZ from age 20, and - from the SSA country from age 20. This needs to add up to the total number of years you need to meet the residence criteria. The total must include 5 years from age 50 (you can use your time from the SSA country for the 5 years too). The criteria is outlined further down the page.

chunks.title: If you don't meet residence criteria using SSA country
chunks.text: You may have spent time living in a NZ Realm country - that is the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau. If so, you may be able to use this time to meet the residence criteria as well. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. International Services Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include time from an SSA country
chunks.text: Select the SSA country below to find out what time you can include towards the residence criteria. If you're ordinarily resident in an SSA country when you apply, you can only use time from that country. The exception to this is Jersey and Guernsey, as you can combine time from both of these. If you want to talk about your situation, contact our International Services team. International Services

chunks.title: Australia
chunks.text: If you meet certain criteria, you can include your time of Australian residence between: - age 20, and - age 67 (the age you qualify for Australian Age Pension). Australian residence means that while you lived in Australia you either: - were an Australian citizen - had an Australian residence class visa, or - were a NZ citizen with a Special Category visa.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include the time
chunks.text: To include this time you must: - have been living in Australia (as defined by Centrelink) for 12 months from age 20, of which at least 6 months were continuous, and - be age 67 or older (the age criteria for the Australian Age Pension).

chunks.title: Canada
chunks.text: You can include time you’ve spent: - living in Canada from age 20 - contributing to the national insurance scheme in Canada from age 20.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include this time
chunks.text: To include this time, it needs to be considered a 'Canadian creditable period' by Service Canada. Service Canadaexternal

chunks.title: Overlapping Canadian creditable periods
chunks.text: You may have Canadian creditable periods under the Old Age Security Act and under the Canada Pension Plan. If any of these periods overlap, we’ll only take them into account once.

chunks.title: Denmark
chunks.text: You can include time you've spent living in Denmark (as defined by Udbetaling Danmark) from age 20. Udbetaling Danmarkexternal

chunks.title: Greece
chunks.text: You can include time you've spent: - living in Greece (as defined by e-EFKA) from age 20 - contributing to the national insurance scheme in Greece. e-EFKA - Electronic National Social Security Fundexternal

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include the time
chunks.text: If you're ordinarily resident in Greece when you apply for NZ Super, you must meet extra criteria to include this time. You must have been ordinarily resident in NZ for 12 months at any time before you apply for NZ Super. If you're ordinarily resident in NZ when you apply for NZ Super, you don't need to meet this extra criteria.

chunks.title: Ireland
chunks.text: You can include time you’ve spent contributing to the Irish insurance scheme from age 20.

chunks.title: Jersey/Guernsey
chunks.text: You can include time you’ve spent contributing to the insurance schemes in Jersey or Guernsey. You can also use your partner’s, or former partner’s, time they’ve spent contributing to these insurance schemes.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include the time
chunks.text: If you're living in New Zealand, to include this time you must have contributed to either scheme for at least 12 months. If you're living in Jersey or Guernsey, to include this time you must: - have been ordinarily resident in New Zealand for at least 1 year from age 20, and - have contributed to either scheme for at least 12 months.

chunks.title: Malta
chunks.text: You can include time you’ve spent contributing to the insurance scheme in Malta from age 20.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include the time
chunks.text: If you're living in New Zealand, to include this time you must: - have at least 1 year of continuous NZ working age residence, and - be ordinarily resident in NZ when you apply. If you're living in Malta, to include this time you must: - have at least 1 year of continuous NZ working age residence - be ordinarily resident in Malta when you apply, and - and be present in NZ or Malta when you apply.

chunks.title: Definition of NZ working age residence
chunks.text: NZ working age residence means that you were living in NZ between age 20 and 65. If you were overseas during this time, you may still have NZ working age residence if you were: - employed outside of NZ and your employer deducted and paid income tax to Inland Revenue in NZ, or - with your partner who was employed outside of NZ and was paying NZ income tax on their earnings.

chunks.title: Netherlands
chunks.text: You can include time you've spent contributing to the national insurance scheme in the Netherlands from age 20.

chunks.title: South Korea
chunks.text: You may include time you’ve spent contributing to the Korean National Pension scheme from age 20.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet to include the time
chunks.text: If you're living in New Zealand, to include this time you must: - have at least 1 year of continuous NZ working age residence, and - be ordinarily resident in NZ when you apply. If you're living in South Korea, to include this time you must: - have at least 1 year of continuous NZ working age residence - be ordinarily resident in South Korea when you apply, and - and be present in NZ or South Korea when you apply.

chunks.title: Definition of NZ working age residence
chunks.text: NZ working age residence means that you were living in NZ between age 20 and 65. If you were overseas during this time, you may still have NZ working age residence if you were: - employed outside of NZ and your employer deducted and paid income tax to Inland Revenue in NZ, or - with your partner who was employed outside of NZ and was paying NZ income tax on their earnings.

chunks.title: United Kingdom
chunks.text: You can include time you’ve spent living in the UK from age 20. You can also include time where you: - lived outside of the UK from age 20, and - were paying contributions to the UK National Insurance scheme.

chunks.title: Before you start the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: Get ready for the Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course, and find out what you need to bring, how to get there and when you start. After you've applied and been accepted for the LSV course, there's some things you need to do to make the most of the course. When the NZ Defence Force get in touch to let you know you're accepted, they give you a detailed list of everything you need to do and what to bring. They also confirm the date you start the course and they organise your transport.

chunks.title: What to bring
chunks.text: NZ Defence Force will give you a list of what to bring. We keep in touch regularly before you start the course, and can help you get everything you need. You need to bring things like: - formal clothes for the graduation dinner – this could be a dress, suit pants or shirt and tie, and you need dress shoes - toiletries like toothbrush, toothpaste, hairbrush and deodorant - some money to buy personal items – there's a shop at the camp and you'll be given times to go there if you need to - if you take medication regularly, you need to bring enough for 6 weeks in the original container. Talk to your doctor or pharmacy and ask for enough to last 6 weeks.

chunks.title: What you wear during the course
chunks.text: You wear military uniforms, footwear and equipment during the course. All of this is given to you when you arrive. You must wear this during the course and return it when you leave.

chunks.title: Cell phones and mobile devices
chunks.text: You can bring a cell phone or mobile device with you, but you won't be able to use it all the time. You need to focus on the course, so you can get the most out of it. You need to hand in your cell phone or mobile device when you arrive at the camp. Make sure your family and friends know you won't be able to access your phone all the time, so they understand you can't reply quickly. You can write letters while you're on the course and post these from the camp. People can also write letters back to you. I wanted to become physically and mentally stronger. I wanted to push myself and become a better person. – Trainee Badger

chunks.title: Getting to the course
chunks.text: NZ Defence Force will organise your transport for you. You don't need to pay for your ticket. Some of the transport options are: - bus - rental van - plane - NZ Defence Force bus or van. NZ Defence Force works out the best way for you to travel, and they will tell you what you need to do and when. They also contact you a few days before you leave, to make sure you're ready. You can't bring your own car to the course, as you are not allowed to park at the camp.

chunks.title: After the course
chunks.text: NZ Defence Force also organises your transport home. Again, you don't need to pay for transport.

chunks.title: Staying in emergency housing
chunks.text: If you're staying in emergency housing, find out your rights and responsibilities, what to do when you leave, and if you have any issues or concerns. Emergency housing is short-term accommodation for people who need it because: - they can't stay where they are, and - they have nowhere else to go.

chunks.title: Cost of emergency housing
chunks.text: In most cases we'll cover the cost of your accommodation for the first 7 nights if you qualify. Then you'll have to start paying for some of the accommodation costs. This is called an Emergency Housing Contribution. Cost of emergency housing

chunks.title: Your rights
chunks.text: Find out your rights while you're staying in emergency housing. Your rights while in emergency housing

chunks.title: What we expect from you
chunks.text: When you're staying in emergency housing, there are things we expect you to do. What we expect you to do when in emergency housing

chunks.title: Your responsibilities
chunks.text: If you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights, there are responsibilities you have to meet from the 8th night. Find out what these are and what happens if you don't meet them. Your responsibilities in emergency housing

chunks.title: Concerns or complaints
chunks.text: Find out what to do if you have concerns or want to make a complaint about your emergency housing supplier. Concerns or complaints when in emergency housing

chunks.title: Steps to Freedom Grant
chunks.text: If you've been released from prison, we may be able to help you get set up in the community with a 'Steps to Freedom' grant.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get a 'Steps to Freedom' grant if: - you've been in prison for 31 days or more and - have now been released, or released on home detention. If you've been released into a residential care facility, you may be able to get the grant for any costs that aren't paid for by the facility. If you have a partner, they must: - earn less than $1,467.61 gross per week - not have any money or assets worth more than $2,351.46.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: You can get up to $350. If you had any money when you were released from prison, this will be taken off the amount of the grant.

chunks.title: What you get it for
chunks.text: It can help pay for any initial costs you have when you're trying to set yourself up in the community, such as: - housing, bond or rent in advance - beds and bedding - essential appliances, for example a kettle or toaster - power, gas or connecting a phone in your home - food - clothing and toiletry items, for example a toothbrush or toothpaste.

chunks.title: In prison
chunks.text: You can apply if you're in prison and about to be released. You need to arrange an appointment with the Work and Income Prisoner Reintegration Coordinator.

chunks.title: Not in prison
chunks.text: If you've recently been released from prison, you'll need to call us to talk about this. Phone us We'll tell you what documents you'll need. You'll also need to provide a release form if you've been in prison in New Zealand, or any deportation documents if you've been in prison overseas, showing proof of any money you had when you were released and how many days you spent in prison.

chunks.title: Payment
chunks.text: Once you've been granted a Steps to Freedom grant, we'll pay this to you through: - your bank account (if you have one) - a Steps to Freedom Card. A Steps to Freedom card is a Westpac debit card, which is pre-loaded with your grant payment.

chunks.title: Stop childcare payments
chunks.text: You need to let us know if you're no longer eligible for childcare. Get in touch straight away so we can stop the payments.

chunks.title: Reasons for stopping payments
chunks.text: Your childcare payments need to stop: - the day after your job or course ends if your children are at school - if your income is above the income limitexternal - after 12 weeks if you stop work temporarily because you have a health condition or are injured - when your child reaches the age limit for the subsidy - 5 for pre-school (or 6 if you're getting a Child Disability Allowance) or 14 for school (or 18 if you're getting a Child Disability Allowance) - when your child leaves the provider or programme - if your child leaves your care - if your child attends childcare for fewer than 3 hours a week - if you leave NZ permanently.

chunks.title: How to stop your payments
chunks.text: myMSD login You can stop your childcare payments online, using MyMSD. You need to log in and select the 'Something has changed' option.

chunks.title: Stop your payment
chunks.text: If your situation has changed so much that you should no longer get your benefit or payment, you need to stop it as soon as possible. If you don't, you may get a debt.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: You need to call us right away if you're receiving: - Unsupported Child Benefit - Orphans Benefit - Child Disability Allowance (CDA) - Special Benefit. Phone us

chunks.title: If someone has died
chunks.text: Please call us if someone getting a benefit has passed away. If they were getting NZ Super or Veteran's Pension you can tell us by filling out our online form. Phone us Register a senior's death with usexternal

chunks.title: NZ Super
chunks.text: To stop your New Zealand Superannuation or Veteran's Pension payment, you'll need to contact Senior Services on 0800 552 002

chunks.title: All other benefits and payments
chunks.text: You can stop any other benefit or payment online, using MyMSD. You need to log in, and select the ‘Something has changed’ option. My MSD You'll need to tell us: - the reason for stopping payment - the date your situation changed - details relating to your change in situation eg, employer name and contact details. You can also tell us if you want to stop your payment temporarily, eg if you've got a short work contract or seasonal work. If you are stopping a main benefit payment (eg Jobseeker Support or Sole Parent Support) you can choose to transfer to the Working for Families payment automatically if you qualify. If you have debt with us, you can arrange debt repayments at the time you stop your payments.

chunks.title: All other benefits and payments
chunks.text: If you get the Youth Payment or Young Parent Payment make sure you also contact your Youth Service provider directly to tell them about your change in circumstances. Find your nearest provider (Youth Service)external

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: It will take up to 5 working days for the change to be processed.

chunks.title: If you're a social housing tenant or on the social housing register
chunks.text: After your benefit payments have stopped, you'll need to continue to tell us about any changes to your income, because it may affect your Income Related Rent or eligibility for social housing. Otherwise: - your rent may be increased to market rent if you're a social housing tenant - you won't be offered a property if you're on the social housing register. Declare income

chunks.title: What happens if you don't tell us
chunks.text: If we find out later that any information you give us is not true, or that you knew information you should have told us and did not tell us, we may stop your payments. You might need to pay money back, we may impose a penalty, and you could be prosecuted.

chunks.title: New Zealand Superannuation
chunks.text: Find out all you need to know about NZ Super. The new residence criteria for NZ Super affect people turning 65 from 1 July 2024. Find out about this change

chunks.title: Who can get NZ Super
chunks.text: If you want to apply for New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super), you need to meet certain criteria. You can read about the criteria on our 'Who can get NZ Super' page. Or you can use our step-by-step guide. Who can get NZ Super Find out if you can get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Apply for NZ Super
chunks.text: You can apply now if either: - your 65th birthday is in the next 12 weeks, or - you're already 65. You can apply online through MyMSD, unless you live overseas. Apply for NZ Super

chunks.title: Living overseas
chunks.text: If you live in the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau, you need to complete and sign an application form. Apply for NZ Super from Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau If you live in another country, call us or email our International Services team. We'll check if you qualify and let you know how to apply. Phone us Email our International Services team

chunks.title: When you get paid
chunks.text: If you apply before you turn 65 or on the day you turn 65, you will be paid from your 65th birthday. If you apply after you turn 65, you will be paid from the date you apply.

chunks.title: How much you can get for NZ Super
chunks.text: New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super) is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. How much you get depends on your situation and what tax code you use. How much you can get for NZ Super

chunks.title: Get other income
chunks.text: If you or your partner get other income as well as NZ Super, it may change the tax code you use. This means you could get less for your NZ Super payments, it depends what tax code you're on.

chunks.title: Payment dates for NZ Super
chunks.text: NZ Superannuation is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. Find out what dates you get paid for this year. NZ Super payment dates

chunks.title: If something changes while getting NZ Super
chunks.text: There are obligations you need to meet while getting NZ Super. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop. This includes telling us about any changes that might affect what you're entitled to or how much you get paid. For example, this could be changes to your: - relationship - address, or - tax code. Changes when you're getting a benefit or payment NZ Super obligations

chunks.title: If you get other income
chunks.text: You can work while you get NZ Super. It doesn't depend on your income or your assets. However any income you do earn can affect other payments you get from us, e.g. Accommodation Supplement. If you get other income, it may also change the tax code you use. This means you could get less for your NZ Super payments, it depends what tax code you're on.

chunks.title: Have a partner included in your NZ Super
chunks.text: If you have a partner and they're included in your NZ Super, there are things they'll need to do as well. NZ Super obligations for partners

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text: If you get NZ Super and go overseas, you may still be able to be paid. It depends if you're going overseas for a holiday or going to live overseas. Going overseas for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Overseas pensions
chunks.text: You or your partner may qualify for a pension from another country - this is called an overseas pension. If you or your partner do qualify for an overseas pension, it may affect payments you get from us. Overseas pensions

chunks.title: Someone getting NZ Super dies
chunks.text: If someone who was getting NZ Super dies, you can tell us by either: - using our online formexternal, or - calling us on 0800 552 002. Find out what happens to payments after someone dies

chunks.title: SuperGold Card
chunks.text: Find out about SuperGold Card and how to get one. The SuperGold Card is for people aged 65 years and older (it doesn't expire). It gives you instant discounts and special offers at thousands of businesses across New Zealand, and in Australia. There's also a Veteran SuperGold Card which is a specially branded SuperGold Card to recognize service to our country in the Armed Forces. The card gives you: - instant savings on everyday essentials like electricity, insurance, food and healthcare - discounts on entertainment, travel and in retail stores - free off-peak public transport. Find out more, or sign up to the newsletter for SuperGold updates, on the SuperGold website. SuperGoldexternal

chunks.title: How to get a SuperGold card
chunks.text: We'll automatically send you either a: - SuperGold Card once your NZ Superannuation is approved, or - Veteran SuperGold Card once your Veteran's Pension is approved. This usually takes a few weeks. You may have to wait a month or 2 if you apply before your 65th birthday. If you don't qualify for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, you can still apply for a SuperGold Card. There are certain criteria you'll need to meet. Visit the SuperGold Card website to apply. Apply for a SuperGold Card (SuperGold)external Apply for a Veteran SuperGold Card (SuperGold)external

chunks.title: If you have a Community Services Card
chunks.text: If you have a Community Services Card, it will stop working when your NZ Superannuation is approved. This is because there's been a change in your circumstances (i.e. your income). You'll need to re-apply for a new card. Community Services Card When you reapply, we'll send you a 'combo card'.

chunks.title: What is a combo card
chunks.text: This 'combo' card is a combination of both your Community Services Card and your SuperGold card. You'll be able to use your 'combo' card for all discounts and subsidies that the 2 cards provides. Your combo card will have the initials 'CSC' on the back, as well as the expiry date. This identifies it as a combo card.

chunks.title: When your combo card expires
chunks.text: When your combo card is due to expire, we'll automatically send you a new one. However, if you get NZ Super and your income is close to the limit for a Community Services Card, we'll send you a renewal application form. You'll need to complete this and return it to us. Then we'll send you a new combo card. Community Services Card

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment - single 18+ deduction tables
chunks.text: Use this table to estimate how much will be deducted from your Supported Living Payment benefit payment if you earn income.

chunks.title: Your deductions
chunks.text: Clients who are receiving Supported Living Payment can receive up to $160 per week before their income will affect their benefit. For clients who earn over $160 per week: - income between $160 and $250 per week, their benefit is reduced by 30 cents for each $1 of income - income over $250 per week, their benefit is reduced by 70 cents for every $1 of income. We calculate this by: - We take the income you get between $160 and $250 (maximum will be $90) and multiply by 0.3. - If your income is over $250, we take your total income and minus $250, then multiply by 0.7 - Then we add these two amounts together. If you have personal earnings, e.g. you're working, you can earn up to $180 a week (before tax), before your payment is affected.

chunks.title: Your deductions
chunks.text: Any other payments you get, e.g. Accommodation Supplement, may also be affected. If you earn over a certain amount, you won't qualify for Supported Living Payment. We call this the 'Gross weekly income cut-out point'. View the gross weekly income cut-out points for Supported Living Paymentexternal

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: Supported Living Payment is a weekly payment to help you if you have, or are caring for someone with, a significant health condition, injury or disability.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: To get Supported Living Payment you generally must: - either: be a New Zealand citizen be a permanent resident, or have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - be a New Zealand citizen - be a permanent resident, or - have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - have lived continuously in NZ for at least 2 years since either: becoming a New Zealand citizen becoming a permanent resident, or getting a residence class visa - becoming a New Zealand citizen - becoming a permanent resident, or - getting a residence class visa - be ordinarily resident in NZ, and - be ordinarily resident in New Zealand when you apply. Ordinarily resident It may also depend on you and your partner's income.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: There are also other criteria you need to meet. They depend on the reason you're applying, which could be because you either: - have a health condition, injury, or disability, or - are caring full-time for someone.

chunks.title: Have a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text: If you're applying because you have a health condition, injury or disability, you must also be: - 16 years or older, and - either: permanently and severely restricted in your ability to work because of a health condition, injury or disability, or totally blind. - permanently and severely restricted in your ability to work because of a health condition, injury or disability, or - totally blind. This means you have either a: - condition affecting your capacity to work for more than 2 years, or - life expectancy of less than 2 years. It also means that you can't regularly work 15 hours or more a week in open employment.

chunks.title: Caring full-time for someone
chunks.text: If you're applying because you're caring full-time for someone, you must also be: - giving full-time care at home to someone other than your partner, and - aged either: 18 years or older and do not have a dependent child, or 20 years or older and have a dependent child. - 18 years or older and do not have a dependent child, or - 20 years or older and have a dependent child. The person you're caring for must otherwise need to receive hospital or residential-level care. Examples of this level of care are: - rest home care - residential disability care - extended care services for severely disabled children and young people - inpatient or residential hospital care.

chunks.title: Check if you can get Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: To find out if you could get Supported Living Payment and what else you might qualify for, use our 'Check what you might get' tool.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: Supported Living Payment is paid weekly. How much you get depends on the reason you're applying.

chunks.title: Have a health condition, injury or disability
chunks.text: If you're applying because you have a health condition, injury or disability, how much you get depends on: - your situation, and - how much you and your partner earn (in some cases we may not count all of your income). We'll let you know when you apply if we won't count some of your income.

chunks.title: Caring full-time for someone
chunks.text: If you're applying because you're caring full-time for someone, how much you get depends on: - your situation, and - how much you and your partner (if you have one) earn.

chunks.title: Rates and income limits
chunks.text: Supported Living Payment cut-out points (Maps and Procedures)external If you get the Supported Living Payment, you'll also automatically get a Winter Energy Payment. This is paid during the Winter months. Winter Energy Payment

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: How you apply depends on whether you're already getting a benefit or not. As part of the application process we'll need to see proof of the reason you're applying. This includes either: - information that confirms your condition and the impact it has on your ability to work, or - medical information from the health practitioner of the person you're caring for. We'll let you know what's needed and how to get this to us.

chunks.title: Not getting a benefit
chunks.text: You can apply online through MyMSD. We'll also check to see if you can get any other help from us, based on the answers you give in your application. MyMSD will tell you what you’ll need to provide, including a medical certificate from your health practitioner. If you want to get child support through Inland Revenue, you can apply through us when you complete your online application. Or you can apply through Inland Revenue. Any child support payments you get will be counted as income for your benefit. Child support Apply online

chunks.title: Already getting a benefit
chunks.text: If you are getting another benefit (eg Jobseeker Support), call us on 0800 559 009. We'll let you know what you need to do.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: Once you've submitted your online form, we'll call if there's anything else you need to do. Apply online

chunks.title: If your application's approved
chunks.text: - We'll let you know when your payments will start. - We'll send you a Community Services Card to help with the cost of healthcare and public transport. - If you have dependent children under 18, you may get a family tax credit. This can be paid with your benefit or from Inland Revenue (it depends what option you chose when you applied for your benefit). Community Services Card Family tax credit (Inland Revenue)external The health and disability support system may also be able to help, eg, time off for caregivers or home support services. Visit the Ministry of Health website for more information. Ministry of Healthexternal

chunks.title: Meet your obligations
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting a Supported Living Payment benefit. If you don't do them, your benefit could reduce or stop. This includes things like: - telling us if something changes - preparing for work - taking part in work ability assessments. If you have a partner, there are things they'll need to do as well. Supported Living Payment obligations

chunks.title: Confirming your circumstances
chunks.text: We must review your circumstances at least once every 52 weeks (one year) to check you're getting the correct assistance and amount. If we need up-to-date information from you, we will send you a Confirming your Circumstances form. It's important to fill it out and return it promptly – if you don't respond by the due date, Supported Living Payments will stop. Confirming your circumstances

chunks.title: Review of income
chunks.text: We must review your annual income each year to check if anything has changed and you're getting the right amount. You may get a form to fill out for this review. It is separate from the Confirming your Circumstances review. Review of annual income

chunks.title: Update us with information about your health condition
chunks.text: Every 2 years we may ask you for updated medical information. This is to check how your health condition or disability currently impacts on your capacity to work. Renew your medical certificate or information

chunks.title: Working while you're getting Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: You can still work while you’re getting a Supported Living Payment, even if it’s just a few hours a week. We can help you prepare for work, find a job or study. Help with work Supported Living Payment - single 18+ deduction tables
