chunks.title: Travelling overseas for more than 26 weeks
chunks.text: If you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension and plan to go overseas for more than 26 weeks, you must apply to keep these payments going. You need to meet certain criteria to apply for this. There are different rules if you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension and you're planning to: - travel overseas for less than 26 weeks, or - live overseas Travelling overseas for 26 weeks or less Living overseas if you get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension There are also different rules if you're going overseas while on a benefit. Going overseas while on a benefit

chunks.title: Getting other payments
chunks.text: You can apply to keep your NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension going while you're overseas for more than 26 weeks. You can't get any other payments from us while you're overseas. Examples of other payments are: - Winter Energy Payment - Accommodation Supplement - Disability Allowance - Temporary Additional Support.

chunks.title: Keep NZ Super/Veteran's Pension going
chunks.text: You need to apply at least 6 weeks before you leave New Zealand.

chunks.title: Who can apply
chunks.text: You can apply to keep getting your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension payments while you’re overseas if you: - qualify for the NZ Super or Veteran's Pension in your own right (i.e. not be a partner included in the payment) - are ordinarily resident in New Zealand when you apply - intend to travel overseas for more than 26 weeks, - tell us all the countries you intend to travel to.

chunks.title: If you used an SSA country to meet residence criteria
chunks.text: When you applied for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, you may have had to use a Social Security Agreement (SSA) country to help you meet the residence criteria. This means you may have included time you spent: - living in a country that NZ has a SSA with, and/or - contributing to a SSA country's pension scheme. If you used an SSA country to meet the residence criteria, you may not be able to keep getting your payments. You need to contact International Services to talk about your situation. International services

chunks.title: Your partner is included in your payments
chunks.text: If you have a partner who’s included in your NZ Super or Veteran's Pension payments, their payments will stop while you're overseas. This is because they won't qualify for their payments. When you return to New Zealand, you will not be able to be include them in your NZ Super or Veteran’s Pension payments again. They will need to apply for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension themselves, once they qualify.

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: The amount you get while you’re overseas depends on the number of months you lived in New Zealand between the ages of 20 and 65. This is a total of 45 years, or 540 months. If you were overseas between the ages of 20 and 65, we may still be able count this time as if you were living in New Zealand. For example, if you or your partner were: - doing missionary work on behalf of a religious body - working overseas and paying New Zealand income tax on earnings. You must have remained ordinarily resident in New Zealand during this time. If you’re not sure whether we would count your time overseas, call us to discuss your situation.

chunks.title: Lived in NZ for the whole 45 years
chunks.text: If you lived in New Zealand for the whole 45 years (540 months) between age 20 and 65, you can get either: - $595.57 gross a week, if you're single, or - $492.14 gross a week, if you have a partner.

chunks.title: Lived in NZ for less than 45 years
chunks.text: If you lived in New Zealand for less than 45 years (540 months) between age 20 and 65, how much you get depends on how many months you lived in New Zealand. For example, if you lived in New Zealand for 18 years between age 20 and 65, this is 216 months. So we would calculate it this way: - if you're single: 216 ÷ 540 x $595.57 (the single rate of NZ Super we use) = $238.22 gross a week - if you have a partner: 216 ÷ 540 x $492.14 (the couple rate of NZ Super we use) = $196.85 gross a week.

chunks.title: Get an overseas pension
chunks.text: If you get an overseas pension, this won't affect your NZ Super payments. You may still be able to get your overseas pension while you're overseas, you need to talk to the organisation you get the pension from.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to apply at least 6 weeks before you leave New Zealand. Call us to book an appointment. International services You'll need to bring: - your passport - another form of identification - your travel itinerary or tickets. You also need to complete the application form and bring it to your appointment.

chunks.title: What happens next
chunks.text: We'll send you a 'client declaration' form every 6 or 12 months (depending on your circumstances). This will be sent to your overseas address and you'll also be able to see it in MyMSD. MyMSD You must complete and return this to us within 4 weeks or your payments may stop. You can post it, or scan and email it to us. International services

chunks.title: Tell us about any change of circumstances
chunks.text: You also need to let us know every time any of your circumstances change. This is so we can make sure we are paying you the correct amount. You can call or email us. International services

chunks.title: How you're paid
chunks.text: You can choose to have payments made directly to either your: - NZ bank account every 2 weeks, or - overseas bank account every 4 weeks. If you choose to be paid to your overseas bank account: - it can take around 4-6 weeks to change your payments to this account. - don't close your New Zealand account until you receive your first payment into your overseas account.

chunks.title: Taxes
chunks.text: Payments are made at a gross rate when you're travelling for more than 26 weeks. You need to contact Inland Revenue before you leave New Zealand so they can organise your tax. Inland Revenueexternal We'll send you a tax certificate every April. This will be sent to your overseas address and you'll also be able to see it in MyMSD. It will show what you have been paid during the previous financial year while you have been overseas.

chunks.title: Trust payments
chunks.text: If you are able to get a regular or one-off payment from a trust you need to tell us about it as it may affect your benefit.

chunks.title: What is this?
chunks.text: Having a trust may or may not affect your benefit and there are a number of things we need to look at so we can find this out. You need to contact us so we can start the process. We'll ask you to fill out a trust questionnaire and there's also quite a bit of information we'll need you to show us. Phone us Here's what you need to get together if possible: - trust financial statements or details of income and expenses - latest rates notice for any properties owned by the trust - latest trust portfolio investment market valuation report and portfolio income report for the last 12 months - details of any other trust investments or income eg term deposits - personal tax summaries and returns. Generally, payments you can receive from a trust will be personal income for benefit purposes.

chunks.title: How your benefit will be affected
chunks.text: You can check how your income will affect your benefit using the income deduction tables. Income deduction tables

chunks.title: Contact
chunks.text: If you need more information or want to discuss this in more detail contact us. Phone us

chunks.title: Social Security Agreement with the United Kingdom
chunks.text: New Zealand (NZ) has an agreement with the United Kingdom to share responsibility for social security coverage. This agreement generally allows you to apply for certain NZ payments (paid by us) or Australian payments (paid by Centrelink). The payments covered by this agreement are different, depending on whether you're living in the UK or NZ. It also allows you to add together your periods of residence in either country so you can meet certain criteria for these payments.

chunks.title: Living in the UK
chunks.text: If you've lived in New Zealand and now live in the UK, you may be able to get some payments. Social Security Agreement with the UK - living in the UK

chunks.title: Living in New Zealand
chunks.text: If you've lived in the UK and now live in New Zealand, you may be able to get some payments. Social Security Agreement with the UK - living in New Zealand

chunks.title: Unsupported Child's Benefit
chunks.text: Unsupported Child's Benefit is a weekly payment which helps carers supporting a child or young person whose parents can't care for them because of a family breakdown.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get the Unsupported Child's Benefit if the child or young person you care for is: - 18 years old or younger - single - financially dependent on you - not able to be cared for by their parents. You must: - be 18 or older and the main carer of the child or young person - have primary responsibility for the day-to-day care of the child - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - not be the child or young person's natural or adoptive parent or step-parent. You and the child or young person must normally live in New Zealand. You'll need to apply for Child Support from the child's parents. This money goes to the government to help cover what we pay you. You'll also need to attend a Family Meeting (if you haven't already had a Family Group Conference) to confirm that there has been a family breakdown and that you'll be the main caregiver for a period of time.

chunks.title: Income
chunks.text: This benefit is not based on your income or any money the child gets from working after school or in the holidays. But other income the child gets, eg from a family trust, ACC, investments or their parents' estate, could affect whether you qualify and the amount you can get. If you're working and are granted the Unsupported Childs Benefit, you may also qualify for the In-work tax credit from Inland Revenue. In-work tax credit (Inland Revenue)external You won't be able to get the Unsupported Child's Benefit at the same time as Board payments from Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children or Working for Families Tax Credits from Inland Revenue (except In-work tax credit) for the same child.

chunks.title: Parent/caregiver involvement
chunks.text: When you apply for an Unsupported Child's Benefit for a child, the parent/caregiver will be invited to discuss the situation. There are some circumstances where this won't happen, for example, when a recent Oranga Tamariki - Ministry for Children Group Conference has been held. Information for parents/caregivers

chunks.title: Child is 16 or 17
chunks.text: In some cases, a child may qualify for their own income support. To find out more: - call us, or - Youth Serviceexternal

chunks.title: How much you can get
chunks.text: How much you get depends on how old the child is and any income they have. Current ratesexternal You will also be able to get a Clothing Allowance. This is paid automatically when you get an Unsupported Child's Benefit. Clothing Allowance

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: Call us to talk about your circumstances and we'll explain how to apply, and what documents you'll need to provide. You'll usually need to provide: - a full birth certificate for the child - a copy of the custody or guardianship agreement - details about the child's income - Family Group Conference Outcomes, Court Orders or Court Approved Plans - names, addresses and phone numbers of the child's parents and their places of work. If you don't have these documents or find it hard to get these, please let us know. Call us

chunks.title: How long do I have to complete my application?
chunks.text: You have 20 working days from when you first contacted us. If we ask for any supporting documents, you'll need to provide them within this time. If you can't complete your application within 20 working days for any reason, please let us know when you talk with us.

chunks.title: When do payments start?
chunks.text: If your application is approved, you'll usually receive your first payment two to four weeks from the date you apply or start looking after the child (whichever is later). You'll need to apply as soon as you become the child's main caregiver as we can't backdate payments.

chunks.title: Other payments
chunks.text: If you get the Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit you may be able to get help with other expenses.

chunks.title: Holiday and Birthday Allowance
chunks.text: You automatically get these 2 payments each year if you already get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit for a child in your care. Use these payments to celebrate important events in the child’s life, like their birthday or Christmas. Holiday and Birthday Allowance

chunks.title: Establishment Grant
chunks.text: Establishment grant is paid automatically when you first get Unsupported Child's Benefit or Orphan's Benefit. This is a once only payment of $350 for each child you're caring for. This money helps you buy things like a bed, bedding and clothing. You won't be taxed on this money, and you won't have to pay it back. Establishment Grant

chunks.title: School and Year Start-up Payment
chunks.text: Help with the costs that mostly happen at the beginning of the year, in particular pre-school and school-related costs such as clothing, school fees and stationery. School and Year Start-up Payment

chunks.title: Extraordinary Care Fund
chunks.text: This fund helps support children to develop their skills and talents. It can also help children who are experiencing difficulties that are significantly impacting on their development. Extraordinary Care Fund

chunks.title: Unsupported Child's Benefit obligations
chunks.text: There are things you need to do when you're getting an Unsupported Child's Benefit. If you don't do them your benefit could reduce or stop.

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: You must tell Work and Income or your contracted service provider (where one is assigned to you) immediately if: - the care and/or support arrangements for the child change - the financial circumstances of the child change - either you or the child intend to travel overseas - you or the child have changes to personal details, eg: name address bank account number - name - address - bank account number - either you or the child have any other change that may affect your benefit entitlement or rate.

chunks.title: If you don't meet your obligations
chunks.text: If there's any reason why you or your partner can't meet your obligations, talk to us straight away. Contact us If you and your partner don't tell us about changes in your life that might affect your benefit entitlement, or rate, then: - your benefit may be reviewed and cancelled - you may have to pay back the total amount of any overpayment that you receive - we may impose a penalty (up to 3 times the value of the overpayment) - you may be prosecuted and fined, or imprisoned.

chunks.title: Urgent or unexpected costs
chunks.text: If you're struggling to meet your living costs, or get an unexpected bill, we might be able to help you, even if you're working.

chunks.title: What we can help you with
chunks.text: - Housing costs Get help to stay in your home.

chunks.title: Housing costs
chunks.text: Get help to stay in your home. - Bereavement Get help to pay for funeral or tangi expenses.

chunks.title: Bereavement
chunks.text: Get help to pay for funeral or tangi expenses. - Car repairs Get help to repair your car.

chunks.title: Car repairs
chunks.text: Get help to repair your car. - Dental treatment Get help to pay for immediate or essential dental treatment.

chunks.title: Dental treatment
chunks.text: Get help to pay for immediate or essential dental treatment. - Fire or theft Get help after a fire or theft.

chunks.title: Fire or theft
chunks.text: Get help after a fire or theft. - Food Get help to pay for food.

chunks.title: Food
chunks.text: Get help to pay for food. - Glasses Get help to pay for eye tests and glasses.

chunks.title: Glasses
chunks.text: Get help to pay for eye tests and glasses. - Home repairs and maintenance Get help with essential home repairs and maintenance.

chunks.title: Home repairs and maintenance
chunks.text: Get help with essential home repairs and maintenance. - Health and disability Get help if you have a health condition or disability.

chunks.title: Health and disability
chunks.text: Get help if you have a health condition or disability. - Moving house Get help with costs if you're moving house.

chunks.title: Moving house
chunks.text: Get help with costs if you're moving house. - Power, gas, water bills or heating Get help to pay an urgent power, gas or water bill, heating costs, or a water tank refill.

chunks.title: Power, gas, water bills or heating
chunks.text: Get help to pay an urgent power, gas or water bill, heating costs, or a water tank refill. - Whiteware Get help to buy or repair whiteware.

chunks.title: Whiteware
chunks.text: Get help to buy or repair whiteware.

chunks.title: Other urgent or unexpected costs
chunks.text: If you have a cost that's urgent or unexpected and not listed here, eg, clothing or bedding, we may still be able to help. We may be able to give you a one-off payment. What payment you may be able to get depends on if you're getting a benefit or not, and what cost you have.

chunks.title: If you're already getting a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get either Special Needs Grant or Advance Payment of Benefit. Special Needs Grant Advance Payment of Benefit Each payment covers lots of different costs. If you get stuck, give us a call on 0800 559 009 and talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: If you're not getting a benefit
chunks.text: You may be able to get either: - Special Needs Grant or - Recoverable Assistance Payment. Special Needs Grant Recoverable Assistance Payment Each payment covers lots of different costs. If you get stuck, give us a call on 0800 559 009 and talk with us about your situation.

chunks.title: Using a payment card
chunks.text: How to use your payment card, where you can use it and what you can buy. Make sure you: - set a personalised PIN before you use it - sign the back of your card - spend the money within 7 days from when it's loaded onto the card (for glasses you have up to 28 days) - use the card at shops that are registered with us and accept payment cards - only spend up to the amount of money on your card. How to set your PIN

chunks.title: Setting your PIN
chunks.text: You need to set a personalised PIN to use your payment card. If you haven't set your own PIN the card won't work. If you have more than one card, you need to set a PIN for each card.

chunks.title: How to set your PIN:
chunks.text: - Log in to MyMSD. - Go to 'My payment cards'. - Select the card you want to add a PIN for. - Enter a 4-digit PIN - don't use a PIN that is consecutive, easily associated with you (like birthdays), or the numbers on your card. - Re-enter your PIN to confirm. - Done! Your PIN is now ready to go. MyMSD Loginexternal Other ways to set your PIN: - call us and say "set my card PIN" - register your voice so you can set your PIN by calling us at any time without waiting to talk to a person - our staff in our service centres can help set your PIN in MyMSD - we have other ways you can contact us if you're deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment.

chunks.title: Reset your PIN
chunks.text: You can reset your PIN by following the same steps above.

chunks.title: Locked card
chunks.text: The card will lock if you enter an incorrect PIN 5 times. You can unlock this by resetting your PIN, or wait until the next day – the card will unlock automatically at midnight.

chunks.title: How to use the card
chunks.text: - At the checkout, swipe the payment card through the EFTPOS terminal. - Select the CHQ option. - Enter your personalised PIN. Make sure no one can see you PIN when enter it. - Sign your receipt – the shop staff will check this matches your signature on the back of your card. Find out how to set your PIN Don't throw the card away after you've used up the balance. Keep it so we can use it again if you need more help.

chunks.title: What you can buy
chunks.text: You can only use your payment card to buy the essential items you applied for. These are things like: - food and groceries - clothes - dental treatment. You can't buy non-essential items like: - alcohol - cigarettes, tobacco or vaping products - gift cards or vouchers (except for phone top-ups) - lotto tickets - non-essential appliances or electronics (such as an air fryer or gaming console). If you're a young person in Youth Service on Money management, there's a few different rules about what you can get: Money management - Youth Service - ratonga taiohiexternal

chunks.title: Keeping your PIN and card safe
chunks.text: Your PIN is a security measure to make sure no one else can use your payment card. Do not write your PIN down, and do not tell anyone else your PIN. This includes police, family members and Ministry of Social Development staff. If you think someone else knows your PIN, reset it or call us. Keep your payment card in a safe place. If you need further payments, we can load them onto this card, so you don't need to go to a service centre to get another one. Never let anyone else use your payment card.

chunks.title: Where you can use it
chunks.text: You can only use payment cards in shops that are registered with us and accept our cards. When you apply we'll talk with you about what help you need, how much money has been granted and which shops you can go to. You can check which shop your payment is for in MyMSD. MyMSDexternal. You may be able to use the card in more than one registered shop, depending on what you've applied for. For example, you can use food grant payments in more than one grocery or food shop.

chunks.title: Money leftover
chunks.text: You can check how much money you've spent and how much is left online in MyMSD. MyMSDexternal. You may have money leftover if you: - haven't spent all the money yet because you're planning to spend it at more than one shop - didn't need to spend all the money. Any money you don't need will stay on the payment card until the 7 days is up. After the 7 days is up it will expire. If the money is for glasses you have up to 28 days to spend it. If you don't spend the full amount on your card, you can't get cash out for the rest. You also can't get vouchers or gift cards for the rest.

chunks.title: Vasectomies
chunks.text: If you're on a benefit or a low income and want a vasectomy, we may be able to help with the cost of travel, accommodation and surgery. - The decision whether to get a vasectomy or not is an entirely personal decision made in consultation with a health practitioner, e.g., a doctor. - You don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may be able to get help if: - assistance is not available from your District Health Board - only partial funding is available from your District Health Board District Health Board - Ministry of Health websiteexternal - you need to travel away from home or pay private fees. You also need to: - be 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Service) Youth Serviceexternal - be a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have no other way to meet these costs. It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: We can pay up to $300 for: - travel - accommodation - surgery. How much you get depends on your situation. You don't have to pay the money back.

chunks.title: How to apply
chunks.text: You need to call us on 0800 559 009 We'll book you an appointment to come in and see us. We'll let you know what you need to bring.

chunks.title: Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Find out all you need to know about the Veteran's Pension.

chunks.title: Who can get Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: If you want to get Veteran's Pension, you need to meet certain criteria. You can read about the criteria on our 'Who can get Veteran's Pension' page. Or you can use our step-by-step guide. Who can get Veteran's Pension Find out if you can get Veteran's Pension - our step-by-step guide

chunks.title: Apply for Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Find out how to apply for Veteran's Pension and what documents you need to provide. Apply for Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: How much you can get for Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: How much you get for Veteran's Pension depends on your situation and what tax code you use. How much Veteran's Pension you can get

chunks.title: Get other income
chunks.text: If you or your partner get other income as well as Veteran's Pension, it may affect your Veteran's Pension payments. Getting other income may also mean the tax code you use could change. This means you could get less for your Veteran's Pension payments, it depends what tax code you're on.

chunks.title: Payment dates for Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: Veteran's Pension is paid fortnightly on a Tuesday. Veteran's Pension payment dates

chunks.title: If something changes while getting Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: There are obligations you need to meet while getting Veteran's Pension. If you don't do them, your payment could reduce or stop. This includes telling us about any changes that might affect what you're entitled to or how much you get paid. For example, this could be changes to your: - relationship - address, or - tax code. Changes when you're getting a benefit or payment New Zealand Superannuation and Veteran's Pension obligations

chunks.title: Have a partner included in your Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: If you have a partner and they're included in your Veteran's Pension, there are things they'll need to do as well. Veteran's Pension obligations for partners

chunks.title: Going overseas
chunks.text: If you get Veteran's Pension and you're going overseas, you may still be able to be paid. It depends if you're going overseas for a holiday or going to live overseas. Going overseas for NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Overseas pensions
chunks.text: You or your partner may qualify for a pension from another country - this is called an overseas pension. If you or your partner do qualify for an overseas pension, it may affect payments you get from us. Overseas pensions

chunks.title: Someone getting Veteran's Pension dies
chunks.text: If someone getting Veteran's Pension dies, the surviving partner or dependent child may be able to get extra help from us. When someone getting Veteran's Pension dies

chunks.title: Violent relationships
chunks.text: If your relationship has ended because of family violence, there are a number of ways we may be able to help you. If you're in immediate danger, dial 111 and ask for the Police. Family violence help and support (NZ Police)external The 'Are you OK' website also has information and services that can help you. You can call them on 0800 456 450. Are You OK (Family Violence Information and Support)external

chunks.title: How we can help
chunks.text: If you are living in or leaving a violent relationship you can talk to Work and Income about how we can help you. We have specialist staff in each region who will help you access the right support services, including financial help from us, depending on your need. This could include: - financial help to get back on your feet - including benefit payments, help with accommodation costs, special needs grants and other assistance - help to find somewhere to live - including information on housing options in your area and, if need be, an assessment for social housing - referring you to other support services and agencies able to help you. We'll also support you to build a better future for you and your family by helping you prepare or look for suitable work. We'll take into account your particular circumstances and what's appropriate for you.

chunks.title: How we can help
chunks.text: Work and Income case managers have been trained to identify and respond appropriately to people who are living in or leaving violent family situations. Talk to us about your situation. The more we understand what is happening for you, the better we can help you. Call us on 0800 559 009 to make an appointment and say "Appointment".

chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy August 2021
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidies August 2021 were a series of 8 payments. These were to help businesses pay employees and protect jobs affected by COVID-19 alert level changes. They were available from 20 August 2021 to 9 December 2021 and are now closed. The COVID-19 Wage Subsidies August 2021 were support for businesses to pay 2 weeks of wages (per application) for their employees. It was to continue support for businesses affected by changes to COVID-19 alert levels and lockdowns. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about these payments. Detailed information can be found in the declarations at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: These payments were available to employers, including self-employed people, whose employees could not work during the COVID-19 alert level changes. The alert level changes lasted from 17 August 2021 until 2 December 2021, when New Zealand moved to the COVID-19 Protection Framework. Employers and self-employed people could apply on behalf of their employees. To get a payment, a business must have: - had at least a 40% decline in revenue over a certain timeframe (this timeframe depended on the time of application, there’s more detail about this in the declarations below) - been registered with the New Zealand Companies Office (except for self-employed people) and operating in New Zealand - physically located and legally working in New Zealand (for self-employed people).

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: State Sector organisations were generally not eligible for COVID-19 payments, however some may have been granted an exception. This could be because they had an exception for a previous COVID-19 payment, or the organisation was a State-Owned Enterprise or Mixed Ownership Model company. The full eligibility criteria is listed in the declarations.

chunks.title: Payment amount
chunks.text: These payments were paid as a 2-week lump sum of: - $600 a week for each full-time employee (20 hours a week or more) - $359 a week for each part-time employee (less than 20 hours a week).

chunks.title: Declarations
chunks.text: The declarations contain the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for each of the Wage Subsidy August 2021 payments. Each Wage Subsidy had its own declaration. chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension was to help businesses pay staff impacted by COVID-19. It was available from 10 June 2020 to 1 September 2020. The Wage Subsidy Extension was support for businesses to pay 8 weeks of wages for their employees. It was to continue support for businesses affected by changes to COVID-19 alert levels and lockdowns. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declaration at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: This payment was available to employers, including self-employed people, whose employees could not work. The business must also have had a 40% decline in revenue: over the period of any month being applied for, when compared to the same month in 2019, andthat loss was attributable to the COVID-19 outbreak.State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the Wage Subsidy Extension, however some may have been granted an exception.

chunks.title: Payment rates
chunks.text: The subsidy was paid at a flat rate of: $585.80 for full-time employees (20 hours or more a week)$350.00 for part-time employees (less than 20 hours a week).If the employee's usual wages were less than the subsidy rate, any difference should have been used to pay wages of other affected staff. If there were no other affected staff, the remaining amount must be repaid.

chunks.title: Paying your staff
chunks.text: The business must have tried their hardest to pay the employee at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension for them. If that wasn't possible, the employee must have been paid at least the subsidy payment rate.

chunks.title: Declaration
chunks.text: The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension. Declaration for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy Extension

chunks.title: COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021
chunks.text: The Wage Subsidy March 2021 was to help businesses pay staff affected by COVID-19 alert level changes. It was available from 1pm on 4 March 2021 to 11:59pm on 21 March 2021. The information on this page is a summary of the key details about this payment. Detailed information can be found in the declaration at the bottom of this page.

chunks.title: Who could get it
chunks.text: This payment was available to employers or self-employed people. Their business must have had or expected to have had a 40% decline in revenue over 14 consecutive days between 28 February and 21 March, compared to a typical 14-day period between 4 January and 14 February 2021. Businesses with highly seasonal revenue could compare their decline in revenue to the same period in 2019. State Sector organisations were generally not eligible to get the Wage Subsidy, however some may have been granted an exception.

chunks.title: Payment rates
chunks.text: The COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021 was paid as a 2-week lump sum of either: - $585.80 a week for full-time employees (20 hours a week or more) - $350 a week for part-time employees (less than 20 hours a week).

chunks.title: Paying your staff
chunks.text: The business must have tried their hardest to pay their employees at least 80% of their usual wages while getting the wage subsidy for them. If that wasn't possible, at least the subsidy rate needed to be paid.

chunks.title: Declarations
chunks.text: The declaration contains the full eligibility criteria, obligations and repayment responsibilities for the COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021. Declaration for COVID-19 Wage Subsidy March 2021

chunks.title: Waiting for public housing
chunks.text: Once you apply for public housing, you'll need to wait until a suitable property becomes available. You'll also need to tell us if your situation changes while you're waiting.

chunks.title: How long you have to wait
chunks.text: The length of time you have to wait depends on: - how urgently you need a property - how quickly a suitable property becomes available - what your needs are - the number of other people waiting with urgent needs. People with the greatest needs are placed first, when suitable properties become available. A suitable property is one that meets your housing needs as agreed during your interview. While waiting for a property, it’s important to keep looking for other options, like rental properties in the private market. Find private housing

chunks.title: Tell us if something changes
chunks.text: While you're waiting to get into a public house, you must let us know straight away about any changes in your and your partner’s (if you have one) circumstances. This could be changes to your: - address and phone number - income or financial circumstances - family or household arrangements. If you don’t let us know, you might not be able to get a property that best meets your needs, or you may no longer qualify for public housing.

chunks.title: How to tell us
chunks.text: Call us on 0800 673 468

chunks.title: Confirm your circumstances
chunks.text: We may contact you and ask you to confirm your circumstances. This is so we can make sure your situation hasn't changed. We will either: - call you and ask you to confirm over the phone, or - text you and ask you to confirm in MyMSD. MyMSD is our online service where you can apply and manage your information online. About MyMSD If we contact you, it's important you confirm your circumstances. Otherwise we may think you no longer need public housing and cancel your application.

chunks.title: Warrants to Arrest payment error
chunks.text: We've found an error where some people's benefits were stopped or reduced too early when they had a Warrant to Arrest. This means we owe some people money.

chunks.title: Who's affected by this error
chunks.text: You may be affected if: - you had an arrest warrant before July 2016, and - your payments were stopped or reduced because of this.

chunks.title: If we owe you money
chunks.text: We're contacting and paying all our current clients. We aren't currently making payments to former clients affected by this error. We want to make sure these payments won't affect other payments people may be getting, eg Working for Families.

chunks.title: Review rights
chunks.text: If you don't understand or agree with a decision we've made, please talk with us so we can explain it. You have the right to ask us to review a decision you think is wrong. You can use the application form on our website, or write to us. We need to get your request within 3 months. If you have a good reason why you can't ask us to review a decision within 3 months, get in touch. We may still be able to review the decision. You can find out more on the review of a decision page of our website, or you can give us a call on 0800 559 009 Get a decision reviewed

chunks.title: What happens to your benefit while you train or study
chunks.text: Find out if your benefit will change while you're training or studying, and what other help you might be able to get. To keep getting your benefit while you train or study, you need to make sure you still meet your benefit obligations. - Obligations are things you need to do when you get a payment from us. - If you don't do them, your payments could reduce or stop. Select a benefit below to find out what kind of training or study you can do while getting that benefit.

chunks.title: Jobseeker Support
chunks.text: To get Jobseeker Support while you train or study, you need to meet your work obligations. Jobseeker Support has 3 types of work obligations: - full-time work obligations - part-time work obligations - work preparation obligations.

chunks.title: Full-time work obligations
chunks.text: This means you need to be available and looking for full-time work, which is at least 30 hours a week. If you're studying or training: - part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you're still available and looking for full-time work - full-time, you can't get Jobseeker Support, as you won't be available for full-time work. You may be able to get payments from StudyLink instead. Studylinkexternal If you're not sure if a course is part-time or full-time, check with your education provider.

chunks.title: Part-time work obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability, you will have part-time work obligations. This means you need to be available and looking for part-time work, which is at least 15 hours a week. If you're studying or training part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you're still available and looking for part-time work.

chunks.title: Work preparation obligations
chunks.text: If you have a health condition, injury or disability that means you can't work or can only work less than 15 hours a week, you will have work preparation obligations. This means you need to do a number of things to prepare and plan for work. If you're studying or training part-time, you can get Jobseeker Support if you can still meet this work obligation. You can read the full list of Jobseeker Support obligations to check all the obligations. Jobseeker Support obligations

chunks.title: Your youngest child is under 3
chunks.text: To get Sole Parent Support while you train or study: - you need to meet your work preparation obligations - your course must help you to find work in the future.

chunks.title: Your youngest child is 3 to 13
chunks.text: You can get Sole Parent Support if you're available, and looking, for part-time work of at least 20 hours a week. You may not have to do this if you're either: - already doing a course when your part-time work obligations started (e.g. when your Sole Parent Support started), or - studying at NZQA Level 4 or higher. You must pass at least half of your training or study. Sole Parent Support obligations You can read the full list of Sole Parent Support obligations to check all the obligations and make sure you're meeting those as well. Sole Parent Support obligations

chunks.title: Supported Living Payment
chunks.text: You can still get a Supported Living Payment while you train or study. This includes people getting Supported Living Payment as a carer. Your payment amounts won't change.

chunks.title: Young Parent and Youth Parent Payments
chunks.text: You can study full-time while getting these payments. Your payment amounts won't change. You may be able to get help from StudyLink as well. Contact your Youth Service provider so they can help you to work out which type of support is best for you.

chunks.title: If your benefit stops
chunks.text: If your benefit stops because your training or study means you can't meet your obligations, you might be able to get a different payment instead. Check if you can get help from StudyLink, including a Student loan or Student Allowance. Use their eligibility test to find out what you can get: Eligibility test (StudyLink)external

chunks.title: What you do on the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: What you do during the Limited Service Volunteer (LSV) course, where it's located, course dates, what you get, and paying for costs. At LSV, you do activities every day to learn new skills and improve yourself. You stay on a NZ Defence Force base in Auckland, Wellington or Christchurch. Your accommodation, food, clothing and travel are all free. If you need medical care, like seeing a dentist or physio, this is free as well. To get the most out of the course, you need to put in as much effort as you can, and push yourself to your limits. This will help you discover your strengths and how you can use these in future. You do this as part of a team. You are also supported by NZ Defence Force staff, a Work and Income staff member, and a social worker.

chunks.title: What you do on the Limited Service Volunteer course
chunks.text: Read more about LSV on this page, or if you're ready to apply, you can do this on the Applying for LSV page. Apply for the Limited Service Volunteer course

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: There's no other course like this that I'm aware of. You know, these guys come here, everyone's got an equal chance here to prove themselves and to learn. We always tell them, once you get used to the routine, you'll honestly love the course. And the last month will change your life. Move! Get your bags! Shoulders back. Heads up. That's the one. Be proud. Focus. One! I'm going to give you fifteen seconds. Move! The first day of LSV is really loud and aggressive. I think from a trainee's perspective, coming in, it can be quite overwhelming and quite scary. But knowing that there's a purpose behind everything we do, it sets up the rest of the six week. Get it in your mind that's going to be your clothing for the next six weeks.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: Make sure when you do this, your head is looking up, your shoulders are back, and you are proud to be here. We always say the first two weeks is the hardest, but if you're here at LSV you're pushed outside of your comfort zone. And when you're outside of your comfort zone you grow as a person, and it shows you what you're able to do as well. Get out any drugs, alcohol, knives, lighters, cell phones, MP3 players, aerosol cans, food, or jewellery, and this includes makeup, okay? This is the stuff we'll be taking from you for safe keeping. You'll get it back at the end. And you'll get it back when you need it. Before this course, I've been waking up at like, three or four PM. But I'm hoping to get, like, a routine from this. Just get up, get out and do things. And not just sit in my bed all day.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: Don't look at me. Look straight ahead. Stay in this position. I will be back with you. I want to change my life, and just make everyone proud. Especially my mum, because that's like the main person I'm trying to make myself proud to. Because she was a police officer. So I want to carry on the path that she took. I can handle discipline, most of the time. And I've done camps and stuff before but not anything this intense. I'm finding it a bit strict, but in a good way. Like, this is the kind of strictness I need right now. Corridor! The first thing about us is that we're military. And you have come to us to learn, okay? So we come across as strict, stern, and we enforce standards. The reason for that is because we get you here, and we want to give you back to society here. Okay? So, we need to hold you accountable for your actions and at all times hold you to the standard that we expect of ourselves. So just because we're holding you accountable, and we're holding you quite strictly to these standards that we give out, doesn't mean that we don't care, doesn't mean that we don't like you. Understand that?

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: Yes Staff. I feel like our 17 to 25 years olds, at that time of their life, their decisions that they make really impact them. So being here at a six-week residential live-in programme, it is tough. It is confronting. It is challenging. But that's the whole point of it, is to get people outside of their comfort zone so the real work can happen. One foot in front of the other. Five, four, three, two, one. It's not about your weaknesses. It's about your strengths. The longest day. The longest day. That massive, massive day. Beast of a day. We woke up at four o'clock. And then from there on, pretty much hell started. So the longest day is a real long day of team building activities. There's a lot of thinking involved. There's a lot of fitness. A lot of mental push, that we try to push them to create new limits in their lives. That way, the next time they find hardship in their lives, they understand that they can push through things that they never knew they could.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: It was quite difficult for me. I haven't done that much fitness ever. I just wanted to stop, walk away and just go home. But I just thought about the feeling of graduating. I'd feel pretty crap if I did all this and then just left. It was kind of just pushing through, and not giving up, for me. [Clapping game] I thought that I would give up at some point. But then I actually pushed myself and tried to remind myself, like, my purpose of why I'm here, why I'm doing this, who I'm doing this for. The challenges I had was really pushing my mental strength. No matter how many times my brain says "no, stop, stop, stop, stop" because I'm not going to stop. I'm going to push through it. I feel like I've actually achieved something. I feel like I can say to my dad "I did this, and this, and this". He's going to be incredibly proud.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: I've learned that my mind's a lot stronger than I realised. So instead of just dwelling in the negative, we're focusing on the positive. And that's the cool thing about here, is that they push forward the positive. So, I never give up. It was pretty intense but the good thing about it was just, like, all the support, encouragement. Everyone that's, like, been pushing everyone to, like, try their best. I got used to being a leader, stepping out of my comfort zone, trying to, like, push everyone to come together. If I can just do my best for this small portion of my life, I could probably change my whole life. It's probably the greatest second chance I've ever been given, coming to LSV. As a platoon, and for myself, we've grown to be pretty good 2.0 versions of ourselves. So, we've raised the bar quite a lot through these six weeks.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: I'm happy. I'm proud of myself and how far I came, because I'm leading my team. Getting the trainees through to the end of the six weeks is a big achievement on its own. Graduation day could be the most proudest day of their life. I thought this was like a six-week bootcamp but it's not like that at all. It's getting them ready for a job, making them employment ready. The job opportunities that the trainees have available to them post-course, they're a whole lot bigger than what they were prior. The skills and attributes that they've developed - things like work ethic, being on time, and being prepared to do any sort of task that they are given - they can actually show the employers that they are capable.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: That's what this course does. It not only gets you out of your shell a bit, it makes you accept you for who you are, and also others. And it gives you those skills so that you can go out, back into your everyday life and be independent. Each and every one of us has grown and developed skills that we wouldn't have known in the big wide world. So once again, I'd like to thank and congratulate you all for making it this far. You can take a man out of Three Platoon, but you cannot take Three Platoon out of the man. Thank you. Teamwork's probably the most essential part of this course, because you're working with people who have completely different backgrounds to you. You make good friends that you wouldn't have actually thought you would have. I was just happy with the way I sort of learned to work with people. And that's just something I can take into, sort of, any area of my life.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: I'm more out there now. I can stand up and take charge. I'm actually proud of myself. I'm the leader of the haka. I'm one of the kotiros. And I never seen myself as that. So, I feel really great and honoured to do that. It's a big change for me. The significance of the graduation parade is huge for the trainees. It's the culmination of all of the successes, all of the hardships, all of the experiences that they've had to bond together. And to see that transformation, that different person marching out in that crisply ironed uniform is basically their way of saying "Yep, this is me now. This is who I am. This is who I believe in. And who I'm proud to be." I'm really grateful that I decided to take this course. It was very challenging at first. But taking big challenges that I never thought I could achieve, it changed me a lot, actually.

chunks.title: What you do on the course
chunks.text: The LSV course is a live-in, 6-week course. The course is free, and if you're getting a benefit your payments will keep going while you're on the course. You: - stay in army barracks for 6 weeks - get 3 meals a day - get gear to wear while you're on the course - do fitness training and team work - learn life skills to help you look after yourself - talk with employers about how to get a job you like, and what they look for when they hire people. Fitness training is a regular activity, and it's designed for all fitness levels. It starts off easy and gradually builds up to be more challenging. Everyone is at a different fitness level but, as a team, you support and encourage each other through the activities.

chunks.title: An average day at LSV
chunks.text: I am most proud of completing every task that was thrown at me. Every mountain that had to be climbed, I climbed. The early wake-ups, the discipline, the mahi – everything about LSV has made me a proud individual. – Trainee Rimene-Macrae

chunks.title: What you get
chunks.text: At an LSV course, you get: - clothes, food and accommodation - any gear you need for the course - free transport to and from camp - free medical care, like dental care - practical and personal support to overcome challenges. You save money while you're at LSV because you don't need to pay for costs like food or power. If you're getting a benefit, your payments keep going while you're on the course. At the end of the course, you: - know how to take care of yourself - have new life skills, like managing your time and money - are fitter and healthier - know how to talk to employers and get a job - have more confidence and are proud of yourself.

chunks.title: Where you stay
chunks.text: There are 3 LSV camps: - Whenuapai Base, in Auckland - Trentham Base, in Wellington - Burnham Base, in Christchurch. Most of the time you go to the base closest to where you live.

chunks.title: Living on the base
chunks.text: You live on the base for 6 weeks and sleep in the barracks on the base. There could be up to 8 trainees in a room and the rooms are divided into men-only and women-only. You must stay at the base for the whole 6 weeks. NZ Defence Force are responsible for you and your safety while you're at the base, and there are strict rules about who can go in or out. This means you can't go home for things like family celebrations or during the weekend. You also can't have visitors during the course, except for your graduation at the end. If there's an emergency, you can leave the base. An emergency includes when a family or whānau member is very unwell or has a bad accident, or if there's a death. You might leave the course for a few days, or you can leave the course altogether. We'll keep in touch and continue to support you, and you may be able to do the course again later.

chunks.title: Living on the base
chunks.text: Just do it! The only person that can change you is yourself. You can’t rely on others to make that decision. What I can say is it will be the best decision you’ve ever made in your life. – Trainee Reynolds

chunks.title: Course dates
chunks.text: The LSV course runs on these dates in 2026.

chunks.title: Cell phones
chunks.text: You can bring a cell phone or mobile device with you, but you won't be able to use this all the time. This helps you focus on the course, so you can get the most out of it. If you bring your phone, it's collected and stored safely when you arrive at the base. You can only use it a few times during the 6 weeks. If there's an emergency, you are given the phone to contact home. You can write letters while you're on the course and post these from the camp. People can also write letters back to you. Before you start, you can give your family or friends the emergency contact details for the camp, so they can contact you in case of emergency.

chunks.title: Hair and jewellery
chunks.text: You can choose if you want to get your hair cut or not. Long hair needs to be tied up. You must remove face and body piercings during the course. You can still wear some other jewellery, like necklaces. Tidy hair and less jewellery protects your health and safety. Your commanding officer tells you what you can and can't wear.

chunks.title: Smoking
chunks.text: Your commanding officer tells you the times when you can smoke.

chunks.title: Leaving the course early
chunks.text: If you want to leave early, you can talk to the NZ Defence Force and the Work and Income staff at the base. They listen and support you, and organise support for you after you leave. If you get very sick or are injured, you may need to leave the course early. You discuss this with staff at the base. You may be able to start the course again later, after you've recovered.

chunks.title: Whiteware
chunks.text: We may be able to help you buy a new fridge, freezer, combined fridge-freezer or washing machine if you’re on a low income or a benefit. We may also be able to help you pay for repairs to your current appliance. - You don't have to be on a benefit to qualify for this help. - You don't have to get a quote. - You'll have to pay the money back. - You should only buy an approved whiteware appliance with this assistance. If you need help with other essential items, please talk with us.

chunks.title: Who can get it
chunks.text: You may get help if you: - are 16 or over (if you're 16-19 and have a Youth Service provider, contact Youth Services) - are a New Zealand citizen or permanent resident - normally live in New Zealand and intend to stay here - have an immediate or essential need. Youth Servicesexternal It also depends on: - how much you and your partner earn - any money or assets you and your partner have. Your income will be assessed either weekly or yearly, depending on the kind of help you qualify for. These income and asset limits usually apply:

chunks.title: Asset limits
chunks.text: These don't include the things you need for day-to-day living, e.g. your home, car, and some payments after a severe weather event. They do include things like money in the bank, or a second property.

chunks.title: What you can get
chunks.text: You can apply for an advance or recoverable assistance payment to buy a: - fridge - freezer - combined fridge-freezer - washing machine. Advance Payment of Benefit Recoverable Assistance Payment If your application is approved, you'll be able to buy your appliance from one of the suppliers we have an arrangement with. They will: - provide a minimum 2-year warranty - deliver and install the appliance - remove your old appliance (if it's clean and empty). The appliance will also be covered under the Consumer Guarantees Act. Consumer Guarantees Actexternal You only need to pay back the money you spend. Any money left on your payment card will automatically return to us, and you won't have to pay it back.

chunks.title: Where you can get it from
chunks.text: We have an arrangement with 4 suppliers for whiteware for you to choose from. They have a range of appliances, models and brands available at MSD prices. These suppliers are: - Big Save - Noel Leeming - Trade Depot - Fisher & Paykel and Haier (through 100% Home, Appliance Plus, Harvey Norman and Heathcotes - these retailers offer only Fisher & Paykel/Haier whiteware through this arrangement). You can go to any of these stores to buy the appliance you've been approved for. Once you're in store, tell the staff you're paying with a Work and Income payment card. They will show you the approved range of appliances and tell you the MSD prices. If an appliance in the approved range is on sale, the sale price is also available to you. The sale price won’t include the cost of delivery, installation, and removal of packaging and the old appliance, so that would be added.

chunks.title: Where you can get it from
chunks.text: You should pay the lowest overall price, whether it’s the MSD price or a sale one (plus delivery, installation, and removal charges). Click on the links below to see the appliances and price ranges for MSD clients: - Big Saveexternal - Fisher & Paykel/Haierexternal - Noel Leemingexternal - Trade Depotexternal The specific MSD prices for individual appliances aren't available online.

chunks.title: Step 1: Call us
chunks.text: You need to call us. Phone us We'll talk with you to understand your situation and how we can help. We'll let you know what information you need to provide and how to get this to us. You do not need to provide quotes.

chunks.title: Step 2: Get a payment card
chunks.text: If your application is approved, we'll load the money onto a payment card for you. If you don't already have one of these, you'll need to visit a service centre to get one, and set a pin on it before you use it. Find a service centre Set a PIN Find out more about payment cards

chunks.title: Step 3: Choose where you'll buy your appliance from
chunks.text: We have an arrangement with 4 suppliers for whiteware for you to choose from. They have a range of different appliances, models and brands available at MSD prices. These suppliers are: - Big Save - Noel Leeming - Trade Depot - Fisher & Paykel and Haier (through 100% Home, Appliance Plus, Harvey Norman and Heathcotes - these retailers offer only Fisher & Paykel/Haier whiteware through this arrangement). You can go to any of these stores to buy the appliance you've been approved for. Tell the staff you're paying with a Work and Income payment card. They will show you the approved range of appliances and tell you the MSD prices. Click on the links below to see the appliances and price ranges for MSD clients:

chunks.title: Step 3: Choose where you'll buy your appliance from
chunks.text: - Big Saveexternal - Fisher & Paykel/Haierexternal - Noel Leemingexternal - Trade Depotexternal The specific MSD prices for individual appliances aren't available online. You can't top up the money available on your payment card with your own funds.

chunks.title: Step 4: Buy the appliance
chunks.text: You'll need to buy your appliance at the store using your payment card. Let the staff know you're an MSD client and are here for an appliance with an MSD price. You can't use your payment card online. If you can't get to a store, tell us when you call to apply. You should only buy the appliance you have approval for. For example, if you get assistance to buy an approved fridge, you can’t buy other items such as an air fryer or a microwave. If you need help with other essential items, please talk with us. If you have been approved to buy multiple items on your payment card, for example a fridge-freezer and bedding, you need to pay for these in separate transactions – even if it’s from the same store.

chunks.title: Step 4: Buy the appliance
chunks.text: If you're not sure how to use your payment card, you can find out how to do this here: Using a payment card Our whiteware retailers tell us about payment card transactions, including the payment card number used. We use this information to make sure clients are using the assistance for the purpose we've discussed with them.

chunks.title: Step 5: Arrange delivery
chunks.text: The store will work with you to arrange for the appliance to be delivered to your home and installed. They will also remove the packaging and take away your old appliance (if it's clean and empty). These services are included in the MSD price. You can't take the appliance away after you buy it. It has to be delivered and installed by the store. If you need to make any changes to your order, get in touch with the store. If there is a refund, the money will be returned to us, not your payment card.

chunks.title: If there's a problem with the appliance
chunks.text: Appliances come with a minimum 2-year warranty. Quotes aren't needed for whiteware repairs.

chunks.title: Appliances purchased on or after 3 September 2025
chunks.text: If you need help with your appliance, contact the store you bought it from. They will talk to you about what needs to be done, and if needed arrange for a service technician to come look at it. If the fault with your appliance isn't covered by the warranty, we may be able to help you pay for servicing and repairs. Call us to apply. Phone us

chunks.title: Appliances purchased before 3 September 2025
chunks.text: If you need help with your appliance purchased from Fisher & Paykel before 3 September 2025, call Fisher & Paykel on 0800 673 424. Discuss the fault and, if needed, arrange a repair service. If the fault with your appliance isn't covered by the warranty, we may be able to help you pay for servicing and repairs. Call us to apply. chunks.title: Who can get NZ Super
chunks.text: If you want to apply for New Zealand Superannuation (NZ Super), you need to meet certain criteria. Use our step-by-step guide to find out if you may meet the criteria for NZ Super. Find out if you can get NZ Super or Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: You may qualify for NZ Super if you: - are 65 or older - either: are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen are an NZ permanent resident, or hold an NZ residence class visa - are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen - are an NZ permanent resident, or - hold an NZ residence class visa - are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, and - have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time. Definition of 'ordinarily resident' Ordinarily resident in SSA country when you apply

chunks.title: If you're working
chunks.text: You can still get NZ Super while you're working. However if you have to change your tax code, your NZ Super payments may be less after tax. If you get any other payments from us, like Accommodation Supplement or Disability Allowance, any income you earn will affect them.

chunks.title: Overseas pensions
chunks.text: If you or your partner qualify for an overseas pension, you must apply for it. This could affect your NZ Super payments. Overseas pensions

chunks.title: You must have lived in NZ
chunks.text: You must have lived in New Zealand for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. The total number of years you need is based on your date of birth. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive. Work out how many years you must have lived in NZ Haven't lived in NZ for required years

chunks.title: What we mean by 'have lived in NZ'
chunks.text: When we say 'have lived in NZ', we mean you were 'resident' and 'physically present' in NZ at the same time. If you left NZ to travel overseas, this period may not be counted as having lived in NZ. Read the definition to find out more. Definition of 'have lived in NZ'

chunks.title: You're a refugee or protected person
chunks.text: If you're recognised as a refugee or protected person, the number of years may be worked out differently. It depends on the age you started living in NZ. Refugees and protected persons

chunks.title: Work out how many years you need
chunks.text: Use the table below to work out how many years you must have lived in NZ.

chunks.title: Example - born in 1961
chunks.text: Your date of birth is 28 March 1961. You must have lived in NZ for at least 11 years from age 20. The 11 years must include 5 years from age 50. The 11 years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive.

chunks.title: Haven't lived in NZ for required years
chunks.text: If you haven't lived in NZ the whole time, you may be able to use another country to meet this criteria if: - it is a country that has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with NZ, or - it is a NZ realm country (the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau). SSA countries are: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, Malta, the Netherlands, South Korea and United Kingdom. Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Wait until you meet the residence criteria
chunks.text: If you don't meet the residence criteria when you're 65, you can wait until either: - you've lived in NZ for the required number of years, or - you can use another country to meet this criteria. Then you can apply for NZ Super (as long as you meet all the other criteria).

chunks.title: Who can get emergency housing
chunks.text: If you need emergency housing, you must meet certain criteria.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: You may qualify for emergency housing if you: - have nowhere to stay tonight or in the next 7 nights, and - agree to meet your responsibilities from the 8th night (if you're in emergency housing for more than 7 nights). You must also meet the residency criteria. This means you need to be either: - getting a main benefit, NZ Super or Veteran's Pension, or - ordinarily resident in New Zealand and either: a New Zealand citizen have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: - a New Zealand citizen - have a residence class visa under the Immigration Act 2009 - recognised as a refugee or protected person under the Immigration Act 2009, or - getting a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your New Zealand partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. Main benefit Ordinarily resident It also depends on your income and any assets you have. We may also look at whether you've caused or contributed to your need for emergency housing. For example: - you moved out of your accommodation without a good reason and didn't have another place to move into, or - you had to move out of your accommodation because you: damaged the property, or didn't follow the supplier's rules of stay.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: - damaged the property, or - didn't follow the supplier's rules of stay.

chunks.title: If you're getting a main benefit
chunks.text: We'll look at the status of your benefit. You can't get emergency housing if it's been suspended, reduced for a certain reason, or cancelled for 13 weeks.

chunks.title: Income
chunks.text: Generally you need to have income under these limits. However, if your income is over these limits, you may still qualify. Contact us to talk about your situation. Phone us

chunks.title: Cash assets
chunks.text: Generally you need to have cash assets under these limits. However, if they're over these limits, you may still qualify. Contact us to talk about your situation. Phone us

chunks.title: Who can get Veteran's Pension
chunks.text: If you want to apply for Veteran's Pension, you need to meet certain criteria. Use our step-by-step guide to find out if you may meet the criteria for Veteran's Pension. Find out if you can get Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: You may qualify for Veteran's Pension if you: - have served in the New Zealand Armed Forces on Qualifying Operational Service - are 65 or older - either: are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen are an NZ permanent resident, or hold an NZ residence class visa - are a New Zealand (NZ) citizen - are an NZ permanent resident, or - hold an NZ residence class visa - are ordinarily resident in New Zealand, the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau when you apply, and - have lived in New Zealand for a certain amount of time. If you are ordinarily resident in a country NZ has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with when you apply for Veteran's Pension, you may still qualify. There may be additional criteria you need to meet, it depends on your situation.

chunks.title: Criteria you need to meet
chunks.text: If you get other income, it may affect your Veteran's Pension payments. Definition of 'ordinarily resident Ordinarily resident in SSA country when you apply If you get other income

chunks.title: You must have lived in NZ
chunks.text: You must have lived in New Zealand for a certain number of years from age 20. This must include 5 years from age 50. The total number of years you need is based on your date of birth. These years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive. Work out how many years you must have lived in NZ Haven't lived in NZ for required years

chunks.title: What we mean by 'have lived in NZ'
chunks.text: When we say 'have lived in NZ', we mean you were 'resident' and 'physically present' in NZ at the same time. If you left NZ to travel overseas, this period may not be counted as having lived in NZ. Read the definition to find out more. Definition of 'have lived in NZ'

chunks.title: You're a refugee or protected person
chunks.text: If you're recognised as a refugee or protected person, the number of years may be worked out differently. It depends on the age you started living in NZ. Refugees and protected persons

chunks.title: Work out how many years you need
chunks.text: Use the table below to work out how many years you must have lived in NZ.

chunks.title: Example - born in 1961
chunks.text: Your date of birth is 28 March 1961. You must have lived in NZ for at least 11 years from age 20. The 11 years must include 5 years from age 50. The 11 years (including the 5 years from age 50) do not need to be consecutive.

chunks.title: Haven't lived in NZ for required years
chunks.text: If you haven't lived in NZ the whole time, you may be able to use another country to meet this criteria if: - it is a country that has a Social Security Agreement (SSA) with NZ, or - it is a NZ realm country (the Cook Islands, Niue or Tokelau). SSA countries are: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Greece, Ireland, Jersey, Guernsey, Malta, the Netherlands, South Korea and United Kingdom. Using SSA countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super Using NZ Realm countries to meet residence criteria for NZ Super

chunks.title: Wait until you meet the residence criteria
chunks.text: If you don't meet the residence criteria when you're 65, you can wait until either: - you've lived in NZ for the required number of years, or - you can use another country to meet this criteria. Then you can apply for NZ Super (as long as you meet all the other criteria).

chunks.title: If you get other income
chunks.text: If you get other income, it may affect your Veteran's Pension payments. Getting other income may also mean the tax code you use could change. This means you could get less for your Veteran's Pension payments, it depends what tax code you're on. If you get an overseas pension, you can still get Veteran's Pension. However this could affect your Veteran's Pension payment. Overseas pension How much you can get for Veteran's Pension

chunks.title: Who can get public housing
chunks.text: If you want to apply to live in public (social) housing, you need to meet certain criteria.

chunks.title: Age
chunks.text: You must be 16 or older.

chunks.title: Residency
chunks.text: If you're getting a main benefit from us (e.g. Jobseeker Support), you meet the residency criteria. If you don't get a main benefit from us, you need to meet one of these residency criteria: - you're a New Zealand citizen - you have a resident visa or permanent resident visa and have lived in NZ continuously for at least 2 years since getting it - you're recognised as a refugee by Immigration New Zealand - you're recognised as a protected person by Immigration New Zealand, or - you either: have a Christchurch Response Visa, or get a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your NZ partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence. - have a Christchurch Response Visa, or

chunks.title: Residency
chunks.text: - get a Special Needs Grant because you came to New Zealand on a temporary visa to be with your NZ partner and your relationship ended due to domestic violence.

chunks.title: Serious housing need
chunks.text: You must have a serious housing need. This means we'll look at things like: - your current housing situation, including: the property's physical condition if the property has basic living facilities over-crowding how secure your tenancy is - the property's physical condition - if the property has basic living facilities - over-crowding - how secure your tenancy is - whether your current property or area is safe for you and suitable for your medical or physical needs - whether you could afford to rent privately - how difficult it is to find a private rental that meets your needs - whether you could manage long term in a private rental.

chunks.title: Income and assets
chunks.text: Generally you need to have: - income under: $807.63 a week (after tax) if you're single with no children $1,242.51 a week (after tax) if you have a partner or children - $807.63 a week (after tax) if you're single with no children - $1,242.51 a week (after tax) if you have a partner or children - cash assets worth less than $42,700. If you have income or assets worth more than this, you may still qualify for public housing. It depends on your situation.

chunks.title: Lump sum payment from a will or estate
chunks.text: Lump-sum payments from wills don't need to be declared as income. But if you get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit you do need to tell us about it.

chunks.title: What is this?
chunks.text: This is a one-off payment when someone dies and leaves you money or you get some money when their property is sold.

chunks.title: How it affects your benefit and allowances
chunks.text: You have to tell us about this payment if you: - get Accommodation Supplement, Temporary Additional Support or Special Benefit - invest the money you get and earn interest, this will be counted as income - get this money as regular payments.
